Noting as a UI-polish candidate for Step 12/the IA-redesign steps, not a Step 5b fix.
8. **No progress bar for speaker diarization — confirmed real, and harder to fix than the other progress gaps in this file.** Checked both diarization call sites (`tabs/workspace_tab.py` line 527 and line 1997): each wraps `diarize.diarize(...)` only in `st.spinner(...)`, no `progress_cb`. Checked why, at the source: `diarize.diarize` (`diarize.py` lines 63–81) makes **one single call** to pyannote's own `pipeline(audio_path, num_speakers=...)` and only gets a result back at the end — unlike Whisper's segment-by-segment processing (which is what makes `core.transcribe_for_timing`'s real progress bar possible), pyannote's pipeline doesn't expose an incremental callback in its public API. This isn't a wiring gap like the other progress-bar-missing spots elsewhere in this file — it's a real API limitation. Best available fix: keep the indeterminate spinner, but add an estimated-duration caption (diarization runtime scales roughly linearly with audio length; a rough "usually N–M seconds for an audio this long" estimate is honest without claiming false precision) rather than a fake animated progress bar.
9. **Whisper default: `large-v3-turbo` vs. `large-v3`, plus confirming GPU memory is actually freed.** User has a confirmed RTX 3080 Ti (12GB VRAM) and asked to weigh the two as the default, given they now have headroom for either. Turbo is a pruned-decoder variant of `large-v3` (far fewer decoder layers) — real, verified tradeoff: meaningfully faster and lighter on VRAM, at some accuracy cost, and Step 6 (merged) already recorded the one language-specific finding checked so far: "reported weaker on Japanese and Korean." **Not independently re-verified this pass for Chinese specifically** (this project's own primary content language) — flagging honestly rather than asserting a number I haven't checked. Since the user's 12GB VRAM comfortably fits `large-v3` (it doesn't need turbo's memory savings to run), and the one verified accuracy finding cuts against turbo for two of the three source languages this app targets, **recommend keeping `large-v3` as the default for all three languages (zh/ja/ko)**, with `large-v3-turbo` staying an opt-in "fast mode" choice (as Step 6 already added it) for whoever wants the speed and can tolerate the accuracy tradeoff — not flipping the default without a verified zh number. **GPU-memory-freeing: confirmed, already covers Whisper.** Read `core.release_gpu_models()` directly (`core.py` lines 168–191): it clears `_whisper_model_cache` (Whisper's own cache, model-size-agnostic — applies identically whether the size is `large-v3` or `large-v3-turbo`), the ASR-backend and forced-aligner caches, runs `gc.collect()`, then `torch.cuda.empty_cache()`. It's called after every GPU stage: post-transcription/alignment (line ~1991), post-diarization (line ~2012), post-re-transcription (line ~493), and post-re-run-diarization (line ~534). VRAM is genuinely handed back after each stage today, for either model size — no action needed there.

**Exit:**
- A test shows a translation job actually uses the Ollama URL configured in Settings, not a hardcoded default.
- A test shows opening a merge preview and then navigating away without confirming leaves the drama's stored lines unchanged.
- A test shows using a re-transcribe result clears that line's result box, and starting a new re-transcribe on a different line doesn't show the previous line's stale text.
- A test shows `js_runtimes` is passed to yt-dlp as a dict, not a list, in both `video_download.py` and `live_translate.py`.
- Manual check: with a real, confirmed-live stream, Live capture starts without the `js_runtimes` ValueError.
- Manual check (item 5): re-run speaker detection with 2+ speakers, add a temporary debug line before the color-picker gate, and report back what `speakers`/`ln.speaker` actually hold at that point — this determines whether the fix is in `assign_speaker_to_line`'s overlap matching or somewhere still unfound.
- A test shows the raw-novel toggle doesn't render at all when `content_mode` is `streamer_vod` or `novel_narration`, and for `audio_drama` renders off by default with the uploader only appearing once switched on.
- Manual check: an estimated-duration caption shows next to the diarization spinner, roughly matching real elapsed time on a real run.

### Step 5c — A global GPU-job guard, prompted by a shared Gemini architecture review
User shared a Gemini-authored review flagging VRAM/hardware saturation as a risk: "Running F5-TTS, OCR model inference, speech recognition..., and PyAnnote concurrently will quickly overwhelm consumer GPUs (8–12 GB VRAM)." Checked what actually guards against this today before deciding whether it's a real gap — it's real, and narrower than it first looks. Step 5 (merged) already clears model caches and calls `torch.cuda.empty_cache()` after each GPU stage *within* one drama's own sequential pipeline (transcribe → diarize → translate → dub never overlap for the same drama). Step 1b's line-writing guard and Step 9b item 3's bulk-translate queuing prevent job *collisions on the same drama's data*, not GPU *resource* contention. Read `background_jobs.start_job` directly: its only dedup is **by `job_id`** — two different job IDs (e.g. a Scanlate OCR job on one drama and a Workspace transcription job on a completely different drama, started from two different tabs) run as fully independent threads with **zero coordination**, and nothing stops both from holding GPU memory at once. This is exactly the scenario Gemini's review describes, and it's real: nothing today prevents it.

This is **not** R3-full (the deferred "single-slot model manager," §3) — that's a bigger, more general architecture (tracking which specific model occupies the GPU, unloading/reloading on demand) explicitly deferred until real OOM crashes are observed. This is smaller and more specific: a **global lock on GPU-touching job *starts***, not a model manager. It doesn't manage what's loaded — it just refuses to let a second GPU-heavy job begin while one is already running, queuing it instead.

1. Add a `gpu_touching: bool` flag when a job is registered (transcription, diarization, OCR, TTS/dub, ML-based Scanlate detection/inpainting, **and Ollama translation** — resolved definitively on a later pass: Ollama translation runs the local `qwen3:8b` model (Step 5's own default), so it's GPU-bound the same as every other local-model stage, no hedge needed. Only cloud-API translation (Claude/Gemini/DeepSeek) is excluded, since those never touch the local GPU at all).
2. Before starting a new GPU-touching job, check whether any other GPU-touching job (any `job_id`, any drama) is currently `running`. If so, don't start it — queue it (reusing the same queue/backoff shape Step 9b's bulk-translate already introduces) and show a clear "Waiting — GPU busy with <job description>" message instead of starting a job that would silently compete for VRAM.
3. This is a **soft** guard, not a hard block: a user on a genuinely high-VRAM machine (24GB+) may never need it and shouldn't be forced to wait unnecessarily — add a Settings toggle ("Limit to one GPU job at a time") defaulting **on** (matches the 8–12GB consumer-GPU assumption Gemini's review and this project's own hardware-budget decisions elsewhere, e.g. Step 5's VRAM-class reasoning, are built around), switchable off by anyone who knows their hardware can handle concurrent jobs.

**Exit:**
- A test shows starting a second GPU-touching job while one is already running (different job IDs, different dramas) queues it rather than starting it immediately, and starting a non-GPU-touching job (e.g. a cloud-engine translation) alongside a running GPU job is unaffected.
- A test shows the queued job starts automatically once the running one finishes.
- A test shows the Settings toggle, when off, allows two GPU-touching jobs to run concurrently as today.
- Manual check: with the toggle on, start a transcription job on one drama and an OCR job on another at roughly the same time, and confirm the second one shows "waiting" rather than starting immediately.

### Step 6 — Transcription quality
1. **Whisper settings** (`core.transcribe_for_timing`).
   - Default to `condition_on_previous_text=False`, and add `no_repeat_ngram_size=3` and a mild `repetition_penalty` (about 1.1). This prevents repeated-phrase loops at the source.
   - Keep `filter_hallucinated_segments` as a backstop.
   - Add `large-v3-turbo` as a model choice. It's much faster, but reported weaker on Japanese and Korean, so label it that way and keep `large-v3`/`medium` as the default for ja/ko.
   - Add an opt-in "fast mode" using faster-whisper's `BatchedInferencePipeline`, which is roughly 4× faster.
2. **Qwen3-ForcedAligner reliability** (`forced_align`).
   - The known issues are zero-duration word spans (Qwen3-ASR #197) and timing that drifts out of sync after about 30 s on longer inputs.
   - Lower the chunk target in `_bucket_into_chunks` from about 280 s to about 60 s.
   - Detect zero-duration or non-increasing timings. For those lines, fall back to the diff alignment (`core.align_transcript_to_timing`) and flag them for review.
3. **Vocal separation** (`audio_preprocess`).
   - Demucs's original repo is archived and no longer maintained.
   - Add an optional `audio-separator` backend using a Mel-Band RoFormer vocal model, which gives cleaner vocals on content with background music.
   - Keep Demucs as the fallback.
4. **Optional audio-derived emotion/event tagging alongside Whisper** — [`FunAudioLLM/SenseVoice`](https://github.com/FunAudioLLM/SenseVoice), checked directly: real, actively maintained (9.4k stars), code MIT-licensed (model weights under the separate FunASR Model Open Source License — note this in Settings next to the option, same pattern as other model-license caveats already in this doc). `SenseVoiceSmall` natively outputs 7-category emotion tags (happy/sad/angry/neutral/fearful/disgusted/surprised) and 8 audio-event tags (BGM/speech/applause/laughter/cry/sneeze/breath/cough) as part of transcription, covering exactly Baihe's actual content languages (Mandarin, Cantonese, English, Japanese, Korean) — not a broader multilingual claim than that, so **not** a Whisper replacement. This is a second, audio-derived emotion signal distinct from `emotion.py`'s existing text-based detection (already wired to Chatterbox TTS delivery in Step 11b) — add as an optional pass alongside Whisper transcription, surfaced next to the existing text-based emotion tag rather than merged with it, since the two can disagree and the user should see both rather than one silently overriding the other.
5. **A cloud ASR option, added after a Gemini-authored review the user shared raised offloading inference to conserve local VRAM.** Confirmed real: today every transcription backend (Whisper via `faster-whisper`, Qwen3-ASR, SenseVoice) runs locally — there's no cloud alternative the way translation already has one (Claude/Gemini/DeepSeek) and TTS already has one (`elevenlabs`, already in `requirements.txt`, hosted, no GPU needed). For someone on a lower-VRAM or GPU-less machine — this project's own manual-check notes have already flagged "no GPU to verify" more than once — offloading the single heaviest local stage (ASR) is a real, not hypothetical, need. Checked pricing directly rather than assuming: [Groq's hosted Whisper Large-v3-Turbo API](https://groq.com) — $0.04/hour of audio (≈$0.0007/minute), no GPU needed, and it's the *same model family* Baihe already defaults to locally, so output shape/behavior stays consistent with what the rest of the pipeline already expects — dramatically cheaper than OpenAI's own Whisper API ($0.006/minute, ~9× more) checked as a comparison point. Add as an opt-in cloud engine choice alongside the existing local backends, same settings/API-key pattern as the cloud translation engines, not a default — this app's local-first design stays the default, cloud ASR is for whoever needs to conserve VRAM specifically.

**Exit:** mocked tests cover the new Whisper kwargs, the smaller chunk size, the zero-duration fallback and separator backend selection, and a test shows SenseVoice's emotion/event tags are surfaced alongside (not merged into) the existing text-based emotion detection. A test shows the cloud ASR option is selectable and its result reaches the same downstream pipeline (alignment, diarization hand-off) as a local Whisper result, using a mocked API response.

### Step 6b — Export formats (VTT and ASS) *(un-deferred by request — was R6)*
SRT already works everywhere, so this is additive, not a fix.
1. **VTT writer** next to `core.lines_to_srt`/`lines_to_bilingual_srt` — same structure, WebVTT's header and timestamp format.
2. **ASS writer** with real style controls — this is the format that makes styled/"clip streamer"-look subtitles possible; VTT and SRT can't carry per-line font/colour/position. Expose, with sensible defaults so nobody has to touch them:
   - font family (a short list of fonts that are commonly preinstalled, plus a free-text field for any font installed on the machine doing the export/burn — note in the UI that an uncommon font must be installed locally or it silently falls back);
   - size, bold and italic on/off, primary (fill) colour, outline colour and outline width, and a basic text-alignment choice (bottom/top, left/centre/right) *(these last two — italic and alignment — confirmed against VideoTranscriber's actual `app.py`, whose ASS style dict already exposes exactly these fields as plain Streamlit widgets, so they're cheap to add now rather than defer)*;
   - one colour per known character (from `characters`/`series_characters`), reusing Step 1e's character list, so each speaker is visually distinct without the user setting each one by hand;
   - a couple of starting **presets** the user can tune from, not a fixed look — e.g. "Clean" (today's plain default) and "Streamer clip" (bold, larger size, thick high-contrast outline — the common shape of Japanese clip-channel subtitles: legible over busy video/gameplay, not an exact copy of any one channel's style). Position/margin stay at sensible defaults, not exposed yet.
3. **Long-cue handling**, shared by all three writers: split a cue over a configurable character-per-line limit (default per source language, e.g. tighter for CJK) at a sentence or clause boundary where one exists, otherwise at the nearest space; never mid-word.
   - Add a defensive overlap clamp right before writing any of the three formats: if line N's end is after line N+1's start (possible after a manual edit or merge, even though `core._lines_from_char_times` already guarantees non-overlap at alignment time), trim N's end back to N+1's start and flag the line for review rather than exporting an invalid cue.
4. **Subtitle reading-speed (CPS) warning** *(idea from Whishper's editor and ZastTranslate's per-script CPS table; genuinely missing — confirmed against the code, since the app's existing `chars_per_second` check in `core.diagnose_line_coverage` only flags mis-segmented ASR on the source side, never whether the translated text is readable in the time it's shown)*.
   - Starting CPS ceiling, read directly out of ZastTranslate's `fitted_cps_config.py` (the one file of theirs that actually resolved when fetched — the rest of that project's claims are unverified, see §6): CJK ≈ 6.0–7.0, Arabic/Hebrew/Hindi/Thai and similar scripts ≈ 7.0, most Latin-script languages ≈ 8.0–9.0, default fallback 7.5. A starting table, not a precision model — adjustable later.
   - Flag any line whose **translated** text exceeds its script's ceiling for its own duration, using the existing flag mechanism so it shows up in the review queue like any other flagged line.
   - Surface the same check next to the style controls in this step's export panel, so a line that's fine to read in the app but too dense as a subtitle gets caught before export, not after.
5. Add format choice (SRT/VTT/ASS) and the style controls above next to the existing export button, defaulting to SRT + "Clean" so nothing changes for anyone who doesn't touch the new controls.
   - **GUI gap:** with this many style knobs (font, size, bold/italic, two colours, outline width, alignment, presets), nobody should have to export-and-check repeatedly to see what they picked. Add a small live preview — render one sample line (a real line from the drama, not placeholder text) with the current style settings as an image or styled HTML block, updating as controls change, so the look is visible before committing to a full export.
6. **Fix: expose hardsub (burned-in) styling, which already exists in the backend but is invisible in the UI.** `video_export.burn_subtitles` already accepts `font_size`/`font_color`/`outline_color`, but section 10's "Export full subtitled episode" calls it with no arguments (`workspace_tab.py` ~line 2819), so every hardsub export silently uses the same fixed look regardless of what's picked elsewhere. Two changes:
   - wire the same style controls from item 2 into that call;
   - when the chosen format is ASS, burn the `.ass` file directly (`ffmpeg -vf "subtitles=file.ass"`, no `force_style` needed — libass reads the per-speaker styles straight from the file) instead of building one flat `force_style` string, so hardsub gets per-speaker colours too, not just softsub.
7. **Shadow distance and other ASS text effects — confirmed missing, added on a later feature-brainstorm pass.** `_subtitle_style_controls` (item 2 above) exposes font/size/bold/italic/colours/outline-width/alignment, but `subtitle_formats._style_line` hardcodes ASS's `Shadow` field to `"1"` — it never reads a shadow value out of the style dict at all, so there's no way to change or disable the drop-shadow distance from the UI. Add a `shadow` slider (0–5, matching ASS's own integer-pixel-offset convention) to the style controls and thread it through `_style_line` instead of the hardcoded literal.
8. **Translator notes as a separate, smaller-styled line — added on the same brainstorm pass, ASS-only.** Today `core._notes_suffix` appends a note as a bracketed suffix on the *same* cue, same font/size as the dialogue (`"...[Qijutang: lit. 'Hall of...']"`) — for SRT/VTT this is the only option (a cue is one plain text block), but ASS can carry two styled lines in one cue (a second `Dialogue:` line with a different `Style` reference, same start/end time). Add an opt-in "Show notes as a separate line" toggle next to the style controls: when on and the format is ASS, render the note as its own smaller-sized line above the dialogue line (reusing the same style dict at a reduced size, e.g. 70% of the main size) instead of appending it inline; off (default) keeps today's inline-suffix behavior everywhere, and SRT/VTT always use the inline suffix regardless of the toggle, since they have no way to represent it.
9. **Add a standalone subtitle-file download to "Export full subtitled episode" (section 10), at the user's direct request** — today that section only produces the burned video, with a caption pointing back up to section 9 for the separate `.ass`/`.srt`/`.vtt` downloads; there's no way to get the sidecar subtitle file for the *whole episode* from the export-the-video section itself. Confirmed this is a small, low-risk addition, not new plumbing: section 10 already calls the exact same `_subtitle_text(field)` closure section 9's own download buttons use (same function, same `_sub_style`/`speaker_colors`/`_export_lines`, all already in scope in section 10's own code), and already has `_base_name` available for a matching filename. Add a `st.download_button` next to the existing video-download button, reusing `_subtitle_text(_field_for[sub_language])`'s output with a filename following section 9's existing `{_base_name}_{language}.{ext}` convention (e.g. `{_base_name}_subtitled_{language}.{ext}`, mirroring section 10's own existing `{_base_name}_subtitled{ext}` pattern for the video file) — so the exported video and its matching subtitle file are named as an obviously-paired set.

**Exit:**
- A VTT and an ASS export of the same drama both load and play correctly in mpv and VLC, with ASS showing distinct per-speaker colours and the chosen font/size/outline.
- A test shows a long line is split at a sensible boundary, not mid-word.
- SRT export is byte-identical to before this step.
- A hardsub export using the "Streamer clip" preset visibly differs from one using "Clean" (checked by hand — burning video isn't something a unit test can judge).
- A test shows burning an ASS file skips `force_style` entirely.
- A test shows a manually-created overlap gets clamped and flagged, not exported as-is.
- A test shows a translated line that's too dense to read in its duration gets flagged, and a normal-length line doesn't.
- Manual check: changing a style control (font, colour, preset) visibly updates the live preview without exporting.
- A test shows the ASS writer's `Shadow` field reflects the chosen shadow value instead of the hardcoded `"1"`.
- A test shows enabling "Show notes as a separate line" on an ASS export produces two `Dialogue:` lines per noted cue (smaller-styled note line above the main line) with matching start/end times, and that SRT/VTT exports are unaffected by the toggle either way.
- Manual check: export a full subtitled episode and confirm a matching standalone subtitle file downloads alongside the video, with the same content section 9's own downloads for that drama would produce.

### Step 6c — Meaning-based subtitle re-segmentation *(idea from VideoLingo)*
A different, upstream problem from Step 6b's export-time character wrapping. Today's line boundaries come entirely from Whisper's VAD (silence gaps) — a line can end mid-sentence just because the speaker paused, or run two separate thoughts together because they didn't. Confirmed VideoLingo's actual mechanism by reading `core/_3_1_split_nlp.py` and `_3_2_split_meaning.py`, not just its README:
1. **Rule-based passes first** (their real order, via spaCy): split on hard punctuation, then on commas, then on sentence boundaries, then split anything still too long at its grammatical root. Adopt the concept using what's already in `segment.py` (jieba/sudachipy/kiwipiepy, already per-language) rather than adding spaCy as a new dependency.
2. **One LLM pass**, only for lines still too long after the rule-based passes — asks it to return `[br]` break markers in a JSON response, not to rewrite or translate anything. Their matching step is worth adopting directly: the model's suggested break text is matched back to the *original* text with `SequenceMatcher` (>0.9 similarity required), retried up to 3 times on a bad match, so a hallucinated or reworded response can't corrupt the real text — it can only fail to find a good split, never silently rewrite content.
3. Re-run alignment (Step 2/3's existing timing-reconstruction path) against the new boundaries so start/end times still line up.
4. Optional per drama, off by default — this changes line boundaries, which is a bigger structural change than Step 6b's export-time wrapping, so it needs to be something the user opts into per drama, not silently different from today's output.
   - **Guardrail:** re-segmenting after translation, notes or flags already exist orphans them — the old line ids (Step 2) no longer map to sensible boundaries. Before running, check whether the drama has any translated lines. If it does, warn plainly ("N lines are already translated — re-segmenting will require re-translating the affected lines") and, on confirmation, clear `.en`/flags/notes only for the lines whose boundaries actually changed, leaving untouched lines alone rather than blanking the whole drama.

**Exit:** a mocked test shows a run-on ASR segment gets split at a genuine clause boundary (not mid-word, not arbitrarily by length), and a normal segment passes through unchanged; timing stays continuous across a split. A test shows re-segmenting a drama with existing translations warns first and only clears translations/notes/flags for lines whose boundaries actually changed.

### Step 6d — Data-corruption bugs from stale line-widget state, found after Step 6c
Reported by the implementing session after finishing Step 6c, relayed by the user with an explicit "out of scope, your call" — worth fixing now rather than letting more work pile onto the same file. Confirmed all three directly against real source (`tabs/workspace_tab.py`), not taken on faith.

1. **"Apply merge" and "Restore" (Version history) don't clear stale line widgets — real, reproducible data corruption.** `_clear_line_widget_state()` exists specifically for this: after an operation renumbers or replaces the line list, Review & edit's per-line widgets (`zh_<idx>`, `en_<idx>`, `speaker_<idx>`, etc.) are keyed by **position**, not line identity — they keep showing whatever they held before, and the next rerun reads that stale box back as an "edit," writing it over whichever line now sits at that position. "Apply re-segmentation" already calls `_clear_line_widget_state()` correctly. **"Apply merge" and "Restore" don't call it at all** — confirmed by direct read. Reproduced exactly as reported: after a merge, the page shows the wrong lines while the database is actually correct, and the next "Save edits" writes a merged-away line's text over a different line. **Fix: call `_clear_line_widget_state()` in both places**, same as re-segmentation already does.
2. **The export panel's overlap-clamp check compounds bug 1 into a real, silent database write.** Confirmed: the overlap-clamp check in section 9 (Export subtitles) runs unconditionally on every render of that section — not gated behind a button — and immediately calls `db.save_lines(picked_id, st.session_state.lines, fields=("flag", "flag_note"))` on any line it thinks overlaps the next one. So stale post-merge/restore timing data (bug 1's symptom) doesn't just display wrong — it gets written to the database as real `flag`/`flag_note` values on the very next page load. This is the actual reason bug 1 is dangerous rather than just visually confusing: fixing bug 1 removes the bad input, but note this as the mechanism, since a future stale-widget bug elsewhere could hit the same unconditional-write pattern.
3. **"Improve translation → Use this" gets silently undone on the next page reload — same bug class as the re-transcribe bug already fixed in Step 5b, missed for the English box.** Re-transcribe's "Use this" explicitly pops `st.session_state[f"zh_{ln.idx}"]` after accepting a result, with a comment explaining exactly why (the `zh_<idx>` widget would otherwise keep showing stale text and overwrite the just-accepted result on the next rerun). **"Improve translation"'s "Use this" has no equivalent pop for `en_<idx>`** — confirmed missing by direct read, exactly the same failure mode, just on the other language's box. This was missed in Step 5b's own PR, which fixed the zh/re-transcribe case but not this parallel en/improve-translation case. **Fix: pop `en_<idx>` after accepting an improved translation, mirroring the existing zh fix exactly.**

**Exit:**
- A test reproduces the original bug: after a merge (or a restore), stale widget content for a renumbered line, if resubmitted, no longer overwrites the wrong line — confirms `_clear_line_widget_state()` runs on both paths.
- A test shows accepting an improved translation via "Use this" survives a rerun without a stale `en_<idx>` box reverting it, mirroring the existing re-transcribe test.
- Manual check: merge two lines, don't touch any text box, and confirm Review & edit shows the correct post-merge lines (not the pre-merge layout) with no unexpected flag written on the next export-panel render.

### Step 6e — Vertical/shorts export *(idea from OpenCreator's "Portrait Render" and ZastTranslate's "Viral Shorts Studio")* *(renamed from 6d — 6d now holds Step 6c's follow-up bugfixes)*
Directly relevant to the "clip streamer" look you asked about earlier — that culture is built around vertical/shorts format specifically, not just subtitle styling.
1. Given a drama (or a selected time range within one), render a 9:16 vertical version: centre-crop by default, with a manual crop-position adjustment per drama rather than trying to auto-detect a face/subject.
2. Burn subtitles using Step 6b's ASS styling (so the "Streamer clip" preset and per-speaker colours carry over), sized and positioned for the vertical frame.
3. Export as its own video file alongside the existing horizontal export — this is additive, not a replacement for the existing "Export full subtitled episode" step.
   - **Guardrail:** nothing stops re-encoding a full multi-hour episode vertically by accident, which is slow and heavy. Before starting, show an estimated time/output size based on the selected range's duration (reuse Step 9b's ETA approach), and for a selection longer than a set threshold (e.g. 20 minutes) show a clear prompt suggesting a shorter clip range instead of a hard block — this is a real, if less common, use case, so don't disable it outright.

**Exit:** a vertical export of a short clip plays correctly, is genuinely 9:16, and its burned subtitles are legible without manual repositioning. A test shows the time/size estimate appears before the job starts, and a long selection shows the "consider a shorter clip" prompt.

### Step 6f — Fix: "Apply re-segmentation" can leave duplicate, orphaned rows in the database — real, confirmed data corruption
**Real, confirmed gap, at the user's live report** — after applying "✂️ Re-segment long lines by meaning," the Review & edit table showed both the original long lines AND their new split pieces, all with real timestamps and (for some) real translated text. The user confirmed **a hard refresh did not remove the duplicates** — ruling out a display/rendering staleness issue (a hard refresh re-fetches straight from the database) and confirming the database itself genuinely contains both the old and new rows.

Dispatched two rounds of read-only Explore agents against the real `baihe-subtitler` branch to find the exact mechanism, per this repo's own standing rule to verify rather than assume. First round confirmed the code, read in isolation, *should* work correctly: `resegment_lines()` (`resegment.py`) never produces both an unchanged copy and split pieces from the same source line, and the Apply handler's `db.save_lines(picked_id, _reseg["lines"])` call (no `fields=` argument) should trigger `save_lines()`'s full delete-orphan sync (`removed = existing - kept`, confirmed by reading the exact conditional in `db.py` — this only runs when `fields is None`, and the Apply handler's call qualifies). So this isn't Step 6d's "no `_clear_line_widget_state()` call" bug class, and it isn't a `fields=`-scoping gap suppressing deletes either — both ruled out directly.

**Second round found the real cause: a stale-snapshot bug, the same class Step 9h already flagged as worth auditing for elsewhere.** `st.session_state.lines` (built into `all_lines`/`edited_rows` and frozen into `_reseg["lines"]` the moment "Preview re-segmentation" runs) is **never re-fetched from the database immediately before Preview computes its result** — confirmed via direct read. If `st.session_state.lines` was already stale relative to the database at that exact moment (the same general staleness class Step 9h confirmed live for the translate-completion path), the line IDs baked into `_reseg["lines"]` don't fully correspond to the database's real current ID set. Since Apply saves that frozen, already-stale snapshot unchanged, `db.save_lines()`'s `kept` set (computed from the stale snapshot's IDs) doesn't match its freshly-queried `existing` set — leaving genuinely-real old rows unrecognized as "should be deleted" and orphaned in the database, while the new split rows get inserted alongside them. This is consistent with duplicates surviving a hard refresh: the corruption is already committed to the database by the time any refresh happens, not a rendering artifact refresh could ever fix.

1. **Re-fetch `st.session_state.lines` from the database (`db.load_line_objects(picked_id)`) immediately before "Preview re-segmentation" builds its input**, not relying on whatever `st.session_state.lines` already happens to hold — closes the actual staleness window, the same fix shape as re-fetching after a translate job (Step 9h) or after merge/restore (Step 6d), just applied one step earlier in this specific flow (before Preview, not only before Apply).
2. **Add a real safety check at Apply time**: before calling `db.save_lines()`, verify the ID set `_reseg["lines"]` expects to replace still matches the database's actual current row IDs for this drama (a cheap `SELECT id FROM lines WHERE drama_id=?` comparison) — if they've diverged (e.g., the user edited something else between Preview and Apply), refuse to apply and ask the user to re-run Preview, rather than silently corrupting data. This is a genuine second line of defense, not a substitute for item 1's real fix.
3. **This is the second confirmed live instance of the "stale `st.session_state.lines` snapshot" bug class this session** (after Step 9h's translate-completion case) — Step 9h's own item 2 already called for auditing other bulk operations for the same pattern; this confirms that audit is not hypothetical. Worth checking merge, restore, and re-transcription's own snapshot-freshness the same way, not just patching this one instance and the translate one.

**Exit:**
- A test reproduces the original bug: seed a stale `st.session_state.lines` snapshot (deliberately missing an ID the database actually has), run Preview against it, attempt Apply, and confirm item 2's safety check refuses rather than silently corrupting data.
- A test confirms Preview re-fetches from the database immediately before computing its result, not relying on a snapshot that could be stale.
- Manual check: apply a real re-segmentation on a real drama and confirm the resulting line count and IDs exactly match what the preview promised — no leftover old rows, no missing new ones — even after a hard refresh.
- **Practical note for the user's own current data, not a code fix**: the re-segmentation panel's own "A snapshot is saved to Version history first" message means the pre-Apply state should be recoverable via **Version history / undo → Restore**, without needing a manual database edit.

**Correction (2026-09-27): the stale-snapshot root cause above is not what actually causes duplicate rows — though the shipped fix still correctly guards against a real, different problem.** An independent Opus-level QC review directly probed `db.save_lines()`'s real behavior with `fields=None`: a snapshot missing a line the database has results in that line being **silently deleted**, and a snapshot taken before a new transcription results in the new transcription being **wiped and the old lines restored** — neither probe produced duplicate rows. So the mechanism described above (stale IDs → orphaned rows left undeleted) doesn't match how `save_lines()` actually behaves; **the real cause of the duplicates the user saw is still unexplained.** The review's own most likely lead, not yet confirmed: stale position-keyed `en_<idx>`/`zh_<idx>` widgets (the same bug class already fixed in Step 6d/9h/9i) being saved back after Apply — consistent with the user's real duplicates having translations on them, which the newly-split pieces never do. **This doesn't mean the shipped fix is wrong or should be reverted** — re-fetching before Preview and refusing on an ID-set mismatch at Apply are both independently correct safety improvements that genuinely prevent two other real silent-data-loss cases (item 1/2 above), confirmed by the same probe. It means the *duplicate-rows* symptom specifically may still be able to recur through a different mechanism this fix doesn't address. **Also found**: Step 6f item 3 explicitly called for auditing merge and restore for the same stale-snapshot pattern — this was never done. Reading `workspace_tab.py`'s "Apply merge" directly confirms it still saves a preview kept in `session_state` with no ID-set check at Apply time: previewing a merge, then re-running alignment, then clicking Apply merge would replace the new transcription with the old pre-merge lines, the same mechanism this step's own probes demonstrated. **Separately, a real UX side effect of this step's shipped fix, found while reviewing it**: since Preview now re-fetches from the database and Apply clears the relevant widgets, any *unsaved* edits sitting in the Review & edit boxes at the moment Preview runs are silently discarded — not a data-corruption risk, but a real, undocumented behavior change worth surfacing to the user in the UI (e.g. a warning if unsaved edits exist before Preview runs), not silently dropping them.

1. **Find the real mechanism behind the duplicate rows** — instrument or directly test the actual reported scenario (translated lines present on the "old" duplicates) rather than assuming the stale-widget lead is correct without checking; the goal is to close the real gap, not just the one this step's fix already (correctly, but incidentally) narrowed.
2. **Complete Step 6f item 3's original audit**: apply the same ID-set-mismatch safety check (already built for re-segmentation) to "Apply merge" and "Restore," which still lack it.
3. **Surface a warning when Preview would discard unsaved Review & edit changes**, rather than silently dropping them — a small, real UX fix found as a side effect of this step's own shipped code.

### Step 6g — Lower the default speech-splitting sensitivity, persist it per drama, and record why an auto-tune isn't built yet
**At the user's direct request and real, confirmed-working test** — after personally lowering "Speech-splitting sensitivity (ms of silence to start a new line)" from the 2000ms default to 300ms (the slider's minimum), the user confirmed it fixed their real complaint (subtitles staying on screen through silence when nothing else was being said) and asked for the default itself changed to 300. Confirmed the exact current default via direct read: `st.slider(..., 300, 3000, 2000, 100, ...)` (`tabs/workspace_tab.py`) — 2000ms is the fourth argument, i.e. the default.

**Also asked directly: "Do I have to manually adjust that or can it auto do that based off flags?"** Investigated rather than guessed. Two real, separate findings:
- **`min_silence_ms` isn't persisted anywhere today — not even per-drama.** Confirmed by direct read: it's a plain local variable, no `st.session_state[...]` key at all — unlike "Expected number of speakers," which Step 4f already fixed to remember its last-used value per drama (`st.session_state[f"expected_speakers_{picked_id}"]`). Every visit to a drama currently resets this slider to the default, regardless of what worked last time.
- **A real signal exists that could plausibly drive an auto-tune, but no such mechanism exists yet, and it would be genuinely novel to this codebase.** "Check line coverage" (`core.diagnose_line_coverage`) already computes a real `long_lines` metric — lines whose duration is both over 12s and over 2.5× their expected reading duration, exactly the over-merging symptom this setting causes — but it's a manual, on-demand button, never wired to `min_silence_ms` automatically. Checked the whole codebase for any existing "try a parameter, measure a metric, adjust" pattern to model this on — none found; the closest analog (`adaptive_style.py`, learning from translation edits) doesn't do parameter search over a numeric setting. Building a real auto-tune (re-run alignment at a few candidate `min_silence_ms` values, pick the one minimizing `long_lines` without over-splitting) is feasible using data that already exists, but is new scaffolding, not a small tweak — scoped as its own item below rather than bundled silently into the quick default-change fix.

1. **Change the slider's default from `2000` to `300`**, at the user's explicit, tested request — a one-line change (`st.slider(..., 300, 3000, 300, 100, ...)`). Update the help text's own "The default (2000ms) merges..." wording to match the new real default, so the in-app explanation doesn't contradict the actual slider position.
2. **Persist `min_silence_ms` per drama**, same `st.session_state[f"min_silence_ms_{picked_id}"]` pattern Step 4f already established for "Expected number of speakers" — so a value the user tunes for one drama (e.g. back to something higher for a drama with genuinely long natural pauses) isn't silently lost on the next visit.
3. **Auto-tune itself is not built as part of this step** — real, non-trivial work, spun out to its own step (**6h**) below rather than rushed in here, once the real cost question (below) made clear it isn't a small tweak.

**Exit:**
- Manual check: a fresh drama's transcription config shows the "Speech-splitting sensitivity" slider defaulting to 300ms, not 2000ms, and the help text's own wording matches.
- A test confirms `min_silence_ms` set for one drama persists across a tab switch and comes back correctly on return, same test shape as Step 4f's `load_last_speaker_count` test.
- Manual check: confirm auto-tune (Step 6h) is NOT bundled into this step's shipped version — explicitly a separate step, not silently dropped.

**Real CLI/UI parity gap found by an independent Opus-level QC review (2026-09-27).** This project's own "rules learned from real bugs" list (in `baihe-subtitler`'s root `CLAUDE.md`) explicitly calls out CLI/UI parity as a class of mistake that's already slipped through once before. Confirmed directly: `cli.py`'s `cmd_align` still calls `core`'s alignment function with no `min_silence_ms` argument, silently falling back to `core`'s own hardcoded default of `2000` — meaning the CLI now splits speech completely differently from the UI's new 300ms default, a real, live divergence between the two entry points for the exact same operation. **Fix**: add a `--min-silence-ms` CLI flag (default 300, matching the UI's new default) and pass it through the same way the UI does, so both paths agree unless a user explicitly overrides either one.

### Step 6h — Auto-tune speech-splitting sensitivity, at the user's follow-up request
Step 6g scoped this out rather than build it quickly; the user then explicitly asked to add it anyway ("Please add it"). Before designing anything, checked the one question that decides the whole shape of this feature: **is trying several candidate `min_silence_ms` values cheap or expensive?** Dispatched a read-only Explore agent against the real `baihe-subtitler` branch to confirm rather than assume.

**Confirmed: genuinely expensive, not a cheap re-segmentation.** `transcribe_for_timing` (`core.py:430-524`) bakes `min_silence_duration_ms`/`vad_threshold` directly into the `vad_parameters` passed into faster-whisper's own `model.transcribe(...)` call — VAD segmentation happens *inside* faster-whisper's own decode pass, not as a separable pre-step this codebase can hook into independently. There's no whisper-decode-result cache anywhere (`core.py`'s only cache is for model *weights*, not transcripts), and no standalone "VAD-only, don't decode" function exists in `audio_preprocess.py`/`diarize.py` either — confirmed by direct search. So **each candidate value requires a full end-to-end re-transcription**, not a cheap recomputation of segment boundaries over already-decoded audio. Separately confirmed: every ASR backend this app currently ships (`faster-whisper`, Qwen3-ASR, SenseVoice) runs **locally** — so today this costs real CPU/GPU time, not real money — but the roadmap already has an opt-in Groq-hosted Whisper cloud option proposed (not yet built); if that ships, repeated auto-tune re-transcription would carry a real per-run dollar cost too, worth remembering when that step is eventually built. **One piece is genuinely cheap**: `core.diagnose_line_coverage(lines)` is a pure, in-memory computation over any candidate line list, no DB commit required — confirmed it can evaluate a "what if" result the same way "Preview re-segmentation" already does for a different transform (`_reseg_key` in `st.session_state`, reviewed before any `db.save_lines` commit).

**Design, given a real per-candidate cost that isn't free:**
1. **"🪄 Auto-tune" is an explicit, opt-in action (a button), never automatic on page load or on every transcription** — the cost (multiple full re-transcriptions) has to be a decision the user makes, not something that silently fires.
2. **Limit to 2-3 candidate values by default**, not an open-ended search — e.g. 300ms, 800ms, 1500ms (spanning the slider's real range meaningfully without an unbounded number of full re-runs). Show a real time estimate before starting, reusing Step 9b's existing ETA approach (already used elsewhere for job-length estimates), scaled by however many candidates are queued — so the user is deciding with real information, not guessing how long this will take.
3. **Run as a real, cancellable background job**, following this project's own established pattern for multi-step long-running work (Step 4d/4e/4g's subprocess-based real-stop mechanism) — each candidate's transcription is itself the kind of long-running GPU-touching work those steps already made stoppable; reuse that mechanism rather than inventing a separate one, and let the user cancel mid-run if the estimate turns out too long.
4. **Never silently apply a result.** Once all candidates finish, show each one's `diagnose_line_coverage` outcome side by side (at minimum: `long_lines` count, plus total line count so "fewer long lines" isn't gamed by producing far more short ones) and let the user pick — same "suggest, don't decide for the user" discipline as Step 8b's clone-reference-clip reasons and every other diagnostic surface in this app. Picking one applies it the same way manually setting the slider already does (including Step 6g's per-drama persistence), not a separate code path.
5. **Real tuning-strategy question, left to the implementing session to decide with real test data, not pre-decided here**: whether to score candidates on `long_lines` count alone, or a combined score also penalizing excessive line-count inflation (a candidate that eliminates every long line by over-splitting into hundreds of fragments isn't actually better) — `diagnose_line_coverage`'s existing metrics may need a small combined-score helper, not a UI-only decision.

**Exit:**
- A test confirms the auto-tune job produces real, distinct `diagnose_line_coverage` results for each of its candidate `min_silence_ms` values on a fixture drama.
- A test confirms cancelling mid-run actually stops the in-progress candidate's transcription (reusing Step 4d/4e/4g's real-stop mechanism), not just hiding the UI.
- Manual check: run auto-tune on a real drama with known over-merged lines, confirm the time estimate shown before starting is in the right ballpark, and confirm picking a suggested candidate correctly applies it (including persisting it per Step 6g's mechanism).
- Manual check: confirm no candidate is ever auto-applied without an explicit user pick.

### Step 7 — Reflect translation mode *(new feature; needs Step 1)*
- **Correction after reading VideoLingo's actual code** (`core/translate_lines.py`), not just its README: it's a **two**-call pipeline, not three — `get_prompt_faithfulness()` produces a `"direct"` (literal) translation, then `get_prompt_expressiveness()` takes that plus the source and produces a `"free"` (natural-reading) one; reflection/self-critique is folded into that second prompt internally, not a separate visible pass. pyvideotrans's own three-step framing is closer to what's below.
- Add an optional "High quality" setting as a genuine **three** separate calls anyway — a deliberate choice, not a copy of VideoLingo's two-call version: making the middle critique its own pass means it can be **stored and shown**, not just silently folded into a rewrite prompt where the reasoning disappears.
  1. **Faithfulness pass:** translate the batch preserving exact meaning, not yet polished for how it reads.
  2. **Reflection pass:** the same engine critiques *that specific translation* — where it's technically correct but reads unnaturally, plus accuracy, pronouns/gender, glossary use, tone and register.
  3. **Expressiveness pass:** rewrite using the reflection, now optimizing for how it reads as a subtitle, not just correctness.
- It works through the same engine interface for every LLM engine: Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek and Ollama.
- It costs about 3× as much, so show the estimated cost (`translate_engines.estimate_cost`) before the user starts it.
- Every pass keeps the id-keyed JSON from Step 1 — **deliberately not** VideoLingo's own matching method, which uses `SequenceMatcher` fuzzy-similarity (>0.9 threshold, errors below it) to associate returned lines back to source lines rather than an id. That's strictly less robust than Step 1's exact id match, so nothing here adopts it.
- Save the reflection critique as translation notes, so the reasons for the final wording can be reviewed.

**Exit:** a mocked engine test shows 3 calls per batch, with ids kept at every pass, and the reflection critique stored as notes.

### Step 7b — Whole-document-first glossary extraction *(idea from VideoLingo)* — ✅ **Merged (PR #23), text corrected to match what was actually built**
`translation_guide.extract_terms_llm` already exists and works. This item was originally written assuming extraction already ran chunk-by-chunk, with a planned whole-document pass meant to feed into each chunk's `known_terms`. **The implementing session re-verified this against current source before building and found that assumption doesn't hold**: there is exactly one real call site (`workspace_tab.py`'s "Extract terms" button), and it makes a single call over a single sample — nothing here is chunked, so there was never a second, per-chunk pass to feed into. Checked VideoLingo's real `core/_4_1_summarize.py` for the actual idea worth adopting regardless: `get_summary()` takes the **combined, whole-document** source content in one call and directly produces the terminology list — `{src, tgt, note}` per term — so the model sees the full story at once before proposing any term, rather than a truncating prefix. That combined-context view is the real mechanism; the "feed into each chunk's pass" framing was never accurate for this codebase.
1. ~~Add a first pass that runs `extract_terms_llm`-style extraction over a combined sample across the whole drama, then feed its output into each chunk's existing per-chunk pass as known context.~~ **What was actually built**: the one real call site's sample (previously `zh_lines[:max_lines]`, a truncating prefix that made any name introduced past the default 400-line cutoff invisible to extraction) now spreads `max_lines` lines evenly across the *whole* drama via a new `_sample_lines_across_text()` — explicitly including both the first and last line — the line-list counterpart of the existing `_sample_across_text()` already used by `extract_glossary_from_novel` for the same reasoning on raw-string input.
2. This is still one call, not a chunked pipeline — the "one extra whole-document call per run, not one per chunk" framing below is moot since there was only ever one call to begin with.

**Exit (as actually met):** a mocked test shows the sample spreads across the whole drama (not just the start, and including the true end), and existing `extract_terms_llm` tests still pass.

Accept sets the character name on that speaker label the same way a manual assignment would; Reject dismisses just that suggestion and never re-shows it for that speaker/episode pair.
