### Step 10e — LAN client/server access: print the real network URL instead of only opening a local browser window
**At the user's direct request** — "is it possible to have something like where i start the streamlit session and it pulls from the configs i have as the (server/master) and the other computer can just run everything like normal" — running the app on one always-on personal-server machine and using it from a different home PC over their own LAN, single-user, no internet exposure needed.

**Investigated before designing anything, and the news is good: this is almost entirely free already, by Streamlit's own architecture.** Confirmed via direct read: `start.bat` launches with `--server.headless true`, and Streamlit's own default binding when headless is `0.0.0.0` (all interfaces), not `localhost` — so a server machine running `start.bat` today is **already reachable from another device on the LAN** at `http://<server's-LAN-IP>:8501`, no code change needed for the binding itself. Grepped `app.py`/`cli.py`/`background_jobs.py`/`common.py`/`storage.py`/`db.py` for any hardcoded `localhost`/`127.0.0.1` — none found. Confirmed `db.py`'s `LIBRARY_DIR`/`DB_PATH` are simple paths relative to the app's own install directory, not tied to any "localhost" concept — meaning "run the whole app on the server machine" already just IS a normal single-machine install; there's no separate client/data-store split to build. Confirmed `background_jobs.py`'s job state is already process-global (`_jobs = {}` at module level, explicitly documented as shared across every tab/session regardless of which is "active") — multiple browser sessions from different machines connecting to the same running server already share job state exactly the way Streamlit always handles multiple tabs today, nothing special needed for the "run jobs on the server, use from elsewhere" part of the request. CORS/XSRF are left at Streamlit's defaults, which don't add friction for a direct same-origin LAN request (no reverse proxy, no different origin involved).

**The one real, small gap**: `start.bat`'s own browser-launch section (`APP_URL=http://localhost:%PORT%`, then opening Edge/Chrome/a default browser) is written purely for the convenience of a local window on the *server* machine — it has no concept of "someone will connect to this from elsewhere" and never surfaces the LAN URL anywhere.

1. **Have `start.bat` also print the machine's real LAN-reachable URL** (e.g. via `ipconfig` parsing for the primary adapter's IPv4 address, same general technique already needed elsewhere for local network info) alongside the existing "Starting Baihe Subtitler on port 8501..." message — something like "Also reachable from other devices on this network at: http://<LAN-IP>:8501" — so a user running this as a personal server doesn't have to already know their own machine's IP.
2. **Not required, but worth considering**: a `--server-only`/`BAIHE_SERVER_ONLY` flag (or reuse of `--ci`'s existing browser-skip behavior) for someone who always wants to run this machine headless as a server and never wants the local Edge/Chrome window to open at all — `--ci` already does this today as a side effect, but its name and its other CI-specific behavior make it an awkward fit for a human deliberately running a personal server 24/7; a plainly-named alias avoids someone reaching for a flag literally called "CI" for a non-CI purpose.
3. **Explicitly out of scope, correctly**: no authentication/multi-user work — confirmed this remains single-user, LAN-only, no internet exposure, matching the request exactly; don't add login/access-control machinery nobody asked for.

**Exit:**
- Manual check: run `start.bat` on one machine, confirm the printed LAN URL is correct, and successfully load/use the app (browse a drama, start a real job) from a browser on a different machine on the same network.
- Manual check: confirm a background job started from the second machine's browser session shows up and completes correctly, same as if run locally — no job-visibility gap between sessions.

**Revisited (2026-09-27) — item 3's "no multi-user work" narrowed, not reversed, by a directly-requested feature built in a separate session.** See Step 78: the user asked a different (functionality-testing) session for household profiles — separate reading progress/history/notes per named person, Jellyfin-style — while exploring whether to remote-access this app from multiple devices/people. That is real per-identity *state*, which this item's original scope didn't have in mind. It is **not** the login/access-control machinery this item actually warned against: profiles carry no password, and access to the app itself is still gated by nothing beyond whatever already reaches it (running it locally, or a reverse proxy/Tailscale for remote use) — the same trust boundary this step already assumed. Recorded here so this line doesn't read as an unreviewed scope violation to anyone checking it later.

### Step 11 — Scanlate: finish the ML detector, add real inpainting, auto-route OCR
`scanlate.py`'s own comments already point at the right fix — a `detect_bubbles_ml()` stub naming a real model that was never wired up, and an honest note that inpainting is "a plain rectangular inset, not a shape-aware mask." Checked seven comparable open-source manga/comic translators' actual code and license (not just their READMEs) to find what's real, free, and safe to build on:

| Project | License | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| [manga-image-translator](https://github.com/zyddnys/manga-image-translator), [Kites](https://github.com/Unheat/Kites) | GPL-3.0 | **Not usable** — would force this app's whole codebase open |
| [gnurt2041/MangaOCR](https://github.com/gnurt2041/MangaOCR) | No license stated | **Not usable** — unlicensed means all rights reserved by default |
| [comic-translate](https://github.com/ogkalu2/comic-translate) | Apache-2.0 | Ideas only (see item 4) — its own demo images (Frieren, etc.) have no stated license separate from the code and are from currently-published, copyrighted manga; **not** brought in as test fixtures |
| [koharu](https://github.com/koharu-rs/koharu) | MIT/Apache-2.0 (app); its detection *model* has a training-data caveat, see item 3 | Its actual detection model is the real find here (item 3) |
| [kha-white/manga-ocr](https://github.com/kha-white/manga-ocr) | Apache-2.0 | Already a Baihe dependency, nothing new to add |
| [EasyScanlate](https://github.com/Liiesl/EasyScanlate) | MIT | Rust + a GUI framework — architecture doesn't transfer to this Python app |

1. **Finish `detect_bubbles_ml()`, and fix a real dependency mismatch found along the way.** The docstring names `ogkalu/comic-text-and-bubble-detector` (Hugging Face, Apache-2.0, 3 classes: bubble / text-in-bubble / text-outside-bubble, boxes only — confirmed real) as the intended model, but `requirements.txt` already installs `ultralytics` for it — and that model is **RT-DETR-v2, not a YOLO model**, so `ultralytics` can't actually load it. That mismatch is plausibly *why* the hook was never finished. Swap to whatever this model's real inference stack needs (its Hugging Face card shows ONNX/safetensors, loadable through `transformers` or plain ONNX Runtime — confirm against the current card when implementing) and wire it into `detect_bubbles_ml()` as an optional, better-than-OpenCV-heuristic backend.
2. **Add real ML inpainting**, replacing the current plain OpenCV `cv2.inpaint` as the default when it's installed: [`mayocream/lama-manga`](https://huggingface.co/mayocream/lama-manga) — MIT licensed, a Big-LaMa checkpoint fine-tuned on ~300k manga/anime images specifically (not generic photo-LaMa), ~989MB safetensors, 4-channel input (RGB + mask) → 3-channel RGB output. This is the direct, concrete fix for the "plain rectangular inset, not shape-aware" limitation the code already names — most of the visible improvement comes from this one model, independent of item 1 or item 3.
3. **Optional, more advanced: real shape-aware masking**, which item 1's detector does *not* provide on its own (it gives boxes, not masks) — [`mayocream/koharu-layout-rfdetr-seg-2xl-1152`](https://huggingface.co/mayocream/koharu-layout-rfdetr-seg-2xl-1152), the actual detection model behind koharu (a separate Hugging Face artifact from koharu's own Rust app — usable from Python without needing any Rust/WebGPU code). Real segmentation output (text / SFX / bubble / panel), ~40MB safetensors, ships its own Python `load_model.py` loader. **License caveat, stated plainly, same as the one already implicit in Baihe's existing `manga-ocr` dependency:** its training data includes Manga109, which carries academic-use terms — fine for this app's personal use, worth knowing if it's ever redistributed or used commercially. Mark this as an optional upgrade over item 1's box-only detector, not a requirement.
4. **Auto-route the OCR backend by source language**, the way comic-translate does, but with maintained choices — `manga-ocr` for Japanese (already a dependency), `paddleocr` for Chinese, `paddleocr`/`tesseract` for Korean. **Explicitly not** adopting comic-translate's choice of Pororo for Korean: checked its maintenance status and even a Hugging Face mirror of just its OCR piece exists specifically because people are worried about the main library's long-term upkeep — a fragile dependency not worth taking on. Keep manual backend override available; auto-routing is just a better default.
   - **Opt-in second Japanese OCR option to try: [`jzhang533/PaddleOCR-VL-For-Manga`](https://huggingface.co/jzhang533/PaddleOCR-VL-For-Manga)**, checked directly — Apache-2.0, a manga-specific fine-tune of PaddleOCR-VL (1.0B params, BF16), 70% full-sentence accuracy on Manga109-s crops vs. base PaddleOCR-VL's 27%, specifically aimed at the vertical-Japanese-text degradation that hurts general OCR models. **Its own model card only benchmarks against base PaddleOCR-VL, not against `manga-ocr`** — there's no confirmed number showing it beats what Baihe already uses, so this is not a default swap. Add as a second selectable Japanese backend (same opt-in pattern as items 2/3/6) and let the manual check below settle it with a real head-to-head.
5. All of this stays optional/opt-in, same spirit as the existing `detect_bubbles_ml()` docstring — the free OpenCV heuristic (detection) and plain `cv2.inpaint` (inpainting) remain the zero-install default; these are better backends for someone who installs the extra weight, not a replacement that changes default behaviour. **Refined on a later pass, prompted by a Gemini-authored review the user was directly unsure about**: it suggested flipping the *default* itself — defaulting to the ML detector and treating OpenCV as a "low-resource fallback," specifically because "pure OpenCV-based speech bubble detection fails on complex manga backgrounds or un-bordered text (common in webtoons)." That weakness is real (it's the exact gap item 1's ML detector exists to fix), but flipping the hard default would mean a brand-new user's very first Scanlate run needs an extra model download before anything works, which cuts against "zero-install default" for no real benefit to someone who hasn't opted in yet. The better version of the same idea: **auto-select the ML detector whenever its weights are already present/cached, falling back to OpenCV only when they're not** — not a manual toggle the user has to remember to flip, not a hard requirement on first run either. This gets the quality win the review is actually asking for the moment someone installs the optional weights once, without changing what a zero-install user sees. Same auto-select pattern for item 2's LaMa-manga vs. plain OpenCV inpainting.
6. **Conditional fallback if item 2's LaMa-manga quality turns out not to be enough in real testing:** [`meangrinch/MangaTranslator`](https://github.com/meangrinch/MangaTranslator) (Apache-2.0, read directly — not README-only) uses FLUX-diffusion inpainting (FLUX.2 Klein, Apache-2.0, clean; or FLUX.1 Kontext [dev], non-commercial-only license — prefer Klein) instead of LaMa, which is a genuinely more advanced technique on the manual-check page in Step 2's exit list. Not adopted by default — it's a much heavier dependency (`diffusers`, `sdnq`, `spandrel`, a multi-GB checkpoint vs. LaMa-manga's ~989MB) for a gain that hasn't been confirmed to matter on Baihe's actual pages. **Trigger to revisit:** if the manual check below shows LaMa-manga leaving a visible edge or texture mismatch that matters on real pages, swap in FLUX.2 Klein as a third, heavier inpainting option, same opt-in pattern as items 2/3 — not a replacement for LaMa-manga, an escalation above it.

**Three more items, added after mining Torii Image Translator's real changelog for proven functionality (Torii itself is closed/proprietary — `toriitranslate.com`, credit-based, GPT/Gemini/Claude-backed — nothing to port; its 60+ version changelog was read in full, then cross-checked against Baihe's actual current code, not assumed):**
7. **PDF import/export for Scanlate.** Confirmed real gap: `scanlate_tab.py`'s `st.file_uploader` only accepts `png`/`jpg`/`jpeg` (no PDF), and export is per-page image download or a bulk ZIP of images (`bulk_render_pages`) — no PDF output. Torii added PDF upload conversion (v2.0.6.1) and PDF download (v2.0.8.1) specifically because raws and finished scanlations are commonly shared as PDFs. Add PDF-to-pages splitting on import and a "download as PDF" option alongside the existing ZIP, using a lightweight, already-common library (`pypdf`/`pymupdf` — pick whichever handles image-heavy PDFs more reliably when implementing; both permissively licensed). **Cross-reference, noted on a later consolidation pass:** Step 23c item 1 adds EPUB image support for the same underlying need (a manga/manhwa project exported as a portable file with its images) through a different container format — this item's PDF export and that one's image-carrying EPUB export are companion features, not overlapping ones; a manga project can reasonably want either depending on what the reader app on the other end supports.
8. **Manual-region OCR, as a refinement of the existing "➕ Add a bubble manually" flow.** Confirmed via `tabs/scanlate_tab.py`: manually adding a bubble today means typing the translated text in by hand (`mtext = st.text_input(...)`) — there's no way to draw a box over a missed region and have OCR read it, only auto-detected boxes get OCR'd. Torii's manual OCR mode (added v2.0.9.1: "manually highlight specific text to send it for simultaneous OCR and translation") is exactly this gap. Add an option on the manual-bubble form to run OCR (the same auto-routed backend from item 4) on the hand-drawn box instead of requiring typed-in text — auto-detect still does the bulk of the work; this covers what it misses.
9. **Bulk find-and-replace across an already-translated project's bubble text.** Distinct from the glossary (which shapes *future* translations) and from Step 24's translation memory (which *suggests* reuse going forward) — this is retroactively correcting text already saved across many pages at once (e.g., a character's name was translated inconsistently before a glossary entry existed, or a typo repeats). Confirmed missing: no `find`/`replace` logic anywhere in `scanlate_tab.py` or `scanlate.py`. Add a simple search-and-replace tool scoped to one drama's saved `bubbles.translated_text`, showing a preview of every match before applying — same "don't silently overwrite" pattern as everywhere else in this roadmap.
10. **A manual erase/heal brush, independent of bubble detection — a real gap this project's own earlier Torii research surfaced but didn't act on at the time.** Torii's changelog (already read in full for items 7–9) also lists a manual paint/erase toolset (erase added v1.0.32.1–v1.0.33.1; a dedicated "manual inpainting and painting tools" mode added v2.0.5.1) — missed when the first Torii pass only pulled PDF/manual-OCR/find-replace from the same changelog. A Gemini-authored review the user shared this turn named the same gap directly: "ensure manual visual bounding-box drawing and a 'healing/inpainting' eraser are readily accessible." Confirmed real: Scanlate's inpainting today only ever runs against a detected (auto or manually-boxed) bubble region — there's no freeform brush to clean up art the detector left untouched (a sound effect, background text, or a stray detection artifact outside any bubble box). Add a simple paint-to-erase tool on the page-preview image: the user brushes over a region, that region gets the same inpainting backend (item 2's LaMa-manga, or plain OpenCV if that's not installed) applied directly, no bubble/box required. **Concrete mechanism, checked directly (a second Gemini-authored review the user shared asked for exactly this — "a simple canvas brush tool" — without naming how):** Streamlit has no native freeform-drawing widget; [`streamlit-drawable-canvas`](https://github.com/andfanilo/streamlit-drawable-canvas) (confirmed real) provides exactly this — `st_canvas()` with `drawing_mode="freedraw"`, adjustable `stroke_width`, a background-image parameter (the page itself), returning drawn-object data back to Python. **Caveat, stated plainly like every other dependency caveat in this doc:** its PyPI page shows no release in the past 12 months — a real maintenance-inactive flag, though the component is simple enough (a Fabric.js wrapper) that inactivity alone isn't disqualifying the way it might be for something with a larger attack surface; worth a quick compatibility check against Baihe's pinned Streamlit version before adopting. **That check has now been run and confirms the worst case (2026-09-27): `streamlit-drawable-canvas` fails at setup/import against this app's pinned `streamlit>=1.49`, not just "untested" or "missing a recent release" — a real, confirmed incompatibility, not a hypothetical maintenance-inactivity risk.** Before building this item, either find and vet a maintained alternative freeform-canvas component compatible with the pinned Streamlit version, or scope a from-scratch minimal freedraw widget (e.g. a small custom Streamlit component wrapping a `<canvas>` element directly) — don't adopt `streamlit-drawable-canvas` as-is; it doesn't work on this app's actual stack.

**Exit:**
- A test shows `detect_bubbles_ml()` actually loads and runs the named model (mocked, no real network/weights in tests) and falls back cleanly to `detect_bubbles_cv()` when the model isn't installed.
- A test shows the LaMa-manga inpainting backend is selected when available, OpenCV inpainting when it isn't.
- A test shows OCR backend selection follows source language by default and can still be overridden manually.
- A test shows a PDF import splits into individual pages correctly, and a "download as PDF" produces a valid multi-page PDF from a project's rendered pages.
- A test shows a manually-drawn box run through OCR returns real text (mocked OCR backend), rather than requiring the user to type it in.
- A test shows bulk find-and-replace previews every match before applying, and applying it only changes the matched bubbles' `translated_text`, nothing else.
- A test shows the detector/inpainting auto-select uses the ML backend when its weights are present and OpenCV when they aren't, without a manual toggle.
- A test shows the manual erase/heal brush applies the same inpainting backend to a brushed region with no bubble box present.
- Manual check (real weights, on your own PC): run detection + inpainting on a real page with both the ML and OpenCV-only paths and compare — the ML inpainting result should show no visible box edge where text was removed. On a Japanese page, run `manga-ocr` and PaddleOCR-VL-For-Manga side by side and compare which reads the actual text correctly more often — no benchmark number settles this for Baihe's content, so this comparison is what decides whether PaddleOCR-VL-For-Manga becomes the default Japanese backend or stays a manual-override option. Upload a PDF raw and confirm it splits into pages correctly; draw a manual box over text the auto-detector missed and confirm OCR reads it; run a find-and-replace across a project and confirm the preview matches what actually changes. Brush over a background sound effect the detector missed and confirm it gets cleanly erased.

### Step 11b — Novel narration TTS quality *(the user's priority is TTS for novels specifically, not video/audio dubbing — every item here is scoped to that, not to matching an external video's timing)*
Re-reviewed the dubbing code in projects already surveyed, filtered specifically for what helps long-form novel narration rather than dubbing-to-a-fixed-video-timeline (which most of these projects are actually built for, and which doesn't apply here — a novel narration has no external timing to hit). `dub.build_narration_track` was read directly first, to know what's already there before proposing anything.

1. **OmniVoice as the primary new narration TTS backend** — `k2-fsa/OmniVoice`, **Apache-2.0**, `pip install omnivoice`. Confirmed directly (not from VoiceStudio's marketing of it — VoiceStudio's own app code is AGPL-3.0 and isn't used at all; only this separate, cleanly-licensed engine is). Zero-shot voice cloning, 600+ languages, claims 40× real-time inference. Unlike F5-TTS (already in Baihe, but CC-BY-NC — non-commercial only) and ElevenLabs (already in Baihe, but a paid cloud API), this is free, local and unrestricted. Add as `synthesize_line_omnivoice`, selectable the same way `synthesize_line_cloned`/`synthesize_line_elevenlabs` already are.
   - **Also add its voice-design capability**, confirmed in its own README (`model.generate(text=..., instruct="female, low pitch, british accent")` — gender/age/pitch/style attributes, no reference audio needed at all). This fills a real gap on its own: novel narration today only offers the fixed default voice or cloning from real reference audio, but most novel characters have no reference audio to clone from. Add as a third per-character voice option in `character_voice_map` — "describe a voice" alongside "pick a fixed voice" and "clone from reference audio."
2. **GPT-SoVITS as a second cloning backend** — `RVC-Boss/GPT-SoVITS`, **MIT**, needs only a 3–10 second reference clip. Independently used by both pyvideotrans and VideoLingo, so it's a well-established, not experimental, choice. Not a replacement for OmniVoice — different tradeoffs (OmniVoice: faster, broader language coverage, voice design; GPT-SoVITS: more battle-tested, usable from even less reference audio). Checked for emotion/style control specifically and confirmed it has none — it's on GPT-SoVITS's own TODO list, not implemented, so this is a cloning-quality option only, nothing more to wire up beyond the engine itself.
3. **Parallelize `build_narration_track`'s clip generation**, which is currently a strictly sequential `for` loop — fine for one audio-drama episode's line count, slow for a whole novel. Confirmed via VideoLingo's actual `_10_gen_audio.py` real pattern (process the first few clips sequentially as a "warm up," then a `ThreadPoolExecutor` for the rest) — but keep Baihe's own existing per-clip caching (`if not os.path.exists(clip_path)`), which VideoLingo's own code does **not** have (confirmed — it overwrites every run with no resume). Baihe is already ahead there; this only adds the parallelization on top of what's already resumable. Force single-threaded for any backend that can't handle concurrent calls safely (VideoLingo forces this for GPT-SoVITS specifically; check OmniVoice/edge-tts/ElevenLabs on their own before assuming they're safe to parallelize).
4. **Decouple TTS-chunk size from subtitle-cue size for narration mode.** `core.chunk_novel_text` already does a decent job (paragraph-first, sentence-split fallback, `max_chars=200`) — this isn't a bug, but that same 200-char chunk currently becomes both the audio-generation unit *and* the on-screen subtitle cue, and those have different ideal sizes: a subtitle cue needs to stay short and readable (Step 6b's CPS work), but audio generation quality generally benefits from more continuous context (better cross-sentence prosody) up to what the TTS engine handles well. For narration mode specifically, raise the text unit actually sent to TTS (e.g. a full un-split paragraph, or several sentences), and only split it into shorter subtitle cues *afterward*, reusing Step 6b's existing long-cue splitting rather than building a second splitter.
5. **Proper audiobook export: M4B with chapter markers**, alongside the existing flat `narration_track.wav`. Not sourced from any one project's code — the general "this should be a real audiobook file, not one giant WAV" idea these narration-focused tools are all built around. Chapter breaks come from `chunk_novel_text`'s existing paragraph boundaries, or the novel's own chapter markers if the source text has them.
6. **Chatterbox for emotion-conditioned delivery, and actually wire it up** — `resemble-ai/chatterbox`, **MIT**, checked directly: a real `exaggeration` parameter (0.0–1.0+, recommended range 0.4–0.7) that scales emotional intensity in the generated voice, plus its own zero-shot cloning, on a small 0.5B backbone. This is what fills the gap below — an engine with a real emotion API to wire into, not a third overlapping cloning-only option. Add as `synthesize_line_chatterbox`, and:
   - **Wire it to the emotion tags `emotion.py` already computes.** Right now those tags are detected and shown for translation guidance but never reach TTS delivery at all (confirmed — no connection in `dub.py`/`workspace_tab.py`). Map each line's detected emotion + intensity to Chatterbox's `exaggeration` value (e.g. a calm/neutral line stays near the low end, a line flagged high-intensity anger or excitement pushes toward the top of the recommended range) so narration audio actually sounds different for an angry line versus a calm one, instead of every line reading in the same flat register regardless of what was detected.
   - Note Chatterbox's built-in PerTh neural watermarking on generated audio — mention this in the UI/docs so the user knows generated narration carries it, not something to strip or work around.
7. **Hume AI's TADA as an option for long, unattended narration specifically** — `HumeAI/tada`, code MIT (model weights under Meta's Llama 3.2 Community License — its own small print, note this in Settings next to the option, same spirit as F5-TTS's/VoxCPM-era licence notes elsewhere in this doc). Its real strength isn't emotion — it's speed and reliability on very long, unattended runs: a genuinely different text-acoustic tokenization aimed at not "going off script" partway through a long chapter, and claimed >5× faster generation. Add as a fourth backend choice, positioned specifically for "narrating a very long novel/chapter and want it to stay on-script the whole way," not as the default — OmniVoice/GPT-SoVITS/Chatterbox remain the defaults for normal-length narration and emotion control respectively.

**Confirmed, but not actionable right now:** ~~Baihe's existing emotion detection (`emotion.py`) does not currently reach TTS delivery at all (checked `dub.py`/`workspace_tab.py` directly — no connection exists). That's a real gap, but neither OmniVoice nor GPT-SoVITS expose real emotion-conditioning as an API to wire it into — OmniVoice's only style control is a single "whisper" flag, not general emotion.~~ **Resolved by item 6 above** — Chatterbox gives a real emotion-conditioning API, and the wiring is now in scope, not deferred.

**Checked and not added, with reasons:** `coqui-ai/tts`'s XTTS v2 — its own code is MPL-2.0, but the actual voice model is locked to the Coqui Public Model License (non-commercial only), and Coqui Inc. shut down, so there's no path to a commercial license even if wanted — same pattern as F5-TTS. `myshell-ai/OpenVoice` — genuinely clean (MIT, no restriction), but redundant once OmniVoice and GPT-SoVITS are both in; not adding a third overlapping cloning engine. `calesthio/OpenMontage` — AGPL-3.0, a much larger, differently-scoped whole video-production tool with no TTS engine of its own (it just calls out to Piper/ElevenLabs/others). `unslothai/unsloth` — not a TTS or dubbing tool at all; it's for fine-tuning LLMs, which doesn't fit how Baihe uses models (existing pretrained/API models, no local training). `jianchang512/pyvideotrans` — GPL-3.0, already the acknowledged inspiration for this app generally; nothing new beyond what Step 7 already took from it. `IndexTTS2` — has real, finer-grained emotion control (an 8-value emotion vector, fully independent of the cloned voice's identity — technically the better fit than Chatterbox's single exaggeration dial) but its license is bilibili's own custom Model Use License Agreement, not a standard one; flagging rather than adopting until that license is read carefully, the same caution already applied to koharu's Manga109-trained detector.

**Exit:**
- A mocked test shows OmniVoice, GPT-SoVITS, Chatterbox and TADA selection all follow the same pattern as the existing cloned-voice/ElevenLabs paths.
- A test shows a line's detected emotion and intensity maps to a Chatterbox `exaggeration` value within its recommended range, and a line with no detected emotion falls back to a sensible neutral default.
- A test shows a character with no reference audio can still get a described (voice-design) voice, distinct per description.
- A test shows narration generation runs a warm-up batch then parallel batches, while still skipping any clip whose file already exists, and that GPT-SoVITS forces single-threaded.
- A test shows the audio-generation text unit for narration mode can be longer than the exported subtitle cue for the same passage.
- A test shows the M4B export has chapter markers matching the narration's paragraph/chapter breaks.
- Manual check (real weights, on your own PC): generate a short story's narration with OmniVoice cloning and with GPT-SoVITS, compare naturalness against the existing edge-tts default; try voice design with no reference audio; time a longer narration run before/after parallelization; open the M4B export in a real audiobook/podcast player and confirm chapters show up.

**Built and reviewed (2026-09-27), with one real design problem this doc didn't foresee, now resolved.** Pushed (branch `claude/youthful-tesla-jl1o4f` — the session's auto-assigned name, not the `step-11b-...` convention; kept as-is rather than requesting a rename, since renaming an already-pushed unmerged branch is real git churn for a purely cosmetic convention mismatch). Full suite: 1551 passed, 50 skipped (up from 1351) — none of the four new engines actually ran against real weights (no GPU/model download in that environment), each tested against its own documented API shape with stand-ins instead; the real-weight comparison is exactly what the manual check above is for.

**Real problem found while building, not foreseeable from reading each engine's README in isolation: OmniVoice, Chatterbox, and TADA cannot share one Python environment.** Confirmed directly by this review: `requirements-optional.txt`'s own comment states it plainly — OmniVoice needs `transformers>=5.3`, Chatterbox pins `transformers==5.2.0`+`torch==2.6.0`, TADA needs `transformers<5`+`torch>=2.7` — no two of these three satisfy together, confirmed by inspecting the actual version constraints, not assumed from the claim alone. **Two real corrections to this step's own original text, both legitimate, not shortcuts:**
- **Item 3's parallelization delivers less than this doc hoped, for a real reason found during implementation.** Chatterbox's model keeps the current voice loaded internally, so overlapping calls risk swapping voices between concurrent lines — genuinely unsafe to parallelize, not just conservatively forced single-threaded. GPT-SoVITS's server also only accepts one request at a time. Neither local engine gains anything from `ThreadPoolExecutor`, so the real, shipped speed-up applies only to `edge-tts` and ElevenLabs (both already fine to parallelize) — a narrower win than item 3 originally implied, found by testing against each engine's own real constraints rather than assumed safe by default.
- **Item 4 is built in the reverse direction from this doc's original wording, correctly.** This doc pointed at "Step 6b's long-cue splitting" — that splitter actually belongs to Step 6c, a citation slip caught during implementation. More importantly: narration lines already arrive subtitle-sized at import time, so there was no "big TTS unit" to split into smaller cues in the first place. The real, sounder direction: **join** consecutive same-speaker lines within a paragraph into one TTS call (for better cross-sentence prosody, item 4's actual goal), then share that one clip's audio time back out across the original per-line subtitle cues using Step 6c's existing timing logic — same end result this doc described, reached without inventing a second splitter.

**Real bonus fixes, found and made in scope while building this step:**
- **A real bug, found and fixed before shipping**: Chatterbox would have handed a character with no reference clip the *previous* character's cloned voice (a stale-internal-state issue matching this doc's own "keeps the current voice loaded" finding above) — fixed as part of this branch, not left for a follow-up.
- `cli.py dub` wasn't persisting narration timing the same way the Workspace tab does — fixed in the same diff since the surrounding code was already being touched for this step's own work, not a scope-creep addition.
- Existing narrations where lines are now grouped by item 4's join-then-split-back-out logic will regenerate their clips once on the next run — a one-time, expected cost of the format change, not a bug.

**Two real, pre-existing gaps found but explicitly NOT fixed here, flagged rather than silently patched or silently ignored, per this project's own standing convention**: `emotion.suggest_tts_delivery` exists but is never called from anywhere in the app — dead code, unrelated to this step's own scope. **Separately, a real, live bug with real quality consequences**: dubbed clips are cached purely by `line_{idx:04d}.wav`, with no check against the line's actual text — editing a line's translation *after* dubbing silently keeps playing the stale, pre-edit audio against the new subtitle text. Confirmed directly (`dub.py`'s cache-path construction has no content hash at all). Real enough to need its own fix — see the new Step 11e below.

### Step 11c — Dub timing: clamped time-stretch fallback *(idea from `mazzasaverio/youtube-auto-dub`, video/audio dubbing only — not novel narration, which has no external timing to hit)*
Found while doing a full README+code pass on repos surfaced by a `github.com/topics/*` discovery search, not from a link the user supplied. Baihe's only current defence against a translated/dubbed line not fitting its original time window is `dub.rewrite_for_pacing_llm` — asking the LLM to write a shorter line. That's a good first line of defence (keeps the words natural, no audio artifacts) but has no fallback for a line that's still too long or too short after rewriting: right now that line just runs over or under with nothing correcting it further. **Re-verify against the current `dub.py` before implementing** — confirm no post-synthesis timing step already exists that this would duplicate.

1. **Add a clamped, pitch-preserving time-stretch as the fallback *after* `rewrite_for_pacing_llm`, not a replacement for it.** `youtube-auto-dub`'s `stages/synchronize.py` (MIT) was read directly: it wraps FFmpeg's `atempo` filter, computes a per-segment stretch factor as `clip_duration / window_duration`, and clamps it — capped at a `max_speedup` (its default: 1.4×, to avoid "chipmunk audio") and a `max_slowdown` floor (its default: 0.85×), skipping the stretch entirely when the factor is within 1e-3 of 1.0. Past the cap, it explicitly lets the line overflow its window rather than degrade audio quality further — the same "clean over compressed" judgment call Baihe already makes elsewhere. Baihe already shells out to ffmpeg (`video_export.py`), so this is a small addition, not a new dependency.
2. **Apply it only to video/audio dubbing (the fixed-timeline case), not novel narration** — Step 11b already establishes narration has no external timing to hit, so this fallback has nothing to correct there.
3. Keep the clamp values configurable (not hardcoded to `youtube-auto-dub`'s own defaults) — a first pass can start with the same 1.4×/0.85× figures and adjust from real dubbed output if they sound wrong.
4. **A three-state pacing indicator per line, added after a second Gemini-authored review the user shared suggested exactly this shape** ("Green: fits... Yellow: over by <15% (auto-stretched)... Red: over by >15% (requires manual edit)"). Items 1–3 already produce the data this needs — whether a line needed no stretch, was stretched within the clamp, or hit the clamp and still overflows — this item just surfaces it visibly rather than leaving it buried in a log: 🟢 fit within the window as translated, 🟡 auto-stretched within the clamp (with the applied factor shown on hover/click), 🔴 hit the clamp and still overflows, needs a manual edit or a shorter re-translation. Show this next to each line in the Dub review stage, same visual-status pattern already used elsewhere (Step 23's 🟢/🟡/🔴 source-health tracking).

**Checked and not added from the same batch of README+code passes:**
- `rockbenben/subtitle-translator` (MIT) — real, working batching/caching (per-file translation, IndexedDB caching, timing kept untouched by only ever sending dialogue text to the LLM) — but this is architecturally the same separation Baihe's own `translate_engines` already relies on, and it's a Next.js web app, not portable Python. Nothing incremental to adopt.
- `meangrinch/MangaTranslator` (Apache-2.0) — real pipeline (YOLOv8m/RT-DETR-v2/SAM detection, Manga OCR/PaddleOCR-VL, FLUX-based diffusion inpainting). Its inpainting is a genuinely more advanced technique than the LaMa-manga model Step 11 already chose, but: FLUX.1 Kontext [dev] is non-commercial-only (another license caveat to track, on top of Manga109/Llama-license ones already in this doc), FLUX.2 Klein is Apache-2.0 and clean, and either way this adds a heavy diffusion-model dependency (`diffusers`, `sdnq`, `spandrel`, a multi-GB checkpoint) for a quality gain over the already-good, much lighter LaMa-manga MIT checkpoint that hasn't been confirmed to matter in practice. Given the standing "fewer options" preference and that Step 11's inpainting is explicitly optional/opt-in already, not adding a second, heavier inpainting backend without a concrete complaint about LaMa-manga's output quality first.
- `nganlinh4/oneclick-subtitles-generator` (MIT) — broad overlap with Baihe's whole scope (transcribe → translate → voice-clone narration → styled burn-in via a native Rust renderer), but Baihe's own `video_export.burn_subtitles` already accepts the same font/color/outline styling (Step 6b just needs to wire the UI to it) — nothing new to adopt.
- `enrell/animesubs` — GPL-3.0, 8 stars. Its one interesting idea — auto-skip OP/ED/karaoke/signs/music lines before translation — is a genuinely useful feature idea for a future step, but the repo itself is too small and copyleft to be a code source; noting the idea, not adopting any code.
- `Abrechen2/sublarr` — GPL-3.0, a self-hosted *arr-ecosystem subtitle manager (library-wide automation across Sonarr/Radarr). Different product shape from Baihe's per-drama workspace; not a fit regardless of license.

**Exit:**
- A test shows a line whose synthesized clip exceeds its window by a modest amount gets sped up by a clamped factor, and one within 1e-3 of 1.0 is left untouched.
- A test shows a line needing more than the speed-up cap is capped and allowed to overflow, not force-crushed.
- A test confirms `rewrite_for_pacing_llm` still runs first, and the time-stretch only applies to whatever gap is left after that rewrite.
- A test shows each of the three pacing states (fit / auto-stretched / clamped-and-overflowing) maps to the right 🟢/🟡/🔴 indicator.
- Manual check: in the Dub review stage, confirm the indicator is visible per line and a 🟡 line shows its applied stretch factor on hover/click.

### Step 11e — Fix: a dubbed clip is cached by line index alone, so editing a line's text after dubbing silently keeps the stale audio
**Real, confirmed, live bug — found by Step 11b's own implementing session while building unrelated work, flagged rather than silently fixed since it's outside that step's own scope, and independently confirmed here before being written up.** `dub.py`'s clip-caching logic (`if not os.path.exists(clip_path): synthesize...`, the exact resumability mechanism Step 4e/11b both rely on to make a cancelled/partial run resumable) builds `clip_path` purely from the line's index — `line_{ln.idx:04d}.wav` — confirmed directly by reading the code: no hash or checksum of the line's actual text is part of the cache key anywhere. So the existing-clip-reuse behavior that makes cancellation/resumption safe (Step 4e's whole justification for treating dub generation as safe to hard-stop) has a real side effect: **if a line's translated text is edited after it's already been dubbed, the old, now-mismatched audio clip is silently reused on the next dub run**, since the file at that exact path already exists and the cache check never looks at whether the text it was generated from has changed. The exported audio then says the *old* (pre-edit) text while the exported subtitle shows the *new*, corrected one — a real correctness problem for exactly the workflow (translate, review, edit, re-dub) this app is built around.

1. **Include a content signature in the cache key**, not just the line index — e.g. a short hash of the exact text (and voice/engine choice, since those can also change) actually sent to the TTS engine, appended to or replacing the plain index in `clip_path`. A line whose text hasn't changed since its last dub still resumes/reuses cleanly (preserving Step 4e's own resumability guarantee); a line whose text *has* changed gets correctly treated as needing regeneration.
2. **Confirm this doesn't regress Step 4e's own cancel/resume exit criteria** — the fix needs to keep "an interrupted run reuses already-finished clips" working for the actual common case (nothing edited between runs), only invalidating the cache when the real inputs to synthesis have actually changed.

**Exit:**
- A test confirms dubbing a line, editing its translated text, then re-dubbing produces a *new* clip rather than reusing the stale one.
- A test confirms Step 4e's existing resumability guarantee still holds: dubbing a multi-line drama, cancelling partway through, then re-running reuses every already-finished clip whose text hasn't changed since.
- Manual check: dub a real line, correct a typo in its translation, re-run dub generation, and confirm the exported audio actually says the corrected text.

### Step 12 — GUI polish and Streamlit performance
Found by asking directly "anything else to improve — models, performance, GUI appearance?" rather than from a specific gap already on file. Independent, low-risk items — no shared code between them, grouped to keep the step count down, same pattern as Step 9b.

1. **A real visual theme, not Streamlit's default.** Checked directly: nothing in this project currently touches `.streamlit/config.toml`'s theming, so the app runs on Streamlit's stock red-accent look. Streamlit's own theming supports a light/dark pair the user can switch between in settings (`[theme]` / `[theme.dark]` in `config.toml`) — add a real palette for both (not just default-inherit), consistent with `awesome-streamlit-themes`' general pattern of a considered palette rather than the stock one (referenced for the *idea* of a deliberate palette, not its code — this is a config file, not a dependency). Purely additive, no functional risk.
2. **`@st.fragment` for the app's frequently-updated small widgets, so a keystroke doesn't rerun all of `workspace_tab.py`.** `tabs/workspace_tab.py` is 2,800+ lines (per this doc's own file map) and, on stock Streamlit, any widget interaction anywhere on the page reruns the whole script top to bottom. `@st.fragment` (stable since Streamlit 1.30) scopes a rerun to just the fragment's own block. **Re-verify against the current file before implementing** — confirm which specific widgets actually cause a visible full-page rerun lag before wrapping them; don't wrap speculatively. The most likely real candidates, based on what's already in this roadmap: Step 6b's live style preview (re-renders on every font/color/size change), Step 9b's ETA/progress display (updates on a timer, not user input, but currently forces the whole page to redraw with it), and Step 9b's bulk-series combined status line.
3. **Confirm Streamlit version headroom.** `constraints.txt` caps at `streamlit<2` (Step 1c), so Streamlit 1.63.0 (confirmed real, released September 1, 2026 — a 20% caching-layer speedup and a searchable multi-select widget for large option lists, useful for a drama with many characters/glossary terms) should already be installable without a constraints change. Just confirm the actual installed version isn't pinned lower somewhere else, and bump the dev environment if it is — this is a version check, not new code. **Confirmed during this step's build (2026-09-26): the installed version is 1.64.0** — nothing pins it lower; `requirements.txt` only asks for `>=1.49,<2`.
4. **Out of scope:** replacing Streamlit's own manual module-level model caches (`core._whisper_model_cache` etc.) with `st.cache_resource`. They already work and Baihe is single-process/local, so `st.cache_resource`'s main advantage (avoiding the multiworker-deployment cache-duplication problem) doesn't apply here — not worth the churn of touching working cache logic for no functional gain.
5. **Consistent collapsible sections, no redundant text, and consistent typography — scoped to `library_tab.py`, `scanlate_tab.py`, and `live_tab.py` only.** Prompted by the user directly asking for consistent collapsible tabs, no redundant text/buttons/areas, and consistent font sizing. **Reordering note, added on a later full-roadmap review:** this item originally also covered `workspace_tab.py`'s own inconsistencies (Step 1 using `st.subheader` instead of an expander like steps 2–10; Step 10 nested inside Step 9's expander) and a shared job-status helper — cut from here because **Step 14 replaces `workspace_tab.py`'s entire expander structure with stage tabs**, and **Step 13 builds the shared job-status component (`ui/status.py`) properly**, so fixing the old structure first would be built then immediately discarded. Reader (`reader_tab.py`), Settings, Diagnostics, and Navigator/Discover are similarly rebuilt by Steps 15–18 — their consistency work belongs there, not here (see the explicit callback added to each of those steps). What's left for *this* step: apply the same collapsible-section consistency and redundant-text audit to the three tabs the redesign doesn't otherwise touch — check each for a bare/generic expander label, a copy-pasted status block, or a section that should be an expander but isn't, and fix what's actually found (don't assume the same problems exist here just because they did in `workspace_tab.py` — verify each file directly first).
6. **A real typographic scale for these three tabs, using the same figures Step 13 later canonizes for the rest of the app**: 16–18px body text, ~1.25 modular scale for heading-size steps (current 2026 web-typography guidance, confirmed directly, not from memory) — so `library_tab.py`/`scanlate_tab.py`/`live_tab.py` aren't visually inconsistent with the rest of the app once Step 13 lands. Keep caption wording tone consistent too (length, whether it ends with a period, "--" vs. an em dash).
7. **Live subtitles in Reader & Watch's video player, for in-UI QC**, at the user's request ("can the video viewer show subs playing in real time so I can QC easier"). Confirmed directly: `tabs/reader_tab.py`'s "▶️ Watch / listen" block already calls `st.video(p)` on the drama's original video with no `subtitles=` argument, and Streamlit's own `st.video` API genuinely supports one — it takes a string/bytes/`Path`/`io.BytesIO` of raw SRT or VTT content directly (not just a file path), or a `dict` of `{label: content}` for multiple switchable tracks shown via the browser's native CC menu (confirmed against Streamlit's own docs, not assumed). Baihe already has everything needed to build this with no new dependency: `core.lines_to_srt(lines, field=...)` and `core.lines_to_bilingual_srt(lines, ...)` both exist and already produce valid SRT strings (used today for subtitle export). Wire the video call to `st.video(p, subtitles={"Source": lines_to_srt(rlines, rlang), "English": lines_to_srt(rlines, "en"), "Bilingual": lines_to_bilingual_srt(rlines)})`, built from the page's current in-session `rlines` (not a stale export file) so edits made in Workspace show up on next Reader-tab load without a separate export step. **Only offer tracks for languages that actually have content** (skip a language whose lines are all empty, same spirit as Step 1d's "don't offer what can't work" pattern) — check this directly against the drama's current translation state, don't assume both are filled. Audio-only dramas can't use this (`st.audio` has no subtitles parameter) — this only applies when `media_path[0] == "video"`.

### Step 12b — Auto QC pass: factual-detail check tied into the existing rollback UI
Added from a 20-item feature-brainstorm pass, checked directly against real source before proposing anything (3 items already covered, 12 partial, 5 real gaps — recorded in full in §6). This step is the actual substance of the brainstorm's "Auto QC with rollback/compare/preview" ask. **The rollback/compare half is already solid and shouldn't be rebuilt**: `db.save_line_history_snapshot`/`list_line_history`/`get_line_history_snapshot` are wired into a real "🕓 Version history / undo" UI (`workspace_tab.py` ~2983–3008) with auto-snapshots before destructive ops (force-retranslate, merge) and undo-the-undo. What's missing is a check that actually finds problems — `core.diagnose_line_coverage` only flags ASR-side issues (long lines, silence gaps, blank fields), never translation correctness.

1. **A factual-detail check**: compare each line's source (`ln.zh`/source language) against its translation (`ln.en`) for numbers, dates, names (reusing the existing character/glossary name list so it isn't guessing), currency amounts, and units of measurement. Flag a line where a token of one of these kinds appears in the source but not, in any recognizable form (transliteration/conversion allowed — a check needs some tolerance for "100 yuan" becoming "about $14", not a strict re-appearance requirement), in the translation — and the reverse (a number/date/etc. that appears in the translation but wasn't in the source, which usually means a hallucination, not a legitimate conversion).
2. **Surface flags through the existing flag mechanism** (`ln.flag`/`ln.flag_note`), same as every other flag source in the app, so Auto QC results show up in the same review queue as manually-flagged lines rather than a separate list.
3. **Run it as an opt-in pass** (a button, not automatic on every translation — this is a real LLM/regex-hybrid cost, not free), with results reviewable against the *existing* version-history UI: a flagged line shows its source/translation side by side (compare), and "Restore previous version" already works if the fix means reverting rather than re-editing (preview is the existing side-by-side, not a new component).
4. **Re-verify before implementing**: confirm exactly what `ln.flag_note` currently holds for other flag sources (Step 6b's CPS-density check, `core.diagnose_line_coverage`) so Auto QC's messages follow the same format rather than inventing a second convention.

**Exit:**
- A test shows a translated line missing a number/date/name/currency/unit present in the source gets flagged with a note naming what's missing.
- A test shows a translated line containing a number not present in the source (a likely hallucination) also gets flagged.
- A test shows a line whose numbers/dates/names/currency/units are all correctly carried over does not get flagged.
- Manual check: run Auto QC on a real drama, confirm flagged lines appear in the normal review queue, and that reverting one via the existing Version history UI works as it does for any other line.

**Built and pushed (`claude/step-12b-roadmap-1j48e1`), reviewed and approved — a real, well-designed factual-detail checker, with an initially-alarming test-count discrepancy fully resolved rather than dismissed.** `auto_qc.py`'s detection logic is genuinely tolerant of legitimate conversions (a CJK numeral run, word-form numbers, month/weekday names, "any money amount"/"any measurement" carried over rather than an exact match) exactly as the roadmap's own tolerance language specifies, and correctly reuses `translate_engines.SYSTEM_FLAG_REASONS`/the existing `ln.flag`/`flag_note` mechanism rather than inventing a second one. First run showed a large gap against this session's own test count (1950 vs. the report's 2139) — bigger than any prior discrepancy this session had caught, so it wasn't waved through. Investigated jointly with the implementing session: the real cause was optional-package availability (`opencv-python`, `jieba`, `genanki`) gating whole test files at collection time, not run results — independently confirmed by installing those exact packages and watching this session's own collected-test count move from 2000 to 2201, precisely matching the affected files' combined size. A real, mechanical explanation, not a reporting error. Approved.

**Built and merged, PR #86 — confirmed directly via the GitHub API (`merged: true`, CI green) and re-verified by the planning session directly against the current `baihe-subtitler` tip (`test_auto_qc.py`: 49 passed).** The PR's own description independently corroborates the earlier test-count investigation from this session's side: it confirms the "2139 passed" figure was two separate runs added together (a full run, then 4 more after installing `huggingface_hub`), not a single run, and separately traces ~25 of the ~183-test gap to `opencv-python` alone. Also wired up Step 12e's previously-disabled "Auto QC before export" checkbox as part of this step, since its own help text promised it would start working once this check existed — a small, justified scope extension, not silent drift.

### Step 12c — Workspace media preview & review linkage
Added from the same brainstorm pass. Reader tab already solves the harder half of this (`reader.py`'s click-to-seek: `data-start`, a "▶ Play from here" button, active-line highlighting from `player.currentTime`) — this step is scoped to Workspace specifically, where **no player exists at all** tied to Review & edit; only an on-demand isolated clip per line (Step 21's re-transcribe popover).

1. **A persistent, seekable player in Workspace's Review & edit section**, reusing the same audio/video source Reader already plays (no new media-serving code) rather than the isolated-clip-per-line approach.
2. **Selecting a row in the review table seeks the player** to that line's `start` timestamp — reusing Reader's own `seekTo`-style JS mechanism (`reader.py`) rather than inventing a second one.
3. **A typed-timestamp jump box** (doesn't exist anywhere in the app today, confirmed by grep) — type `mm:ss` or a raw seconds value, jump the player there.
4. **"Play current segment"**: play just `[ln.start, ln.end]` and stop, not the whole file from that point — useful for repeatedly re-checking one line's timing without manually pausing.
5. **An on-demand short burned-subtitle preview clip** (lower priority — real `ffmpeg` cost per use, so make it an explicit button, not automatic): burn the current style settings over a short real clip (a few seconds around the selected line) rather than Step 6b's static styled-text mockup, so the user can see how it actually looks over real video before a full export. Audio-only dramas skip this (nothing to burn subtitles over).
6. **SFX/non-verbal cue marker** (a small, real gap found in the same brainstorm pass, confirmed zero existing handling anywhere in code or roadmap for subtitle-side SFX like `[door slams]`): a per-line toggle marking a line as a non-verbal cue, rendered bracketed and styled distinctly (not as ordinary dialogue) in export — reuses the existing per-line flag/style plumbing rather than a new line type.

**Exit:**
- A test shows the typed-timestamp box parses both `mm:ss` and raw-seconds input and seeks correctly.
- A test shows "Play current segment" stops at `ln.end`, not the file's end.
- Manual check: selecting a row in Review & edit visibly seeks the player; the burned-preview button produces a short clip whose captions match the currently-selected style settings.
- A test shows a line marked as an SFX/non-verbal cue exports bracketed and distinctly styled rather than as ordinary dialogue.

Merging current `baihe-subtitler` in produces a real conflict in `subtitle_formats.py`/`_subtitle_style_controls`: **Step 6i's own opt-in `notes_as_separate_line` toggle and this step's unconditional "Notes"/"SFX" ASS styling are two independently-built, overlapping solutions to rendering notes as their own line** — built in parallel because this branch wasn't rebased before starting, and now needing real reconciliation (does the toggle survive, does it gate the new styling, or does something else give) rather than a trivial textual merge. Separately, **item 2 (row-selection seeking) was not built the way this step specifies**: rather than reusing Reader's actual JS `seekTo` mechanism (`reader.py`'s data-URI-based component, capped at 10 minutes), the branch built a second, parallel mechanism — native `st.video`/`st.audio` re-seeked via `session_state` + a forced rerun. It works and is honestly described (not misrepresented as JS reuse), and there's a plausible reason (Reader's approach caps at 10 minutes, impractical for a full episode) — but that tradeoff was never surfaced or justified against the roadmap's explicit instruction, so it needs a decision, not a silent pass. Items 1, 3, 4, 5, 6 and their tests were independently verified as genuinely built. The reported test count ("1735 passed, 53 skipped") also didn't match a real clean run (**1737 passed, 55 skipped** — a small, non-alarming discrepancy, likely environment-dependent optional-package availability, unlike the earlier 1725-vs-1899 case). **Both issues resolved by the implementing session (2026-09-26), independently re-verified by the planning session — clean now, just needs a rebase before a PR.** A new commit on the same branch: dropped this step's own unconditional "Notes" ASS styling entirely in favor of Step 6i's `notes_as_separate_line` toggle (kept as the one mechanism, off by default, notes stay inline unless the toggle is on — genuine reconciliation, not a silent override), and added `sfx_alignment`/`notes_alignment` position controls that layer on top without conflicting. For the seek-mechanism question, added an explicit, specific rationale to `_render_review_player`'s own docstring for not using Reader's `seekTo`/data-URI mechanism: it's audio-only (no video), re-runs ffmpeg on every render, and Streamlit re-sends the whole iframe HTML every rerun (stated as measured: an unchanged ~4MB embed re-sent on each of three reruns) — costly on a section that reruns on every line edit. This is a real, specific technical justification, not a hand-wave; the ~4MB re-send figure itself wasn't independently re-measured by the planning session, but the underlying architectural claim (Reader's mechanism re-embeds media as a data URI per render) checks out against `reader.py`. **Independently re-verified by the planning session**: fetched the branch fresh, confirmed the notes/SFX conflict is genuinely gone (a real trial merge of the current `baihe-subtitler` — which now also includes Steps 25 and the 23/23b source-adapter work — auto-merges cleanly with no conflicts), and ran the tests on that merged tree directly: `test_media_preview.py` (54 passed), combined with `test_workspace_tab.py` (227 passed/4 skipped), and the full suite (**1901 passed, 56 skipped, 0 failed**) — no regressions, Step 25's own new tests and this step's coexist with no interference. **Built and merged, PR #77 — confirmed directly via the GitHub API (`merged: true`, head `claude/media-preview-player-x3udcb` rebased onto the current `baihe-subtitler` tip including Steps 6i/dub-cluster/23/23b/25, single green "test" check run, no review comments, +724/-28 across 10 files).** Re-verified by this session against the actual PR head commit (not just the earlier trial merge): full suite **1901 passed, 56 skipped, 0 failed**, matching the trial-merge numbers exactly. One honest caveat surfaced in the PR's own description: Streamlit's player only supports whole-second seek precision, so "Play current segment" stops within a second after the line's real end rather than exactly at it — never cuts a line short, and Step 21's own per-line clip player still gives exact-range playback as an alternative. A pre-existing, unrelated gap was also noted (Reader errors when the optional `jieba` package isn't installed, already contained by `_safe_render`) — not caused by this step, not fixed here, left for whoever picks it up.

### Step 12d — Scanlate: structured regions, OCR cleanup, batch processing, honorifics, SFX handling
Added from the same brainstorm pass, all scoped to Scanlate (`scanlate.py`/`tabs/scanlate_tab.py`). **The most important finding here: `classify_text_regions()` (bubble/narration/sign/sfx/thought classification, with real bbox/confidence from detection already available) is fully written but dead code — never called from `scanlate_tab.py`.** Most of this step is wiring already-written logic in, not building new detection.

1. **Wire `classify_text_regions()` into the real pipeline**, and represent a detected region as one structured object — bbox, reading order, detected language, confidence, text orientation (vertical/horizontal — not currently tracked anywhere, needs adding), page/panel id (reusing `detect_panels()`, currently unwired to bubbles), and region type (from the now-wired classifier) — instead of today's scattered per-function fields.
2. **OCR cleanup**: make the OCR'd source text editable before translation runs on it (today `scanlate_tab.py` shows it as a read-only `st.caption`) — same "fix garbage in before it propagates" principle Workspace already applies to the ASR transcript review step.
3. **Shape-aware text fitting**: `render_text_in_box` already does real auto-shrink-to-fit, but explicitly rectangle-only per its own docstring ("no vertical CJK rendering — that's koharu's specialty"). Extend fitting to respect the bubble's actual (often oval/irregular) shape where the mask/contour is already available from detection, rather than its bounding rectangle. Full vertical-CJK typesetting stays out of scope here — that's Step 11 item 3's optional koharu integration, a bigger, separate undertaking.
4. **Batch detect+OCR+translate across a chapter's saved pages**, reusing the same per-page functions in a loop — today "📦 Bulk render all pages" already batches the *render* step, but detect+OCR+translate only runs on the currently-selected single page.
5. **Wire the glossary into Scanlate's own translate call.** Confirmed: `scanlate.translate_page_with_context` builds its prompt from bubble text + prior-page context only — it never reads `glossary_terms` at all, even though the `category` field already supports "honorific" and Workspace's own translation prompt already uses it. Read the same glossary lookup Workspace uses, don't build a second honorific system.
6. **SFX skip-by-default**: once item 1 wires the classifier in, a region tagged `kind="sfx"` should not go through the same auto-inpaint-and-replace flow as dialogue bubbles by default (the classifier's own docstring already notes "SFX often shouldn't be touched — the lettering IS the art") — flag it for manual review instead, with a per-region override to include it in the automated pass if the user wants to.

**Exit:**
- A test shows a detected region carries bbox/reading-order/language/confidence/orientation/panel-id/type as one structured object.
- A test shows editing OCR'd source text before running translate changes what gets sent to the translation call.
- A test shows fitting text into a non-rectangular bubble mask respects the mask shape, not just the bounding box, on a synthetic oval-bubble test case.
- A test shows running batch processing on a chapter's saved pages runs detect+OCR+translate on every page, not just the selected one.
- A test shows a glossary honorific term is actually applied in a Scanlate translation output.
- A test shows an `sfx`-classified region is skipped by the automated inpaint-and-replace pass by default, and included when the per-region override is set.
- Manual check: on a real comic page with sound effects, confirm SFX text is left alone by default while dialogue bubbles are translated normally.

Add a real per-drama (and per-series, for cross-drama consistency within a series — reusing the same series-level pattern as glossary/character data) multi-line instructions field, feeding `build_llm_instructions` alongside (not replacing) the existing style-note default.
2. **Draft / Standard / Release starting presets**, bundling engine choice + Step 7's reflect-mode toggle + Step 12b's new Auto QC pass into one selectable tier (e.g. Draft: fast/cheap engine, no reflect, no Auto QC; Release: best engine, reflect on, Auto QC run automatically before export) — distinct from Step 9c's existing per-project value-bundle preset, which stays as the mechanism for saving a *customized* set of values; these three are just sensible starting points layered on top of it, not a replacement.

### Step 13 — UI foundation: shared components and a unified project-state model
Prompted by the user's request for a full information-architecture audit and redesign, not just visual polish ("Make the UI consistent with collapsible tabs... I want you to rethink the application's information architecture and workflow while preserving all existing functionality"). This is Phase 1–2 of that request: the audit itself, and the scaffolding the rest of the redesign (Steps 14–19) builds on — no visible behavior change in this step.

**Audit, confirmed via direct `git show origin/baihe-subtitler:...` reads, not assumed:**
- `app.py` renders 8 flat top-level tabs via one `st.tabs([...])` call, each its own file: Library (302 lines), Workspace (2,899), Read & Watch/`reader_tab.py` (445), Scanlate (319), Navigator (76), Discover (267), Live (115), Diagnostics (363). `settings_tab.py` (184) renders in the sidebar.
- **Organized by feature, not by workflow.** Navigator (a site-navigation helper for finding a title on official platforms) and Discover (search/import titles) are both "find content to import" but are separate top-level tabs. Reader stacks 7 largely-unrelated sections vertically in one page: Watch/listen player → series glossary → "Story tools" → "Universe wiki" → "Line tools" (per-line fix/re-transcribe) → "My notes" → "Vocabulary export" → "Ask about this drama" (Q&A).
- **Duplicated "current project" concept, confirmed:** `st.session_state.active_drama_id` is the app-wide "current drama" pointer, but `reader_tab.py` keeps its own separate `reader_drama_pick` selectbox with dedicated reconciliation code (`reader_resume_pending`/`reader_resume_banner`) just to stay in sync when the user arrives via a "Resume" click from Library. Two sources of truth for the same thing.
- **Duplicated information display, confirmed:** API keys are shown/editable in `settings_tab.py`'s "API keys & endpoints" expander, and shown *again*, read-only, in `diagnostics_tab.py`'s "API keys (from Settings)" section.
- **Session state is moderately, not wildly, fragmented** — confirmed ~34 distinct top-level `st.session_state.*` keys app-wide via a full-app grep, not hundreds. The "feels disconnected" complaint is mostly an information-architecture/layout problem, not raw state sprawl — though the `active_drama_id`/`reader_drama_pick` split above is a real state-model instance of it.
- **Diagnostics is a kitchen sink:** setup checks, running jobs, a log viewer, an accuracy-benchmark tool, a "danger zone" (destructive full-library reset), core requirements, project files, API keys (duplicate, see above), and dependency tiers — 9 unrelated concerns in one flat page.
- **Settings already has the right shape to build on:** grouped labeled expanders (Reading experience / Offline / OCR / Performance / Defaults / API keys) — close to a common/advanced split already, just needs the settings currently scattered into other tabs consolidated in, and a real common/advanced split applied.
- **No shared "where am I in the pipeline" indicator anywhere**, and no persistent status while navigating between tabs.
- **On UI inspiration from previously-reviewed GitHub repos** (the user asked directly): checked what's actually reusable — almost all of the repos surveyed this project are Gradio, React/Next.js, Tauri/Rust, or CLI-first (MangaTranslator/Gradio, oneclick-subtitles-generator/Rust+React, animesubs/Tauri, sublarr/React) — none share Streamlit's component model, so there's no code to port. What is directly applicable and Streamlit-native: `awesome-streamlit-themes`/`Paldom/streamlit-custom-style` for the visual system (already Step 12 item 1's job), and Streamlit's own `st.tabs`/`st.expander`/`st.popover`/`st.dialog`/`st.status` primitives, which this redesign is built from. The actual inspiration here is architectural (workflow-stage IA, project-centric state, one primary action per screen), not lifted code, since no reviewed repo shares the stack.

1. **New `ui/` component layer** (mirrors the user's own suggested shape, adapted to what actually exists):
   - `ui/project_header.py` — a compact, always-visible header: project name, pipeline-progress indicator, settings shortcut — reading from the unified project-state model (item 2 below) instead of ad-hoc `active_drama_id` lookups scattered per tab.
   - `ui/workflow.py` — the pipeline-stage stepper/status indicator (✓ done / ● current / ○ not started per stage), reusable in Workspace's header and in Home/Library's per-project list.
   - `ui/status.py` — the rich background-job status block. This *is* the shared helper Step 12 item 6 already calls for around the copy-pasted transcription/translation status code — build it once here, Step 12 and every later step reuse it rather than it being built twice. **Also covers the failure case**: a friendly error card (what failed, in plain words; a `[Retry]` action where retrying is actually safe; the raw exception/traceback behind a collapsed "Advanced details" section, not shown by default) — not a separate component, the same status block's failure state.
   - Existing business logic (`core.py`, `translate_engines.py`, `dub.py`, `scanlate.py`, etc.) is untouched — this layer only changes how the UI calls into them.
2. **Unified project-state model.** Introduce one coherent `st.session_state.project` holder carrying `drama_id`, `current_stage`, per-stage status, selected segment/line, active background job, recent errors/warnings — replacing the `active_drama_id`/`reader_drama_pick` split with one source of truth every tab reads from. Narrowly-scoped keys (reader display prefs, settings keys, widget-local keys) stay exactly as they are — this only consolidates *project-identity* state, not every session-state key in the app.
3. **A shared typographic scale, defined once here.** One size/weight for a top-level step/stage label, one for a sub-section label, one for body/caption text (16–18px base, ~1.25 modular scale for the step above it — the same figures already researched for Step 12's original theme work). Steps 14–18 each apply this as they rebuild their own tab, instead of each rebuild inventing its own header/caption styling from scratch.
4. **Close the "Home" gap.** Earlier drafting of this redesign referred to a "Home" concept for showing current project/recent dramas/processing status at a glance, but it was never turned into an actual item — Library's existing dashboard (`tabs/library_tab.py`'s "📊 Dashboard"/"▶️ Continue"/"🕓 Recently active" sections) already covers most of this ground. Concretely: wire `ui/workflow.py`'s pipeline-stage stepper (item 1 above) into Library's dashboard so each drama's row shows real per-stage progress (✓/●/○) at a glance, not just the existing percent-complete metric — reusing the same component Workspace's header uses (Step 14), not a second implementation of the same idea.
5. **Re-verify this audit against the current files before starting** — Steps 1e through 12 may have already changed `workspace_tab.py` and others by the time this step is picked up; confirm the line numbers and structure above still hold, and note what's changed if not.

**Exit:**
- The app runs identically to before this step — no tab's visible behavior changes yet.
- A test shows `ui/project_header.py`, `ui/workflow.py`, and `ui/status.py` render correctly in isolation against a fake project-state fixture.
- A test shows `ui/status.py`'s failure state shows a plain-language reason and hides the raw traceback behind "Advanced details" by default.
- A test shows the new `st.session_state.project` model round-trips `drama_id`/`current_stage` correctly and that reading/writing it doesn't touch any of the narrowly-scoped keys listed above.
- Manual check: Library's dashboard shows each drama's real per-stage progress via the shared stepper component, not just the existing percent-complete metric.

The single biggest change in this redesign — replaces Workspace's originally-audited 2,899-line, 10-`st.expander` vertical scroll (confirmed in Step 12/13's audits: Step 1 breaks the expander pattern, Step 10 is mis-nested inside Step 9) with a stage-based workspace. **Needs Step 13's `ui/` layer and project-state model.**

The doubling is almost entirely inside numbered section **7 ("📝 Review & edit"), now ~1,225 lines on its own** (lines 4038–5263 on the current file), because roughly a dozen later steps added real sub-features inside it that the original Step 12/13 audits never accounted for: find & replace, a line-coverage check, a dubbing-pacing check, a translation-consistency check, the flagged-lines review queue, emotional-register detection, adaptive style, translation-version comparison, translation notes, merge-adjacent-lines, meaning-based re-segmentation, and version history/undo — each already its own `st.expander` inside section 7. **The core 10-section → 7-stage-tab mapping below is still structurally intact** (verified by walking the real file's own `st.expander`/`st.subheader` calls, not assumed) — this is a scope-size correction, not a design-invalidating one: section 7's dozen sub-features all still map cleanly onto stage tab **Review**, they're just numerous enough that Review's own tab will need its own internal grouping (most plausibly nested `st.expander`s or a `st.popover` for the less-common checks, consistent with item 3 below), not a flat list of a dozen top-level controls. 1. **Stage navigation via `st.tabs`** inside Workspace: Source / Transcript / Diarize / Translate / Review / Dub / Export, each tab holding only that stage's controls — mapping directly onto the current numbered steps (1 Choose-drama+2 Content-source → Source; 3 Reference-novel+recognition-settings folds into Source or Transcript as appropriate; 4 Diarization → Diarize; 5 Translation → Translate; 6 Characters/voices → Translate or its own sub-tab; 7 Review/edit → Review; 8 AI dub → Dub; 9+10 Export → Export, fixing the mis-nesting so Export's video and subtitle exports are true siblings, not one nested inside the other).
