Fix as part of this step's typography pass (item 3 below): render as a real table (`st.dataframe`/`st.table`, three columns: name, version/status, source link) instead of a caption loop — a table gives natural alignment and scannability a stack of identically-styled caption lines can't, and groups "not installed" rows visually distinct from real version numbers without extra styling work. **Two specific fixes, at the user's direct request from a real screenshot of this exact panel (2026-09-26):**
   - **Hyperlink the model's own name, not the raw URL text.** Today's markdown produces `**Whisper (faster-whisper)**: `1.2.1` — [https://github.com/SYSTRAN/faster-whisper](https://github.com/SYSTRAN/faster-whisper)` — the full URL is spelled out in the visible text as well as the link target, doubling the visual noise item 2 already flagged. Change to `[**{name}**]({url})` (or the table equivalent: the name cell itself is the link) so the URL is still one hover/click away but never printed out in full.
   - **Give every row a consistent visual "installed vs. not" signal, not just differently-worded text.** Confirmed via `diagnostics.get_model_engine_versions()` directly: an installed "package"-kind entry's `version` is a real version string (`importlib.metadata.version(...)`), a "repo"-kind entry's `version` is its Hugging Face repo id(s) (also effectively "installed," just versioned differently), and a genuinely-missing package's `version` is the literal string `"not installed"` — three different value shapes in the same field, styled identically today (plain `st.caption`, no color or icon logic anywhere in the render loop). Add a real installed/not-installed boolean the render step branches on (not a string match against `"not installed"`, which is fragile if that literal ever changes) — a ✅/version-number pairing for installed rows (package *or* repo kind both count as installed) and a ✗ with `"not installed"` styled in a clearly muted/non-affirmative color (e.g. Streamlit's own gray secondary-text color, explicitly not green — green anywhere on this row was never meant to signal "missing," confirmed nothing in the current code intentionally colors it, so any perceived green is Streamlit's own markdown/theme default, not a deliberate signal to preserve) for not-installed rows, so the two states are scannable at a glance rather than requiring reading the word itself.
3. **GPU/VRAM live display, confirmed genuinely missing.** Checked the whole app directly — no `nvidia-smi`/`torch.cuda.memory_allocated`/`pynvml` usage anywhere, despite `torch` already being a dependency for every GPU-touching stage. For a local-GPU-dependent app, a simple current-usage readout (GPU name, VRAM used/total, current model occupying it) is worth adding to Diagnostics' routine-checks view — `torch.cuda.get_device_properties`/`torch.cuda.memory_allocated` cover this without a new dependency; fall back to "GPU info unavailable" cleanly when CUDA isn't present rather than erroring. **Extended on a later pass, prompted by a Gemini-authored architecture review the user shared flagging "PyTorch version mismatches, CUDA dependencies" as a setup bottleneck.** `diagnostics.py` already checks ffmpeg is on PATH and reports which optional Python packages are installed (`OPTIONAL_DEPENDENCIES`, confirmed real), but nothing reports whether the installed `torch` build's CUDA version actually matches what the GPU driver supports — a torch/CUDA mismatch is a real, common setup failure this app can't fully prevent (that's what `pip install torch` from PyTorch's own site-specific index exists to solve) but can at least surface clearly instead of leaving the user with a cryptic runtime error. Add `torch.version.cuda` (what torch was built against) alongside `torch.cuda.is_available()`'s own result to this same panel, and when CUDA is unavailable despite an NVIDIA GPU being present (detectable via `nvidia-smi` on PATH), show a specific "torch was installed without matching CUDA support — reinstall following pytorch.org's own selector for your driver" message rather than a bare "GPU info unavailable."
4. **Keyword filter on the existing log view.** Checked directly: `applog.tail(50)` just dumps the last 50 raw log lines with no filtering. Not a structured-logging rewrite (that would touch every log call site across the app for a benefit this single-user local app doesn't clearly need) — just a text filter box over what's already there, so finding "what happened with drama X" doesn't mean reading 50 lines by eye.
5. **Use Step 13's typographic scale and give each regrouped section a specific label**, same reasoning as Step 14 item 6.
6. **Make Diagnostics' own sections collapsible too, at the user's direct request — same pattern as Discover (Step 17 item 1), Library (Step 22 item 5), and Read & Watch (Step 15).** Wrap each regrouped section in `st.expander`, defaulting the routine-health-checks group (Check my setup, Running jobs, Model & engine versions) open and the less-frequently-needed ones (Downloaded model cache, the accuracy-benchmark tool, and especially the danger-zone reset — already moved behind its own sub-section by this step's main goal) collapsed by default, so a routine visit doesn't require scrolling past everything else first.
7. **Item 3's torch/CUDA-mismatch message, confirmed as a live, real problem on the user's own machine (2026-09-26), not just a hypothetical.** The user has a confirmed real NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080 Ti (12GB VRAM, driver reports CUDA 13.3) — but a real pasted error trace showed their installed `torch` is `2.13.0+cpu`, the CPU-only build, despite the GPU being present and otherwise idle. Traced why directly: `requirements.txt` pins `torchaudio>=2.0` and `constraints.txt` caps `torch<3`/`torchaudio<3`, but nothing anywhere in `requirements-install.bat` or `start.bat` ever passes PyTorch's own `--index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu<version>` — a bare `pip install torch` on Windows always resolves to the CPU-only wheel from PyPI's default index, silently, with no error and no warning. This is a real install-time gap, one level upstream of item 3's diagnostics-panel message (which only surfaces the mismatch *after* it's already happened): `requirements-install.bat` should detect an NVIDIA GPU (`nvidia-smi` on PATH, same detection item 3 already uses) *before* installing torch, and when found, install from the matching CUDA index instead of the plain PyPI wheel — turning a silent, easy-to-miss footgun into a working GPU install by default for anyone who actually has the hardware for it. Confirmed this is exactly why the user's vocal-separation and diarization runs have been slow (see Step 4g) — not a bug in either of those, just unused hardware. **For anyone already on a CPU-only build today** (this app-level install-time fix only helps future fresh installs) — see Step 18c item 6's one-click "Install GPU PyTorch" Diagnostics button, the same underlying reinstall exposed as an in-app action instead of a manual terminal command. **Resolved on the user's own machine (2026-09-26).** The manual `cu128` command (corrected from an initial `cu124` attempt that failed outright — no Python 3.14 wheels on that index, see the correction above) was run directly, and — after a separate follow-up `torchvision` version-mismatch warning (`torchvision 0.28.0 requires torch==2.13.0`, resolved by reinstalling `torch`+`torchaudio`+`torchvision` together from the same `cu128` index so pip picked a matched set: `torch 2.11.0+cu128` / `torchvision 0.26.0+cu128`) — the user confirmed via a direct `torch.cuda.is_available()` check: `2.11.0+cu128 True NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080 Ti`. Real, live confirmation that this fix works end-to-end, not just in theory; the remaining open items are the in-app one-click version (Step 18c item 6) and the install-time default fix (this item, item 7) for anyone else who hits the same CPU-only-by-default gap.

### Step 18b — App Assistant: point to the real setting, or say so and hand off a report
At the user's direct request, prompted by a real pattern repeated across this session: they'd describe something they wanted to do or thought might be broken ("can Save as preset not be hidden in Translation," "where is speech-splitting sensitivity," "subtitles appear before the speaker sometimes"), and each time it took a manual grep of the real source to find the actual UI location or confirm/rule out a real bug. The user asked for an in-app version of exactly that process, modeled on the existing "💬 Ask about this drama" Q&A (`qa.py`'s `ask_about_drama`, `reader_tab.py`) but scoped to the app itself.

Checked `qa.ask_about_drama`'s real mechanism before designing anything: a single LLM call, grounded in real context passed into the prompt (the drama's own transcript lines, capped at `max_lines`), with an explicit system-prompt instruction not to invent details the context doesn't cover — the same "grounded, say 'don't know' rather than guess" discipline `metadata_lookup.extract_metadata_llm`'s "use null for anything not found" already establishes elsewhere in this app. The one real design problem specific to this feature: what grounds it. A hand-maintained "here's what settings exist" document would drift out of sync with the UI exactly the way this roadmap's own §5 rule 1 discipline exists to prevent for git/PR state. Checked whether a "contact developer" channel already exists (`README.md`, no issue tracker/contact link found) — this is a personal-use, two-Claude-session project (planning + implementing), so "escalate" here realistically means handing the user a structured report to paste into one of those sessions, not a public support channel. The existing "📋 Copy diagnostics for support" button (`diagnostics_tab.py`) already builds exactly that kind of redacted report.

1. **New module `app_help.py`** (parallel to `qa.py`), `ask_about_app(question, engine, chat_history=None)`.
2. **Grounding, generated from the app's own real structure, never hand-maintained prose.** Walk every `tabs/*_tab.py` module's real `st.subheader`/`st.expander` calls and their adjacent `st.caption`/`help=` text via a small introspection helper (regex or `ast`-based extraction over each module's source), regenerated from the real files every time it's used — this produces the same kind of grounding context `ask_about_drama` gets from the transcript, but for "where is X" and "does this setting exist" questions.
3. **System prompt, same discipline as `qa.ask_about_drama`/`metadata_lookup.extract_metadata_llm`**: answer only from the real section/setting list provided; if nothing plausibly matches, say so plainly — never invent a setting name or location that isn't in the grounding context. This is the one non-negotiable behavior: a wrong-but-confident pointer to a nonexistent setting is worse than an honest "I don't see one."
4. **When it can't answer (or the pointed-to setting didn't fix the issue)**: offer a "📋 Copy a report for the developer" action extending `diagnostics_tab.py`'s existing redacted-report builder with this question/answer exchange — one structured paste-able block (question asked, what the assistant found or didn't, redacted diagnostics), not a vague "contact support."
5. **UI**: same chat pattern as "Ask about this drama" (`st.chat_input`/`st.chat_message`, per-session history in `st.session_state`), placed in Diagnostics near "Copy diagnostics for support" — cross-cutting (about the app, not one drama), same natural home as "something's wrong, help me sort it out."

**Exit:**
- A test confirms the grounding context is built from a real, current fixture of tab-module source (not a hardcoded string) — a section added to a fixture module shows up in the grounding context without any change to `app_help.py` itself.
- A test confirms the system prompt causes the engine to decline rather than answer when asked about a setting that doesn't exist in the grounding context (mocked engine returning a plausible-sounding but fabricated answer should be caught by the prompt's own instruction, verified via a fixture question with no real match).
- Manual check: ask it a real "where is X" question for a setting that exists, confirm it points to the correct real location; ask an unanswerable question, confirm it says so honestly and offers the report-copy action instead of guessing.

### Step 18c — In-app Install buttons for optional dependencies
At the user's direct request ("If the app is already running, how can I easily install [audio-separator, demucs], or anything else in the future?") — today that means opening a separate terminal, activating the venv by hand, running `pip install`, and reloading. Checked `diagnostics.py` before designing anything: `OPTIONAL_DEPENDENCIES` is already a real, maintained dict of every optional package the app can use — `{pip_package_name: (import_name, feature_description, tier)}` — confirmed the dict **key is already the real pip install name** in every entry (e.g. `"audio-separator": ("audio_separator", "...", "feature")`, hyphenated pip name vs. underscored import name, already kept straight). This is exactly the data an install button needs — no new mapping to invent, a real action wired onto data that already exists, same "data already exists, no UI surface" pattern Step 22's series-sharing gap found.

1. In Diagnostics' "🧩 Model & engine versions" panel, add a small **"Install"** button next to every entry whose `tier` is `"feature"` or `"engine"` (never `"required"` or `"dev"`) that's currently reported not-installed.
2. Clicking it runs `pip install <the real dict key>` as a subprocess against the **venv's own `python -m pip`**, not a bare system `pip` — reuse whatever path-resolution `start.bat`/`portable.py` already use to find the venv's interpreter. Stream output into a `st.status`/expander (same "show real progress, don't just spin" discipline already used elsewhere in this app) so a failure is visible, not silently swallowed.
3. After a successful install, re-run the same version-detection check and refresh the row in place — no full app restart required, and this covers "anything else in the future" by construction, since it reads the same real dict every other optional dependency already lives in, not a hardcoded list.
4. **Explicitly out of scope**: uninstalling, upgrading, or version-pinning from this UI — install-only.
5. **A real failure mode worth documenting plainly, not glossed over**: confirmed live during this session — `pip install audio-separator` failed on the user's actual machine with a genuine build error (`diffq-fixed`'s Cython build: `'bitpack.pyx' doesn't match any files`), a broken/incomplete source distribution on PyPI, not a bug in this app. The install button must surface the real pip error text (per item 2's streamed output), not swallow it into a generic "install failed" — this is exactly the scenario that finding validates. **Separately, a real setup-guidance gap found from the same incident**: `README.md` states "Python 3.9+" with no upper bound, while CI itself pins `3.11` and the user's real environment is Python 3.14 — new enough that several packages (this `diffq-fixed` case included) don't yet ship prebuilt wheels for it, forcing a source build that can fail this way. Worth a README correction recommending a specific, wheel-covered version (matching whatever CI actually tests against) rather than an open-ended "3.9+," so this class of failure is less likely to begin with — noted here since it surfaced directly from testing this feature's real failure path, not treated as its own step.
6. **A one-click "Install GPU-enabled PyTorch" action, a deliberate exception to item 1's feature/engine-tier scoping — added after the user directly hit this on their own real machine (2026-09-25, see Step 18 item 7).** `torch` is `tier="required"`, correctly excluded from the generic Install-button loop (item 1) — but "required and already installed" isn't the same claim as "installed in the right build," and the CPU-vs-CUDA wheel mismatch this app can't prevent at install time (Step 18 item 7) is exactly the case item 1's model doesn't cover: nothing to install, something to **replace**. When the same `nvidia-smi`-on-PATH detection item 3 already uses finds a real NVIDIA GPU but `torch.cuda.is_available()` is `False`, show a distinct button (not folded into the generic per-package loop) reading something like "GPU detected but PyTorch is CPU-only — Install GPU PyTorch," next to the mismatch message item 3 already added. Clicking it runs, via the same venv-`python -m pip` subprocess mechanism as item 2 (same streamed real output, same "never swallow the real error" discipline): `pip uninstall torch torchaudio -y` followed by a CUDA-index install — reuse `constraints.txt`'s existing `torch<3`/`torchaudio<3` caps so this reinstall can't drift outside the version range the rest of the app already assumes. **The index URL must be picked by the running interpreter's own Python version, not hardcoded to one value — confirmed the hard way (2026-09-26).** First tried `cu124` on the user's real machine (Python 3.14) and it failed outright (`ERROR: Could not find a version that satisfies the requirement torch (from versions: none)`) — checked PyTorch's real package index directly and confirmed why: `download.pytorch.org/whl/cu124/torch/` only publishes wheels through `cp313`, nothing for `cp314`. `cu128`'s index does carry real Windows `cp314` CUDA wheels (confirmed directly: `torch-2.9.1+cu128-cp314-cp314-win_amd64.whl` and the matching `torchaudio-2.9.0+cu128-...` build both exist), and this matches a real, open PyTorch issue (`pytorch/pytorch#169929`) describing exactly this CPU-only-on-3.14 failure mode as a known current gap for anyone on a Python 3.14 CUDA index older than `cu128`. **Fix: this action must check `sys.version_info` (or just try `cu128` first, since it's currently the earliest index with 3.14 wheels, confirmed 2026-09-26) rather than assuming a fixed CUDA index tag works for every Python version** — the two vary independently (CUDA-driver compatibility vs. Python-ABI wheel availability), and this app already has more than one real Python-version-related install friction point (Step 18c item 5's `diffq-fixed`/README "3.9+" gap is the same underlying class of problem: a very new Python version outrunning what packages have published wheels for). After it completes, re-run the same CUDA-availability check and refresh the message in place, same as item 3's pattern — no restart required.

**Exit:**

### Step 20 — UX polish: keyboard shortcuts, toast feedback, transcript search
Found by asking directly "anything else to improve UX?", separate from the information-architecture work in Steps 13–19 — these are smaller, additive interaction improvements, not IA changes, so they can land as their own step rather than folding into an already-large step.

1. **Native keyboard shortcuts for Review & edit's most-repeated actions.** Confirmed directly: Streamlit 1.52+ supports a native `shortcut=` parameter on `st.button` (e.g. `st.button("Save", shortcut="ctrl+s")`) — no third-party component needed, and Baihe should already be well past 1.52 (Step 12 confirmed 1.63.0 headroom). Checked the app for any existing use — none (`grep`'d every file for `shortcut=`, zero hits). Add shortcuts to the handful of actions a reviewer repeats dozens of times per session: save the current line's edit, jump to the next/previous flagged line (reusing the existing `_jump_to_line_button` helper's logic), play/pause the current line's audio clip. **Re-verify the installed Streamlit version supports `shortcut=` before implementing** — it's a recent addition, don't assume without checking against the actual installed version.
2. **`st.toast` for transient confirmations, instead of (or alongside) static inline messages.** Confirmed directly: `st.toast` is a real, stable Streamlit API, and its 2026 update fixed it staying visible across an immediately-following `st.rerun()` — relevant here because several of Baihe's own actions call `st.rerun()` right after showing a message. Checked `workspace_tab.py` for current usage: zero `st.toast` calls anywhere in the app, but 48 `st.success`/`st.balloons` calls in `workspace_tab.py` alone — most of these are small "saved"/"done" confirmations that would read better as a transient toast than a message that sits in the page until the next rerun clears it. Not a blanket replace-everything pass — keep `st.success`/`st.error` for anything the user needs to actually read and act on (a real warning, an error with next steps); use `st.toast` only for pure confirmations ("Line saved," "Export complete").
3. **Full-text search across a drama's transcript.** Confirmed directly: today, jumping to a specific line only works from a flagged-item list (`_jump_to_line_button`, used from pacing/consistency/coverage check results) — there's no way to type a word or phrase and jump to where it appears. For a long drama, finding "that one line with X" currently means paging through the Review table manually. Add a search box in Review & edit that filters/jumps using the same underlying line list `_jump_to_line_button` already works against, reusing its page-jump logic rather than building a second navigation mechanism.
4. **Checked and not pursued: a dynamic browser tab title reflecting background-job progress** (e.g. "42% — Translating..." in the tab bar, so the user can tell status while alt-tabbed away). Checked directly: this is a real, long-standing, unresolved Streamlit limitation (multiple open GitHub issues going back years, no clean native mechanism — `st.set_page_config`'s title can only be set once, early in the script). Available workarounds are JS-injection hacks with known reliability problems. Not worth building a fragile workaround for a nice-to-have when Step 14's persistent in-app status indicator (Step 13's `ui/status.py`) already covers the "can I tell what's running" need while the user is actually in the app.

**Exit:**
- Manual check: the shortcut keys work for save/next-flagged/prev-flagged/play-pause in Review & edit, and don't fire while typing in a text field (native `shortcut=` behavior, per Streamlit's own docs — re-verify this is actually true of the installed version before relying on it).
- A test shows a pure-confirmation action (e.g. saving a line edit) shows a toast, while a real warning/error still shows a message the user has to see and act on, not just a toast.
- A test shows searching for a word/phrase in Review & edit's search box jumps to the correct line, using the same page-jump logic as the existing flagged-item jump buttons.
- Manual check: confirm the transcript search actually finds a term known to exist only in one specific line of a real drama, and lands on the right page.

### Step 20b — Richer Anki export: sentence context and audio, not just an isolated word
Prompted by a Gemini-authored review the user shared: "Allow users to click a word or sentence in the Interactive Reader to export an .apkg card containing: Front: Foreign sentence + audio clip snippet. Back: Target translation + target word definition + Pinyin/Furigana." Checked what already exists before treating any of this as new, since Baihe already has Anki export — `vocab_export.py` (`export_vocab_csv`/`export_vocab_apkg`, the latter already using `genanki` and already wired into `tabs/reader_tab.py`) turns the Reader's click-to-define history (`db.vocab_lookups`) into cards, front = word + reading (pinyin/furigana, already there), back = definitions. **Real gap confirmed by reading the actual card-building code**: cards are word-only — no sentence context, no audio, no translation on the card. Baihe already has the pieces this needs elsewhere in the app: sentence-level `zh`/`en` line data, and an audio-slice extractor already used for other per-line audio needs (`extract_audio_slice(audio_path, start, end, slice_path)`, the same function Step 21's per-line playback also uses). `genanki` itself already supports embedding media files in a `.apkg` — no new dependency for the audio part either.

1. **Extend the export, don't replace it.** Keep the existing word-only card type (still useful for a quick vocab drill), and add a second, richer card type: front = the full source sentence the clicked word/term appeared in + an embedded audio clip of that line (via the same `extract_audio_slice` Step 21 already relies on, for audio_drama/video_drama media types that have a real audio track — a novel-type drama has no audio, so its cards are text-only, same front/back shape minus the clip), back = the line's translation + the word's definition + its reading.
2. **Click-to-export granularity**, matching the review's ask directly: the Reader's existing click-to-define popover (already the entry point to `db.vocab_lookups`) gets an "Add to Anki export" action right there, rather than only a bulk end-of-session export.
3. **Media-type-aware**, per item 1 — don't silently produce an audio-less card and call it the same feature when a novel has no source audio to draw from; the UI should make clear which card type is available for which drama.

**Exit:**
- A test shows the richer card type embeds an audio file in the exported `.apkg` for an audio/video drama, and omits the audio field cleanly (not a broken/missing-file reference) for a novel drama.
- A test shows the sentence-level card's back field contains the line's translation, the clicked word's definition, and its reading, all three present.
- A test shows the existing word-only export still works unchanged — this is an addition, not a replacement.
- Manual check: click a word mid-sentence in the Reader on a real audio drama, export it, and confirm the resulting Anki card plays the right audio clip and shows the right sentence/translation/definition.

### Step 21 — Review workspace: per-line audio playback and save-status
Found by cross-checking the user's segment-editor spec against the actual Review & edit code directly, not assumed. Two concrete, confirmed gaps, both in the same section of `workspace_tab.py` (the per-page line-editing table around lines 2069–2156), so grouped as one step.

1. **No per-line audio playback in Review & edit, confirmed by direct check** (`grep -c "st.audio(" tabs/workspace_tab.py` returns 0 — the whole file has no per-line clip player anywhere, only the full-episode player in Reader's "Watch/listen" block, Step 12 item 8). A reviewer working through source/translation text has no way to hear the exact audio a line came from without leaving Review & edit entirely. Add an audio snippet per row, extracted on demand (reuse `core.extract_audio_slice`, already used by the existing "🎙️ Re-transcribe" button in the same row's `🔧` popover) rather than pre-extracting a clip for every visible line on page load — the same lazy-on-click pattern the row's popover already uses for re-transcription, not a new pattern. **Watch performance**: extracting+rendering an `st.audio` widget for all 40 rows on a page eagerly would be slow and memory-heavy; keep this behind the row's existing `🔧` popover (or a dedicated small "▶" button) rather than always-rendered.
2. **No indication of unsaved changes, confirmed by direct check.** Edits to a page's `start`/`end`/`zh`/`en` fields only persist to the database when the explicit "💾 Save edits (this page)" button is clicked (confirmed: `db.save_lines` is only called from that button's handler in this section, nowhere else). There is currently no visual signal that a page has unsaved edits at all — a reviewer who edits several lines, gets distracted, and navigates to another page or closes the tab loses those edits silently. Two parts:
   - **Minimum fix: a save-status indicator**, matching the user's own requested vocabulary ("Saved" / "Unsaved changes" / "Saving..." / "Save failed") — compare the page's current in-widget values against what's actually in the database (not just session state, since `st.session_state.lines` is already updated by the splice-back logic a few lines above regardless of whether it's been saved) to detect a real unsaved diff.
   - **Stretch, only if the minimum fix ships clean:** autosave when navigating away from the page (page-number change, tab switch) using the existing `db.save_lines` call, not a periodic timer or per-keystroke save — a keystroke-level autosave would multiply database writes for no real benefit in a single-user local app and fights Streamlit's per-rerun-on-interaction model. **Re-verify this is worth the complexity before building it** — the status indicator alone may be enough; don't build autosave speculatively if the indicator resolves the actual problem (forgetting to click Save).

**Exit:**
- A test shows a lazy-loaded audio snippet plays the correct time range for a given line, and that nothing extracts audio for a line until its playback control is actually used.
- A test shows the save-status indicator correctly reflects "unsaved changes" when a page's widget values differ from what's in the database, and "saved" immediately after a successful `db.save_lines` call.
- Manual check: edit a few lines without saving, navigate to Diagnostics and back, and confirm the indicator still shows unsaved changes (session state alone isn't mistaken for "saved").

Prompted by the user's "unified local translation platform" vision doc, cross-referenced against the actual `db.py` schema before designing anything — a genuinely good finding, not assumed. **`series_characters` and `glossary_terms` are already keyed by `series_id`, not `drama_id`** (confirmed directly in `db.py`'s `CREATE TABLE` statements, with the schema's own comment: "shares a glossary across multiple dramas of the same series"), and **`dramas.media_type` already includes `manhwa`/`manga`/`manhua` alongside `audio_drama`/`video_drama`/`novel`** (confirmed in `workspace_tab.py`'s `MEDIA_TYPE_OPTIONS`). ### Step 22b — Add "anime" content type; add series assignment to the drama-creation form *(follow-up to Step 22, at the user's direct request)*

Two real, concrete gaps, both confirmed by reading `tabs/workspace_tab.py` directly, not assumed:

- Manual check: create an anime movie and assign it to the same series as an already-existing anime show's episodes; confirm the series view lists all of them together while the movie remains its own separate, independently-openable drama.

**Built and merged autonomously, PR #80 — confirmed via the GitHub API, CI green, matches spec exactly.** All three roadmap items covered by real tests, including item 3's "no code needed, falls out of the existing model" claim.

### Step 23 — Source-adapter architecture (interface only, no site-specific code)
Second half of the user's raw-source vision (§0), scoped down to what's responsibly buildable this pass. Checked the two reference projects directly before designing anything, not assumed:
- **[`keiyoushi/extensions-source`](https://github.com/keiyoushi/extensions-source)** — confirmed real: Apache-2.0, 4.7k stars, 1.7k forks, actively maintained (646 open issues, ongoing contribution). It's a **Kotlin/JVM extension system for Mihon/Tachiyomi** — different language/runtime from Baihe, so no code ports directly, but its per-site scraping patterns (what endpoint, what parsing, what auth each real site actually needs) are genuine, inspectable, battle-tested reference material — same "read the real technique, reimplement in our own stack" approach already used for every other integration in this roadmap.
- **OpenToon / OpenNovel — confirmed NOT open source, but their real shipped functionality is checkable and worth mining even without the code.** Checked their actual app store listings and marketing pages directly (not assumed): **OpenToon**'s core workflow is "copy any chapter URL, drop it in, start reading" — a generic paste-a-URL-and-fetch import, plus tap-any-bubble-to-edit-the-translation and offline local storage. **OpenNovel**'s is "translate from popular sites or import EPUBs in seconds," a glossary keeping names/terms consistent, and linking official cover art. Checked each against Baihe's actual current code before treating anything as a gap: per-bubble translated-text editing already exists (`tabs/scanlate_tab.py`, `st.text_area` per bubble, "💾 Save bubble edits"); EPUB import/export already exists in full (`epub_io.py`); cover art already exists (`dramas.cover_art_filename`) and adapter-returned metadata (Step 23 item 1's `get_series()`) can already carry a cover URL, so no new item needed there; the glossary is already richer than OpenNovel's (§0). **One real, confirmed gap**: Scanlate currently only accepts manual file upload (`st.file_uploader`, `tabs/scanlate_tab.py` line 27) — there's no lighter-weight "paste a page/chapter URL and fetch it" path that works on an arbitrary site without a registered adapter. Added as item 8 below.

**Explicitly not done this pass, and why:** vetting the ToS/robots.txt/anti-bot posture of the ~20 official JP/CN/KR publisher platforms named in the user's spec (Shonen Jump+, Naver Webtoon, KakaoPage, Tencent Comics, etc.). That's a genuine multi-site legal/technical research project on its own — several are large commercial publishers with real anti-scraping incentives (paid content, official apps), a categorically higher-risk starting point than sites a community-maintained extension list has already converged on as realistically accessible through ordinary HTTP/HTML access. Doing shallow "checked" claims on 20 sites in one pass would be exactly the kind of unverified research this roadmap has avoided everywhere else.

1. **The adapter interface** — `search()`, `get_series()`, `get_chapters()`, `get_pages()`, `download_page()`, with optional `login()`/`refresh_session()` for sources that need them; no adapter is required to implement every method. Each adapter declares its own content types (`manga`/`manhua`/`manhwa`/`novel`) and capabilities, so the same interface serves image sources and text sources without forcing one to pretend to be the other. **A structured `SourceCapabilities` record, added on a later pass after the user asked for a graduated status model instead of a flat supported/disqualified label**: every adapter (and every generic-fallback attempt against an unregistered site) reports platform, content types, languages, which access-ladder tier actually worked, whether auth is required vs. merely supported, and a status drawn from a real set — `VERIFIED`, `VERIFIED_WITH_AUTH`, `BROWSER_ASSISTED`, `PARTIALLY_SUPPORTED`, `AUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED`, `MANUAL_VERIFICATION_REQUIRED` (an active challenge was hit, item 2's hand-off flow applies), `PROTECTED` (a specific technical protection — a signed/expiring token system, encrypted tiles, etc. — was found; nothing attempts to defeat it, this status just records that it exists), `TOS_PROHIBITED` (the narrower line from §6's policy-revision note — a specific, written anti-scraping-and-AI-use clause, not generic boilerplate), or `UNTESTED` (no real investigation done yet — the honest default for most of the candidate list, not a synonym for unsupported). **Technical findings and contractual findings are recorded as two separate fields, never collapsed into one verdict**: a `technical` block (browser-accessible, extraction method, known protections) and a `terms` block (what was actually read, quoted where possible, and what's still unverified) — the app states facts, it doesn't decide for the user whether a given personal use is appropriate.
2. **The access-method ladder, simplest-first**: direct HTTP/API → HTML parsing → an existing, already-authenticated browser session/cookies → a rendered browser page, stopping at whichever level actually works for a given source. **Refined on a later pass, after the user clarified the intended distinction**: this never means solving or algorithmically defeating a CAPTCHA or an active anti-bot challenge (Cloudflare's challenge page, a "verify you're human" JS check, etc.) — no code in this system ever does that, full stop. What it does mean: when ordinary HTTP hits exactly that kind of challenge, **stop automated requests immediately, detect and name what was hit, and hand off to the user** ("A browser verification page was detected. Automatic challenge solving is disabled. Open the page in your browser and complete whatever verification the site asks for." — `[Open in Browser]` / `[Retry]` / `[Cancel]`). If the user completes that verification themselves, in their own real browser, exactly as the site intends, and the resulting page or session becomes legitimately reachable to them — the importer resumes from that already-established, human-obtained session (reusing its cookies or the rendered DOM), same as the existing browser-assisted tier, just reactively triggered instead of only offered upfront. **The distinguishing line stays exactly where it was**: a human proves they're human, to the site, the normal way; the app never does that on their behalf. A source that's genuinely inaccessible even after that (e.g. the resource itself needs an account/paywall the user doesn't have) still reports "unavailable," not a further workaround. **DRM stays a separate, harder line, never crossed**: no decryption, no stream-cipher circumvention, ever. But it's judged **per requested resource, not per site** — a site that happens to DRM-protect some of its content elsewhere doesn't disqualify a different, genuinely-plain resource on the same domain; check whether the *specific* thing the user pasted a URL for is itself DRM-protected before refusing it, the same "verify, don't assume" discipline used everywhere else in this project. **Formalized into a named, numbered tier enum on a later pass, at the user's request** — the ladder above was always these tiers in substance, just not given stable names a `SourceCapabilities.access_method` value or a diagnostics message could cite directly: `STATIC_HTTP` → `RENDERED_BROWSER` (Step 23g/`page_fetch.fetch_rendered`) → `AUTHENTICATED_BROWSER` (Step 23k's persistent-profile session, for a source the user has already logged into) → `USER_ASSISTED_BROWSER` (distinct from the authenticated tier: this is the reactive challenge/manual-verification hand-off two sentences up, where the human actively drives that one specific request rather than a session being reused automatically) → `OFFICIAL_API` → `UNAVAILABLE`. **`OFFICIAL_API` is a new, explicit check, not just a name for something already covered**: before falling through to `UNAVAILABLE`, check whether the source publishes a real, legitimate public API and whether it actually covers what was asked for — reusing the exact lesson already learned the hard way vetting syosetu.com, which has a real official API that's confirmed metadata-only, not chapter text, so the API existing didn't make the site usable for what this app actually needs. An API tier that only partially covers a request (metadata via the API, content via a different tier or not at all) is a real, valid outcome — not a reason to skip checking, and not a reason to treat the whole source as solved once *a* legitimate channel is found.
2b. **Diagnostics must attribute a failure to the specific tier and reason it happened at, never collapse it to "blocked."** A failed static-HTTP request doesn't mean the source is universally unreachable — it might mean only that tier failed, and `RENDERED_BROWSER` or `AUTHENTICATED_BROWSER` would succeed. Track and surface, per attempt: which tier was tried, what specifically happened (a real HTTP status/error, a detected active challenge, a detected auth requirement, a detected DRM/protected-resource signal), and whether a higher tier was attempted as a result — reusing Step 23g's Source Diagnostics view and its "reason, not a bare status" principle rather than building a second diagnostics surface for this. **Made concrete on a later pass, with a named failure-reason taxonomy and a real, non-blacklisting status set, each grounded in a case already hit this session rather than left abstract**:
   - **Failure reasons** (one of): `HTTP_ERROR`, `TIMEOUT`, `RATE_LIMIT`, `JAVASCRIPT_REQUIRED` (Bilibili Manga's confirmed SPA-only structure), `EMPTY_SPA_SHELL` (same case — a real fetch returning an empty shell plus a "enable JavaScript" notice, not just a plain fetch failure), `AUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED`, `PURCHASE_REQUIRED`, `COOKIE_REQUIRED`, `GEO_RESTRICTION` (newtoki/manatoki/booktoki, dropped from consideration for exactly this reason), `CDN_RESTRICTION`, `CLOUDFLARE_CHALLENGE` (69shuba, rawkuma.net — both confirmed via a direct `cf-mitigated: challenge` header), `BOT_CHALLENGE`, `IP_REPUTATION_BLOCK` (the real, still-open ambiguity on `baozimh.com` — a maintained extension exists with no visible bypass code, so the gatekeeper may be specific to this research environment's IP rather than universal), `ACCESS_DENIED`, `DRM_DETECTED`, `ENCRYPTED_RESOURCE`/`SIGNED_RESOURCE` (Bilibili Manga's confirmed signed image-token system; manhuaku's confirmed AES-plus-obfuscation scheme), `UNKNOWN`. Capture real evidence per attempt (HTTP status, response headers, final URL after redirects, page title, DOM text length) rather than inferring beyond what was actually observed.
   - **A `technical_status` value that never collapses to a binary blocked/not-blocked**: `DISQUALIFIED` (a real, confirmed line crossed — e.g. `TOS_PROHIBITED`), `UNRESOLVED` (nothing has actually succeeded yet, but nothing's been ruled out either — `beqege.cc`'s current state), `BLOCKED_IN_CURRENT_ENVIRONMENT` (a real, distinct status this project needed and didn't have — exactly `baozimh.com`'s situation: confirmed blocked from here, twice, with a real reason to suspect it isn't blocked universally), `BROWSER_ACCESSIBLE`, `AUTHENTICATED_ACCESSIBLE`, `PARTIALLY_SUPPORTED`, `SUPPORTED`.
   - **An automatic browser-comparison test when static HTTP fails**: run the same URL through `RENDERED_BROWSER` immediately, and record both results side by side (`Static HTTP: FAILED — HTTP 403` / `Browser: SUCCESS — chapter detected, 38 image resources`) rather than a single pass/fail per source — this is what actually produces a `BROWSER_ACCESSIBLE` verdict instead of a bare failure.
3. **Source-health tracking** (🟢/🟡/🔴, last success/failure, error type, response latency) and **conservative, human-paced request behavior by default — made concrete on the same later pass**: distinguish ordinary rate limiting (HTTP 429, transient 5xx, throttling — exponential backoff, capped retries, eventually stop) from an active anti-automation challenge (item 2's case — never retried automatically at all, always handed to the user). Concrete starting defaults, all configurable in Settings: **1–3s delay between requests to the same source, 1 request at a time by default (no parallel flooding), max 3 retries with exponential backoff.** A comic chapter's 50–100 page images and a novel's chapter-range import (item 13's multi-chapter selective-import UI) both go through this same paced queue, never fired as a burst — a multi-chapter import shows real progress ("Chapter 37 / 500 — waiting before next request...") with cancel available at any point, not a silent, instant bulk fetch. This is content *acquisition* for URLs the user themselves provides one at a time, not an autonomous crawler that discovers pages on its own across a domain — the ladder and the pacing above exist to keep it that way structurally, not just by policy.
3b. **A transparent "Source Access" status view**, so the user can always see what the app is actually doing to a source rather than a bare progress bar: access method in use (Normal HTTP / Browser session), request count so far, how many results came from cache, current action, and the live request delay — plus the challenge hand-off screen from item 2 when that's what's actually happening. Reuses `background_jobs.py`'s existing status/progress plumbing rather than a new tracking mechanism. **Per-tier "Test Now" buttons, added on a later pass at the user's suggestion — a real, small UI addition, not a new architecture.** A `SourceCapabilities` record sitting at `UNTESTED` is a passive fact until someone actually imports something from that source; add explicit `[ Test Static ]` / `[ Test Browser ]` / `[ Test Authenticated ]` buttons on a source's own detail view (alongside `[ Open in Browser ]` and `[ View Diagnostics ]`, item 2's existing hand-off actions) that run exactly one access-ladder tier against a real, user-chosen page and update that tier's field on the record with the result — the same tiers and the same `SourceCapabilities` fields item 1/2b already define, just triggerable on demand instead of only as a side effect of a real import. This is the concrete fix for "stuck at UNTESTED forever because nobody's imported from it yet": a candidate can now be moved off `UNTESTED` deliberately, one tier at a time, without needing a real content import to trigger it — same principle already applied in this planning session's own vetting notes (re-testing a stalled candidate with a fresh, specific technique rather than leaving it marked unresolved indefinitely).
4. **A configurable raw-content cache** (don't retain / temporary / keep originals / keep translated / keep both), content-hashed to avoid re-downloading the same page. This isn't primarily about saving money on reprocessing (re-OCRing or re-translating an identical page costs very little either way) — it's about not re-hitting a rate-limited, possibly-ToS-sensitive external source repeatedly for content that hasn't changed. Re-fetching costs the *source* something (load, a repeated hit against a site that may already be watching for bot traffic); re-processing costs Baihe very little. The cache modes control local retention/disk-space tradeoffs, not a translation-cost decision — that's a separate, already-covered case (Step 24's translation memory handles "don't pay to re-translate identical text twice").
5. **Scheduled chapter checking**, added after checking how Mihon itself (not just the Keiyoushi extension layer) actually does this: Mihon's `LibraryUpdateJob` runs as a periodic background job (user-configured interval, hourly granularity) with optional constraints (Wi-Fi-only, charging-only), re-fetches each tracked title's chapter list from its source, and diffs it against the last-known set to find new chapters — a simple, well-proven pattern, not anything sophisticated enough to need Mihon's own code. Baihe's version: a background job (reusing `background_jobs.py`) that periodically calls an adapter's `get_chapters()` for each tracked series, diffs by chapter id against what's already known, and **notifies the user of new chapters — it does not auto-download or auto-queue them for OCR/translation by default** (per this project's standing "destructive/data-affecting actions need a separate, explicit confirmation" pattern; auto-queueing is an opt-in setting, off by default). Reuses the same per-source rate-limit/backoff from item 3, so a check cycle doesn't hammer a source any harder than a manual fetch would.
6. **Multi-source search.** The `search()` method (item 1) is per-adapter; this adds a top-level search that fans a query out to every enabled adapter concurrently, tags each result with which source it came from, and merges them into one result list — deduplicating by normalized title, not assuming sources agree on formatting. Each adapter's own rate-limit still applies per-source; a slow or failing source degrades that source's results, not the whole search.
7. **Out of scope for this step, on purpose:** any actual site-specific adapter. This step ships with zero working sources — it's the interface and the plumbing, tested against a fake/mock source only.
8. **Generic "paste a URL" import, inspired by OpenToon's actual proven workflow (functionality only — no code to port, since it's closed-source).** A page/chapter URL pasted into Scanlate is fetched with a plain HTTP GET, its HTML scanned for image tags matching common manga-page patterns (largest images in reading order, same heuristic every generic manga downloader uses — no per-site knowledge), and the results fed into Scanlate's existing upload pipeline exactly like a manual file upload. This is deliberately **not** a registered adapter — no `search()`/`get_chapters()`, no source-health tracking, no scheduled checking — it's a one-off fetch for whatever URL the user hands it, and it's expected to fail cleanly (clear "couldn't find page images here" error, not a crash) on sites with heavier anti-bot protection or non-standard page structures. Complements, doesn't replace, the structured adapter system (items 1–6): a registered adapter is worth building for a site used repeatedly; this is for a one-off chapter from anywhere. **Content-vs-chrome filtering made explicit, on a later pass, after the user asked directly whether this already excludes page UI (nav/buttons/ad banners), not just prose:** "largest images" alone isn't a sufficient filter — an ad banner or a hero/promo image can be as large as a real page. Add real exclusion heuristics before ranking by size: reject images below a minimum height (manga/manhwa pages are tall; UI icons and buttons aren't), prefer a consistent aspect-ratio cluster (real chapter pages from the same source are usually near-uniform in shape; a one-off image with a very different ratio is more likely a banner/logo/avatar), reject an image whose exact URL or hash repeats identically across multiple different chapters/pages of the same series (a real page is unique per chapter; a site logo, nav icon, or recurring ad creative isn't), and reject images served from a different domain than the page itself where practical (a common signal for third-party ad content). None of this is per-site knowledge — same "no per-site logic" scope as the rest of this item — just a better content-detection filter before the existing "largest images, reading order" heuristic runs.
9. **The same generic "paste a URL" idea for novel text, confirmed by OpenNovel's own changelog** ("more intelligent website text detection — you can now translate almost any website"). Same shape as item 8 but for prose: fetch the URL, extract the main readable text (a standard "reader mode"/readability-style heuristic — strip nav/ads/comments, keep the largest contiguous text block — no per-site knowledge), and feed it into Workspace's existing novel-import path (`tabs/workspace_tab.py`'s raw-novel upload, same as a pasted/uploaded `.txt`). Same scope limits as item 8: no adapter registration, one-off fetch, fails cleanly rather than crashing on a page it can't parse.

**Six more items added on a later pass, checking a much larger "universal importer" spec the user pasted against this step's real, already-built scope.** Most of that spec turned out already covered here almost verbatim (the access ladder already includes a browser-assisted tier as the last resort and already refuses to defeat DRM/CAPTCHAs/anti-bot exactly as the spec asks; `translate_engines.build_llm_instructions` already passes both preceding *and* forward context, covering the spec's "context-aware translation" ask for novels/subtitles, and Scanlate's `translate_page_with_context` already does the same for comics via prior-page context; `scanlate.py`'s `inpaint_region` already writes to a new output path rather than overwriting the source page, with OCR/translation data in structured DB rows — the same non-destructive guarantee the spec's four-folder layout asks for, just via DB + separate render output instead of files; `video_download.py` already calls `yt_dlp.YoutubeDL` directly, which covers thousands of sites out of the box, so "GenericVideo" is already solved, just not integrated with the items below; the spec's KR/JP/CN site list is largely the same set already recorded as vetted/unvetted candidates just above). **Six real, confirmed gaps, on top of an already-substantial step:**
10. **No unified "paste any URL" front door.** Items 8/9 and the registered-adapter system all assume the user already knows what kind of content a URL is and which tool to open (Scanlate for a comic link, Workspace's upload for a novel link). Add one entry point — a URL box reachable from Library/Home — that fetches enough of the page to detect content type (video/novel/comic) and, where recognizable, platform, then shows a preview (title, chapter/episode, detected language, content type, chapter count if knowable) before the user commits to "Import."
11. **Video isn't part of that front door yet.** Not a rebuild — `video_download.py`'s existing `yt_dlp.YoutubeDL` call already handles arbitrary video URLs. Route a detected video URL from item 10's front door into the existing download path with the same preview treatment items 8/9 already give novel/comic content, instead of leaving video as a separately-discovered feature.
12. **No chapter-ordering intelligence.** Nothing today sorts "Chapter 1, 2, 10" correctly instead of lexicographically ("1, 10, 2"), or recognizes CJK chapter markers (第1章/第十章/第001話) or non-numeric ones (Prologue, Interlude, Side Story) and preserves the original title alongside a normalized sort key. A small, shared utility any adapter's `get_chapters()` output and item 13's UI below can use.
13. **No multi-chapter selective-import UI.** Item 5's scheduled chapter-check only notifies of new chapters — there's no "browse this series' table of contents, check the chapters you want, import selected" view built on the `get_chapters()` interface that already exists. Add one, reusing item 12's ordering utility to display the list correctly and Step 23's existing rate-limit/backoff so a multi-chapter import doesn't hit a source any harder than the per-chapter fetches already do.
14. **Generic novel-text extraction (item 9): use `trafilatura` instead of a single hand-rolled heuristic — checked directly, real and worth adopting.** [`adbar/trafilatura`](https://github.com/adbar/trafilatura) confirmed: Apache-2.0 (current releases; pre-1.8.0 was GPLv3+, irrelevant now), ~6.9k stars, actively maintained (v2.2.0, July 2026), pip-installable, lxml-based. Its real pipeline matches the spec's multi-strategy ask: a rule-based main-content/boilerplate extractor with `jusText`/`readability-lxml` as fallbacks, plus metadata pulled from HTML meta tags, OpenGraph, and JSON-LD — exactly items 8/9's "reader mode" heuristic, but a maintained, battle-tested implementation instead of hand-building 10 strategies. **One real caveat, not glossed over**: CJK support is functional but needs the optional language-detection extra installed (or an explicit `target_language="zh"` passed) to avoid a warning (confirmed via a real GitHub issue, #119) — no independent CJK-extraction-quality benchmark was found, so this should be spot-checked against a real Chinese novel site before treating it as equivalent-quality to its English extraction. Swap item 9's generic novel-text extraction to use it, keeping the same "feeds into the existing raw-novel upload path, fails cleanly" scope.
15. **No developer docs for the adapter system.** Add `docs/content-sources.md` (per adapter: URL patterns, content type, language, auth needs, extraction strategy, known limitations, test status) and `docs/adding-source.md` (how to add a new adapter without touching the translation engine) — Step 23's own interface is already designed for exactly this kind of extension, but nothing documents how to use it that way yet.

**Source-vetting policy re-confirmed and refined, at the user's explicit request — a large spec checked against this step's real, already-built architecture before anything was added, same discipline as every other pasted spec this session.** The user's concern: technical accessibility and policy/permission status must never collapse into one verdict, or a site with generic ToS boilerplate ends up looking as unusable as one with a real, explicit ban. **Most of what was asked for already exists, checked directly against this step's own text above and Step 23k's, not assumed:**
- **Technical and policy findings are already two separate fields, not one** — item 1's `SourceCapabilities` record already keeps a `technical` block and a `terms` block apart ("the app states facts, it doesn't decide for the user whether a given personal use is appropriate"), and Step 23k item 3 already extends this to **six** separate fields tracking distinct facts: `access_method`, `authentication_required`, `purchase_required`, `technical_protection`, `automation_permission`, and `ai_ml_use` — already more granular than the four-field model requested, not less.
- **"UNTESTED" already means untested, not "maybe possible"** — item 1's status set already includes a real `UNTESTED` value distinct from every disqualifying/blocking status, and item 1's own text calls it "the honest default for most of the candidate list, not a synonym for unsupported."
- **The access-method ladder already tests in escalating order and item 2b already forbids collapsing a failure to a bare "blocked"** — `STATIC_HTTP → RENDERED_BROWSER → AUTHENTICATED_BROWSER → USER_ASSISTED_BROWSER → OFFICIAL_API → UNAVAILABLE`, with a named failure-reason taxonomy (17 real, session-grounded values) and an automatic browser-comparison test when static HTTP fails — this already implements "don't stop at step 2 just because `requests` failed."
- **Authenticated browser is already a first-class, normal tier, not a fallback hack** — Step 23k already builds exactly the persistent-Playwright-profile / manual-login / save-state workflow requested, with the same "never ask for a password, never bypass authentication, never defeat CAPTCHA/DRM" boundaries already stated as non-negotiable there.
- **Purchased content is already something this system tests rather than assumes unsupported** — Step 23k item 5 already extracts "the full resource set... novel text..., comic page images incl. `srcset`/`<picture>`/lazy-load/embedded manifests, and... audio/video/subtitle resources where legitimately exposed to the session" once authenticated, explicitly not DRM-bypassing.
- **The LLM already doesn't make the access decision** — Step 23g's confidence/profile system does semantic extraction and DOM interpretation; `SourceCapabilities`'s policy fields are set from what was actually read in a site's real terms, never from an LLM's own opinion about whether a site "seems" prohibited.

**One real, useful field this system didn't have, now added to item 1's `SourceCapabilities` record**: **`content_access_status`** (`TEXT`/`IMAGES`/`VIDEO`/`AUDIO`/`SUBTITLES`/`METADATA`/`MIXED`/`UNKNOWN`) — what resource types were actually confirmed reachable for a given source, independent of the access tier that reached them. Step 23k item 5 already produces this information; it just wasn't a structured field on the capabilities record before.

**Explicit test order, made concrete rather than left implicit in the ladder's prose**, for whoever implements a new adapter or the generic fallback: DNS/connectivity → static HTTP → inspect the returned HTML → embedded JSON/JSON-LD/metadata → detect an SPA shell → `RENDERED_BROWSER` → inspect the rendered DOM → inspect image/video/audio/subtitle resources → if authentication is required, prompt for an authenticated browser session (never a password) → retry authenticated → record exactly what content is exposed → deterministic extraction first → LLM semantic extraction only as the fallback Step 23g already scopes it as. Not stopping at step 2 because `requests` failed, not stopping because a site is JS-heavy, not stopping because login is required — already the ladder's own behavior, now written as an explicit checklist.

**A real, specific correction this pass surfaced, worth fixing rather than leaving as a live inconsistency**: several of this session's own §6 vetting-note verdicts called a site flatly **"disqualified" for hitting an active Cloudflare/WAF challenge, with no separate written ToS clause found disqualifying it** — that's exactly the technical/policy conflation the user is describing, just in this chat's own vetting language rather than the app's data model. **Qidian, 69shuba, hachiraw.net, and Rawkuma (rawkuma.net)** were each disqualified on a purely technical finding (an active challenge Step 23's own line refuses to defeat automatically) with no confirmed contractual violation independently established for any of them. **Corrected**: these are `BLOCKED_IN_CURRENT_ENVIRONMENT`-shaped, not `DISQUALIFIED` — eligible for the existing `USER_ASSISTED_BROWSER` hand-off (the user completes the real challenge themselves, in their own browser, exactly as already specified in item 2), not written off. Retitled in the summary table below. **Sites disqualified/declined on an actual, independently-confirmed policy finding are unaffected by this correction and stay exactly where they were** — Ridibooks (explicit ToS ban, separate from its own Cloudflare wall), Naver/Novelpia/Postype/Toptoon/Toomics/Ciweimao/JJWXC/Alphapolis/Everystar/KadoComi/Magazine Pocket/comic-zenon.com/kmanga.kodansha.com (real, quoted clauses) and Tencent Comics/hongxiu.com/Young Champion/miuraw.com/takecomic.jp/GANMA!/POPO (a named ClaudeBot/GPTBot block) all have their own independent, already-confirmed evidence, not just a technical wall standing in for a policy verdict.

### Step 23b — First real source adapter: manhuagui (zh)
Builds the first actual adapter against Step 23's interface, now that the user has confirmed (personal, single-user use) that a raw-aggregator source is an acceptable starting point. Picked from Keiyoushi's actively-maintained zh list (not the official-publisher list) per Step 23's own stated default. Checked directly before designing anything:
- **Keiyoushi's `manhuagui` extension source** (`src/zh/manhuagui`, real Kotlin/OkHttp code, read directly) confirms the real access method: plain HTTP GET/POST via OkHttp, a spoofed desktop-Chrome user-agent, a rate limiter (10 requests/10s on the main site, 4/s on the CDN — reused directly for Baihe's own rate-limit setting), and **no Cloudflare handling and no JavaScript execution anywhere in the extension** — confirms this site is reachable through the access ladder's HTTP/HTML tiers alone, never needing the browser-rendering fallback tier. Four mirror base URLs are configured (`www.manhuagui.com`, `tw.manhuagui.com`, `www.mhgui.com`, `tw.mhgui.com`) — useful as an automatic fallback list if one mirror is unreachable.
- **Chapter list decoding needs one real technique, not a simple HTML parse**: the site returns its chapter list LZString-compressed and Base64-encoded, decoded client-side in the browser's JS. A real, MIT-licensed Python port exists — [`lzstring`](https://pypi.org/project/lzstring/) (`decompressFromBase64`, API-compatible with what the site needs) — confirmed installable, though its last PyPI release was 2018; acceptable given it's a small, self-contained decoder with no dependency surface to go stale, but noted honestly rather than presented as actively maintained.
- **robots.txt re-checked directly with `curl` (real content this time — the earlier WebFetch result genuinely was a tool artifact, not a misreading of real content).** `www.manhuagui.com/robots.txt` is real, generated via the mcanerin.com robots.txt generator (a common, legitimate tool — its boilerplate header comment doesn't mean the file itself isn't the site's own). It explicitly disallows a long list of **named** crawlers: SEO/indexing bots (AhrefsBot, SemrushBot, MJ12bot, DataForSeoBot, etc.), search engines (Baiduspider, YandexBot, Sogou, 360spider, etc.), and — worth being direct about — **named AI/LLM crawlers specifically: `GPTBot`, `ClaudeBot`, `Claude-SearchBot`, `meta-externalagent`, `Bytespider`, `CCBot`**. The **generic catch-all** (`User-agent: *`) is separate and much lighter: `Crawl-delay: 10` plus two disallowed admin paths (`/yzadmin/`, `/lib/`) — no blanket disallow for unnamed clients. Keiyoushi's own `manhuagui` extension (already confirmed, item above) sends a plain desktop-Chrome user-agent string, not any of the specifically-named/disallowed bot identifiers, so it falls under the lighter catch-all rule, not the named-bot block list — the same posture a real browser or any generic HTTP client has. **Stating this plainly rather than deciding it away**: the site has gone out of its way to name and block AI crawlers specifically, which is a real, deliberate signal, even though a non-self-identifying personal-use client technically isn't one of the named entries. Given the user's already-given personal-use, aggregator-acceptable confirmation for this specific adapter, and that Keiyoushi's own actively-maintained community extension already operates the same way, this isn't being treated as a new blocker — but it's a more complete picture than "unverified," and worth knowing plainly rather than glossed over.
- **Adult-content cookie flag** (`isAdult=1`) exists in the source extension for R18 content access — default this **off** in Baihe's adapter, matching the app's existing content-handling defaults elsewhere; don't send it unless a future setting explicitly opts in.

1. Implement `search()`/`get_series()`/`get_chapters()`/`get_pages()` against manhuagui using Step 23's interface — plain HTTP/HTML tier only, reusing `lzstring` for chapter-list decoding and the same rate-limit numbers found above.
2. Mirror fallback: if the primary base URL fails, retry against the next configured mirror before marking the source unavailable, using the same backoff/health-tracking Step 23 already built.
3. No `login()`/`refresh_session()` needed — the extension requires no authentication for standard content.

**Exit:**
- A test (against a recorded/mocked response, not a live network call, matching this repo's existing test-mocking convention) shows `search()` and `get_chapters()` correctly decode a sample LZString-compressed chapter list.
- A test shows a failed request to the primary mirror falls back to the next configured mirror.
- Manual check: search for a real title on manhuagui through the new adapter, pull its chapter list, and download one page through into Scanlate's existing pipeline with no changes needed there (same check as Step 23's own manual check, now against a real source instead of a mock).

Pagination uses a `<div class="pagination2">` block with 目录(TOC)/上一页(prev)/下一页(next) links. The TOC page lists chapters as `<ul class="list clearfix"><li class="mulu"><a href="...">`. URL pattern: `/<category>/b/<id>.html` for the TOC, `/<category>/b/<id>_<n>.html` for each page.

No auth wall was hit in testing, but that's a small sample, not a guarantee.
