### Step 25y — Fix: EPUB export doesn't escape line text, producing invalid XHTML on lines containing `&`/`<`/`>`
Found by the same fourth adversarial pass. **Independently re-verified by direct code read** against the real merged `epub_io.py`, and cross-checked against this codebase's own established convention for the same class of embedding.

**The bug (`epub_io.py`'s `export_epub`, `_line_html()` helper, ~lines 122-140).** Line/translation text is embedded directly into XHTML content via plain f-strings — `f"<p>{before}</p>"` and `f"<p>{tail}</p>"` — with no `html.escape()` call anywhere in the function or file. Any source or translated line containing a literal `&`, `<`, or `>` character (e.g. dialogue quoting "Tom & Jerry," a stage-direction-style bracketed aside, or any AI-generated translation that happens to produce one of these characters) produces invalid, non-well-formed XHTML inside the exported `.epub` — EPUB content documents must be valid XML, so this can make the exported book fail to open or render correctly in strict e-reader software. **Confirmed as a real regression relative to this same codebase's own convention, not a novel oversight**: `reader.py` and `subtitle_formats.py` both correctly call `html.escape()` before embedding the same kind of AI-generated text into HTML/VTT output — `epub_io.py`'s export path is the one place this was missed. Reachable via Workspace's EPUB export button (`tabs/workspace_tab.py`, novel-narration mode's export section).

1. **Call `html.escape()` on `before`/`tail` before wrapping them in `<p>...</p>`** in `_line_html()` — matching the exact pattern already used in `reader.py`/`subtitle_formats.py`.
2. **Re-verify before fixing**: confirm the image-token-splitting logic around it still works correctly with escaped text (the `[[IMG:...]]` token itself is parsed out before this point, so escaping the surrounding text shouldn't affect it — but verify against the real function shape at implementation time).

**Exit:**
- A test confirms a line containing `&`, `<`, and `>` characters, once exported, produces valid, parseable XHTML content (parse the generated chapter content with an XML parser and confirm it doesn't raise).
- A test confirms the existing `[[IMG:filename]]` image-embedding still works correctly on a line that also contains the special characters above.
- Manual check: export a drama with narration text containing an ampersand or angle bracket to EPUB and open the result in a strict e-reader (or validate with `epubcheck`) to confirm no XHTML parse errors.

**Merged as PR #114** — opened and merged directly by this planning session after independent verification: base was exactly current `baihe-subtitler` tip, diff read in full (exactly the `html.escape()` fix asked for), all 10 tests in `test_epub_io.py` pass against a real `ebooklib` install (a real environment-contamination false alarm was caught and corrected during this review — a stale pre-fix `epub_io.py` this session had left directly in `/tmp` was shadowing the real fixed file under pytest's rootdir mechanics; once cleaned up, the fix verified correctly the first time), full suite clean (2608 passed, 46 skipped, 0 failed).

### Step 25z — Fix: four destructive actions have no confirmation step, violating this project's own established guardrail rule
Found by the same fourth adversarial pass. **Independently re-verified by direct code read** against the real merged code for all four; each confirmed exactly as a single click with zero confirmation. This project's own standing rule (set by the Uninstaller design, restated in this repo's `CLAUDE.md`): "Destructive or data-affecting actions need a separate, explicit confirmation, defaulting to No." Every other destructive action already in this codebase follows it — Library's "Reset the entire library" requires a checkbox *and* typing `RESET`; Library's bulk-delete requires a "Confirm delete" checkbox; Sources' video-import-overwrite (Step 25s) requires an explicit "I understand this replaces..." checkbox — these four are the ones that don't.

1. **`tabs/workspace_tab.py`'s "🗑️ Delete this drama"** (~line 1695) — the single most commonly-clicked destructive action in the app with the largest blast radius: one click calls `db.delete_drama(picked_id)`, which deletes the drama's entire database row and `shutil.rmtree()`s its whole on-disk directory (source audio/video, dub tracks, page images, exports — everything), with no confirmation of any kind. Highest priority of the four.
2. **`tabs/workspace_tab.py`'s "🗑️ Remove current audio/video"** (~line 1823) — immediately `os.remove()`s the drama's real source audio/video file(s), no confirmation. Notably inconsistent with Step 25s, which added a confirmation checkbox specifically for *overwriting* this same file via a Sources video re-import, but a direct in-place "Remove" of it was left unguarded.
3. **`tabs/workspace_tab.py`'s "🗑️ Remove raw novel context"** (~line 1803) — same pattern, smaller blast radius (one context file).
4. **`tabs/translate_tab.py`'s "🗑️ Clear history"** (~line 178) — immediately calls `db.clear_translate_history()`, no confirmation. Lowest severity of the four (standalone-translate log entries only, not drama/line data), but the same missing-guardrail shape.
5. **Add the same confirmation pattern already used elsewhere in this codebase** (a checkbox, defaulting unchecked, that must be ticked before the destructive button itself is enabled/shown — matching Library's existing "Confirm delete" pattern) to all four. "Delete this drama" (item 1), given its size, may warrant the heavier "type to confirm" pattern Library's full-reset already uses — planning session's call at implementation time.
6. **Re-verify before fixing**: confirm each of the four locations' exact current line numbers/shape before changing them.

**Exit:**
- A test confirms each of the four destructive buttons is disabled (or hidden) until its confirmation step is explicitly completed.
- A test confirms completing the confirmation step and then clicking still performs the real deletion/removal (the guardrail doesn't silently break the underlying action).
- Manual check: for each of the four, attempt the action without confirming (confirm nothing happens), then confirm and complete it, verifying the expected data is actually removed.

**Merged as PR #116** — opened and merged directly by this planning session after independent verification: base was exactly current `baihe-subtitler` tip, diff read in full for all four (item 1 correctly uses the heavier checkbox-plus-type-DELETE pattern, items 2-4 use the checkbox-only pattern), all 16 new/touched tests pass (disabled-until-confirmed and performs-the-real-action-once-confirmed for each), full suite clean (2633 passed, 46 skipped, 0 failed).

### Step 26 — Voice bank: reuse a cloned voice across projects
From a user request, explored on branch `claude/iqiyi-ai-vertical-shorts-mzim4n` (2026-09-26, `docs/handoff-voice-bank-translate-zh-narration.md`; nothing built there). Goal: sample voices from audio dramas already in the library, then reuse those clips for characters in other projects (mainly novel narration) without copying files and transcripts by hand.

**Re-verified against the current `baihe-subtitler` tip, confirmed accurate:** clone settings live per-character in the `characters` table (`db.py` ~164–170: `ref_audio_filename`, `ref_text`, `clone_engine`, `voice_design`, `tts_voice`, `offline_voice`). "🎯 Auto-extract reference clips from this audio" (`tabs/workspace_tab.py:3633`) runs `dub.extract_reference_clips` (`dub.py:459`), writing `<drama_dir>/voice_refs/<SPEAKER>.wav` and auto-filling `ref_text` from the matching transcript line (`tabs/workspace_tab.py:3638–3654`). Manual upload is `tabs/workspace_tab.py:3829` ("Upload clone reference for …"), saving `clone_ref_<label>.<ext>` in the drama folder. `series_characters` (`db.py:227`) remembers names/aliases/notes per series and Step 8's voice fingerprints, but stores no voice data. OmniVoice doesn't need `ref_text` (transcribes the clip itself, `dub.py:257`); GPT-SoVITS and F5-TTS do. There's a single shared `library.db` across all dramas (`db.py:18`, `DB_PATH`), the natural home for a library-wide table — `series_characters` already lives there as precedent. **CLI parity checked and doesn't apply**: `cli.py` has no command that reads or writes character voice/clone fields at all today, so there's no existing CLI path for this step to keep in parity with.

**Decided (open questions from the handoff doc, answered directly rather than left for a later ask):**
- **A bank entry is just a voice, not tied to a character.** Fields: name, the clip (a copy, not a reference — see below), `ref_text`, preferred engine, optional voice-design text, language, notes, and where it came from (source drama + speaker), for provenance only.
- **One clip per voice for this version.** Matches what exists today (one `ref_audio_filename` per character); revisit only if a specific engine's quality clearly needs more.

1. A `voice_bank` table in the shared library DB, plus a copied clip file under the library folder (not a reference into the source drama's folder) — so deleting the source drama doesn't break a bank entry.
2. "💾 Save to voice bank" next to each character's clone reference in Workspace, in any project — copies the clip and the fields listed above into a new bank entry.
3. "Use a voice from the bank" on each character, in any project — copies the bank entry's clip into that drama's folder and sets the matching clone fields (`ref_audio_filename`, `ref_text`, `clone_engine`, `voice_design` — the bank's own field list per the "Decided" note above; `tts_voice`/`offline_voice` are edge-tts/Piper *fallback* voice names, unrelated to cloning, and a bank entry never stores or sets them).
4. A preview button (play the clip in place) and delete/rename on each bank entry. Natural home: a new collapsible section in the Library tab (no new top-level tab needed for this alone — consistent with keeping the tab bar from growing without cause).
5. A short, visible note wherever a bank entry is created or applied: voices cloned from commercial audio dramas are for personal use only.

**Exit:**
- A test shows saving a character's clone reference to the bank creates an entry with a copied clip file (not a path into the source drama's folder).
- A test shows applying a bank entry to a character in a different drama sets that drama's clone fields and copies the clip into that drama's folder.
- A test shows deleting the source drama afterward leaves the bank entry's own clip intact.
- Manual check: sample a clone reference from an existing drama, save it to the voice bank with a name, then open a different (or new) drama, apply that bank voice to a character, and confirm it dubs correctly with no manual copying of files. Preview a bank entry's clip, then rename and delete an entry and confirm both take effect.

### Step 26b — Standalone translate section (kr/jp/cn ↔ English)
From the same exploration session and handoff doc. Goal: a separate place to paste source text and get a translation, without creating a drama or project — in both directions (ko/ja/zh → English, and English → those three).

**Re-verified against the current `baihe-subtitler` tip, confirmed accurate:** translation only runs inside a drama today. The system prompt is hardcoded to translate "into natural, idiomatic English subtitles" (`translate_engines.py:355`) and assumes the baihe/GL genre and a medium — there is no path from English into zh/ja/ko anywhere in the app. `source_language` is a per-drama field, `'zh'`/`'ja'`/`'ko'` (`db.py:121`). Engines live in `translate_engines.ENGINES` (`translate_engines.py:1506`); `TRANSLATION_ONLY_ENGINES = {"deepl", "google", "nllb", "libretranslate"}` (`translate_engines.py:1528`) can't take instructions or context, so they're the ones most likely to already support English→CJK — the others (Claude/DeepSeek/Gemini/Ollama) depend on prompting, and Ollama specifically depends on the model. The tab bar is nine tabs wired in `app.py:90` (Library/Workspace/Reader/Scanlate/Sources/Navigator/Discover/Live/Diagnostics) — no existing tab is a natural fit, so this needs its own.

**Decided (open questions from the handoff doc, answered directly):**
- **Save a history** (source text, output, engine, date) — not a button to turn a result into a novel project. Keeps this a standalone utility rather than coupling it to the project/drama system; a "start a project from this" hop can be reconsidered later as its own small step if the workflow turns out to want it.
- **No series glossary/character-name context in this first version**, matching the handoff doc's own suggested default. The optional series picker is a small, separate follow-up once the basic tool is in use.

1. A new tab with a text box plus paste/upload (`.txt`/`.md`/`.epub`; `core.load_novel_text_for_context` may help for `.epub`), source/target language pickers where one side is always English and the other is zh/ja/ko, and an engine picker reusing the Settings-configured keys.
2. Output shown side by side, with copy and a `.txt` download.
3. A history list (source snippet, output, engine, source/target languages, date) persisted in the shared library DB, viewable and clearable from the same tab.
4. Chunk long text using the existing id-keyed request/retry helpers (`translate_engines._request_translations_with_retry`/`_parse_id_keyed_json`) — never match results back by position, per this project's own standing rule.
5. A new, generic system prompt — not subtitle-specific, not genre-locked. The existing drama-translation prompt (`translate_engines.py:355`) stays unchanged.
6. A new prompt path for English → CJK, plus a check of which configured engine actually supports the requested direction (DeepL/Google/NLLB do both ways; Ollama depends on the model — surface this rather than silently failing or mistranslating).

**Exit:**
- A test shows a zh/ja/ko → English request and an English → zh/ja/ko request both produce output using the correct direction's prompt.
- A test shows long input is chunked and reassembled by id, not by list position.
- A test shows an engine that doesn't support the requested direction is refused with a clear reason rather than silently attempted.
- A test shows a completed translation is saved to history and appears in a history listing.
- Manual check: paste a short Korean, Japanese or Chinese passage and translate it to English, then paste a short English passage and translate it into each of the three languages. Confirm the output is readable and check the saved history shows both.

**Built and pushed (`claude/step-26b-roadmap-re56bo`), reviewed by the planning session — real, well-built, but one genuine gap, not approved yet.** Independently verified: fetched fresh (stale by three merges — missing 23i, the direct CLAUDE.md push, and 23j; trial merge of the current tip confirmed clean, no real conflict). Diffed against the real merge-base: 9 files, +848/-19, matching the branch's own scope closely. Verified the specific technical claims directly, not assumed: `standalone_translate` correctly reuses the existing id-keyed retry/parse helper (`_request_translations_with_retry`) via each LLM engine's own `translate_batch` (confirmed in `ClaudeEngine.translate_batch`) — with no `line_ids` passed, it falls back to 1..n positional numbering, which is correct here (one self-contained chunk request, not cross-request line data persisted across saves), not a reintroduction of the "match by position" bug. `standalone_direction_support`'s English→CJK gating is sound: DeepL/Google/NLLB allowed both ways (they take an explicit source+target pair), Ollama allowed with an honest quality-caveat warning, LibreTranslate refused outright (its `translate_batch` has no source-language parameter at all) rather than silently attempted. `db.py`'s new `translate_history` table matches the roadmap's own decision exactly — library-level, history saved and clearable, no "turn into a project" button, no series-glossary context in v1. ### Step 26c — Narrate in the original language, with bilingual subtitles
From the same exploration session and handoff doc. Goal: novel narration read aloud in the original language (Chinese, and ideally Japanese/Korean too), using voices sampled from audio dramas (Step 26), with subtitles from the translation.

**Re-verified against the current `baihe-subtitler` tip, confirmed accurate:** narration always speaks the translation today — `dub._narration_steps` (`dub.py:800`) and `build_dub_track` (`dub.py:676`) both read `ln.en`, as do the chapter-title, time-splitting and "voiced" filter logic (`dub.py:950–996`). The module's own docstring says "generates an English AI dub track" (`dub.py:2`). GPT-SoVITS hardcodes `"text_lang": "en"` (`dub.py:287`); `_GPT_SOVITS_LANGUAGES` (`dub.py:274`) already maps zh/ja/ko, but only for the reference clip's `prompt_lang`. Default edge-tts voices are all English (`DEFAULT_VOICE_POOL`, `dub.py:32`; `build_narration_track`'s own default, `dub.py:825`, is `en-US-AvaNeural`). Confirmed the field-naming question the handoff doc itself flagged: `ln.zh` is the app's generic source-text field regardless of the drama's actual `source_language` — it holds Japanese or Korean text too when that's the source, not literally Chinese-only (`core.py`'s `Line`/`LINE_FIELDS`).

**Decided (open question from the handoff doc, answered directly):**
- **Bilingual subtitles (source + English), not English-only.** Once the audio itself switches to the original language, English-only subtitles would leave the source text visible nowhere at all — bilingual keeps both, consistent with how the rest of the app already treats source-plus-translation, and reuses Step 6b's existing bilingual export path (already confirmed working, used again as recently as Step 12's Reader captions) rather than building a second one.

1. A per-drama setting, "Narrate in: original language / translation," defaulting to "translation" so existing behavior is unchanged for every drama that doesn't opt in.
2. In original mode: speak `ln.zh` (confirmed generic, holds ja/ko source text too) instead of `ln.en`; pass the drama's `source_language` to GPT-SoVITS's `text_lang` instead of the hardcoded `"en"`; default edge-tts to a voice in the source language instead of `en-US-AvaNeural`; split time within a unit by the length of the source text; use source-text chapter titles in the M4B; include the narration language in the clip cache signature so switching modes regenerates clips rather than serving stale ones from the other language.
3. Subtitles stay bilingual (source + `ln.en`), timed to the source-language audio — verify against the `.srt` and M4B output specifically, since the audio's timing now comes from the source text, not the translation.
4. Translation becomes optional in original mode for the audio itself (narration should still work with no `ln.en`), but bilingual subtitles need it — warn clearly when a line has no translation yet rather than silently dropping it from the subtitle track.
5. Scope check, confirmed by re-reading the doc's own reasoning: dubbing a **video** in its original language doesn't make sense (the video already has the original audio) — this step stays scoped to novel narration only, not `build_dub_track`'s video-dub path.
6. Before offering OmniVoice/Chatterbox/TADA in original mode, confirm each actually supports Chinese/Japanese/Korean (not just English) — hide or warn on any that don't, rather than letting a silent bad-quality clone through.

**Exit:**
- A test shows original mode speaks `ln.zh` and passes the drama's real `source_language` to GPT-SoVITS's `text_lang`, not the hardcoded `"en"`.
- A test shows the clip-cache signature changes when the narration-language setting changes, so switching modes doesn't serve a stale clip.
- A test shows exported subtitles in original mode are bilingual (source + English), not English-only.
- A test shows narration still produces audio when a line has no translation yet, with a clear warning that its subtitle will be incomplete.

### Step 27 — Diagnostics: show whether each dependency is on the latest version, and add an Upgrade action
Found by direct code read of `diagnostics_tab.py`/`diagnostics.py` at the user's request, checking whether Diagnostics' dependency panel does what it visually implies. **Confirmed by direct code read, not inferred from the UI or from README claims.**

**What's already real and working, confirmed directly:** `diagnostics.OPTIONAL_DEPENDENCIES` covers ~40 packages across four tiers (Core/Translation engines/Optional features/Development), each shown with ✅/❌ installed status and an "N/M installed" count per tier. The "⬇️ Install" button (`diagnostics_tab.py`'s Dependencies section) genuinely streams real `pip install` output live via `diagnostics.stream_pip_install`, then automatically re-runs diagnostics and calls `st.rerun()` on success — so a freshly-installed package does take effect without a manual app restart, since it was never imported before and Python's own import system just needs it present on disk at next import time.

**The real gap: nothing anywhere checks whether an installed package is current, and there is no upgrade path.** Confirmed by reading both halves of the page that show any version information at all:
1. **The dependency list itself** (`diagnostics.check_all_dependencies()`) only ever returns `{"installed": bool, "powers": str, "tier": str}` per package — no version field exists in this data structure at all.
2. **The separate "🧩 Model & engine versions" section** (`diagnostics.get_model_engine_versions()`) does read each installed version via `importlib.metadata.version()` — but its own caption states this plainly: *"No network call -- this doesn't check whether something newer exists, only what's here right now."* Confirmed no PyPI (or other registry) query exists anywhere in `diagnostics.py`.
3. **The "⬇️ Install" button only ever appears for a currently-missing package** — `diagnostics_tab.py`'s own gating condition is `installable = tier in INSTALLABLE_TIERS and not info["installed"]`. An already-installed-but-outdated package has zero path to update from this page; there is no "Upgrade" button anywhere. The one exception, confirmed separately, is the dedicated "⚡ Install GPU PyTorch" button, which unconditionally uninstalls+reinstalls torch/torchaudio for the CPU-vs-GPU-build mismatch case specifically — not a general version-freshness mechanism.

1. **Add a real "is this outdated" check.** For each installed dependency, compare the installed version (`importlib.metadata.version()`, already available) against the latest available version — query PyPI's JSON API (`https://pypi.org/pypi/<name>/json`, a simple unauthenticated GET) for standard packages. Cache the result for the session (or a short TTL) rather than querying on every page load, and make this an explicit opt-in action (a button, matching the existing "🔍 Check pyannote access" pattern which is the one check on this page that already makes a network call only on click) rather than automatic — consistent with this page's own stated "no network call" default.
2. **Show the result per dependency**: current version, latest version, and a clear up-to-date/outdated indicator — extending the existing per-package row, not a new UI section.
3. **Add a real "⬆️ Upgrade" action** for an outdated (but already-installed) dependency, reusing the existing `stream_pip_install`/`_run_pip_stream` machinery with `--upgrade` added to the pip args — same live-streamed-output, same auto-rerun-on-success pattern the Install button already uses, so this is additive to existing infrastructure, not a new install mechanism.
4. **Respect the existing exclusivity constraints already documented in this file** (OmniVoice/Chatterbox-TTS/hume-tada can't share one environment; torch/torchaudio version caps from `constraints.txt`) — an Upgrade action must not silently violate a constraint this same file already established elsewhere.

### Step 28 — Fix: three real gaps found in a final review of the `sources/` adapter package — two ToS-check bypasses and a credential-redaction gap for path-embedded tokens
Found by a dedicated adversarial pass over the whole `sources/` package, dispatched now that the entire 23-series adapter batch is complete. **All three independently re-verified by direct code read** against the real merged code before writing this up.

**Gap 1 — the Sources tab's "Test Now" diagnostic buttons send a real live request with zero ToS enforcement (`sources/ladder.py`'s `test_tier()`, lines 369-389; called from `tabs/sources_tab.py`'s "Test Static"/"Test Browser"/"Test Authenticated" buttons, ~lines 803-824).** `test_tier()` calls `tier_fn(url)` — `static_tier`/`rendered_tier`/`authenticated_tier` — directly, with no `check_terms()`/`apply_terms()` call anywhere in the function or its caller. Every other action path that touches the network (`generic_import.fetch_page`, `pipeline.run_import_job`, `chapter_check.check_series`, `registry.multi_search`, `auth_browser.manual_login`/`verify`, the series-browse button in `sources_tab.py`) calls `check_terms()` first — this is the one that doesn't. The buttons themselves aren't even conditionally hidden for a prohibited source, since the `caps` used to render them comes from `load_capabilities()` with no `apply_terms()` applied. Currently dormant only because every shipped adapter declares `tos_prohibited: False` — the gap is real and reachable the moment any adapter's default (or a future one) sets it `True`, exactly the class of bug Step 25q already fixed once for search/browse/tracked-series-checking.

**Gap 2 — `front_door.import_video()` is the one adapter-invoking "import" action path in the package with no `check_terms()` call of its own (`sources/front_door.py:160-196`; the same-file `preview()` does call it, but that's a separate, earlier call for a different purpose — building the preview, not gating the actual download).** Unlike `pipeline.run_import_job`, which deliberately *re-checks* `check_terms()` per chapter specifically so the download action doesn't rely on an earlier UI step having checked, `import_video()` goes straight from `registry.find_for_url(url)` to `adapter.download(url, ddir, options=...)`. `BilibiliSource.download()` (`sources/adapters/bilibili.py:305-383`) has no such check either. Separately, `_real_url_resolver()` (same file, lines 168-172, used to expand a `b23.tv` short link before download) makes a bare `requests.head()` call, bypassing `sources/http.py`'s shared `SourceClient` transport (and therefore its pacing/rate-limiting) entirely. Currently dormant because Bilibili's own capabilities set `tos_prohibited: False`, but this is a structural gap that would silently ignore a future restricted VideoSource adapter's terms.

**Gap 3 — `ai_extract.prompt_safe()`'s credential redaction only matches query-string-shaped tokens (`key=value` after `?`/`&`/`#`/`;`), not the same kind of session-derived token embedded as a raw URL path segment (`sources/ai_extract.py`'s `_SENSITIVE_PARAM` regex, lines 321-324; `translate_engines.redact_secrets`'s `_SECRET_PATTERNS`, lines 265-271, layered on top, has the same narrower shape — a `?key=` param, an `Authorization:`/`Bearer` header dump, or an `sk-`/`AIza` prefix).** A CDN URL carrying a signed token as a path component with no `=` at all (a common real shape, e.g. `https://cdn.example/priv/<signed-token>/page1.jpg`) passes through both redaction layers untouched. This is reachable whenever the adaptive extraction pipeline's LLM-fallback tier builds a prompt containing image/media/link URLs from an authenticated-browser session (`sources/auth_browser.py`) — `ai_extract.py`'s own module docstring claims "session-derived credentials inside ordinary URLs ... are blanked before any prompt leaves the app," a guarantee that only actually holds for the query-string-shaped case.

1. **Fix Gap 1**: add a `check_terms()` call to `test_tier()` (or its caller in `sources_tab.py`) before invoking any tier function, and apply `apply_terms()` to the capabilities record used to render/enable the three buttons, so a prohibited source's diagnostic buttons are disabled the same way its real import path already is.
2. **Fix Gap 2**: add a `check_terms()` call to `import_video()` before dispatching to `adapter.download()`, matching `pipeline.run_import_job`'s own "re-check at the actual action, don't rely on an earlier preview" pattern. Route `_real_url_resolver()`'s HEAD request through the shared `SourceClient`/`sources/http.py` transport instead of a bare `requests.head()` call.
3. **Fix Gap 3**: extend `_SENSITIVE_PARAM` (or add a second pattern) to also match a high-entropy-looking path segment following a plausible marker (e.g. a long base64url/hex-like segment between path separators) — re-verify the real shape of a genuine signed-URL path token from an actual CDN before writing the pattern, rather than guessing a regex that's either too narrow (misses the real shape) or too broad (redacts legitimate path content like a real chapter/page slug).
4. **Re-verify before fixing**: confirm the exact current line numbers/shape of all three locations before changing them.

**Exit:**
- A test confirms `test_tier()` refuses to run any tier against a source whose capabilities are `tos_prohibited`/`automation_permission: EXPLICITLY_RESTRICTED`, the same way `generic_import.fetch_page` already does.

### Step 29 — Fix: two real gaps in `dub.py`'s clip-cache crash-safety and edge-tts/Piper-fallback signature
Found by a dedicated adversarial pass over `dub.py`, dispatched because it's flagged elsewhere in this roadmap as the single most complex file in the app (four/five TTS backends, parallelized generation, emotion→delivery mapping) and had never had its own deep review pass. **Both independently re-verified by direct code read**, including confirming the exact Python `wave`/`soundfile` write-then-patch-header-on-close behavior the first finding depends on.

**Bug 1 — `build_dub_track` writes each clip directly to its final cache path with no atomic temp-file/rename step, unlike `build_narration_track`, so a Cancel or kill mid-synthesis can leave a corrupted-but-loadable clip that survives the "already generated" reuse check and gets silently baked into the mix forever (`dub.py`'s `build_dub_track`, ~lines 695-724, vs. `build_narration_track`'s `generate()`, ~lines 895-916).** `build_narration_track` deliberately writes to a `.partial.wav` temp name and only `os.replace()`s it into place after a successful synth call, with its own comment explaining this is specifically so a kill mid-write (`background_jobs.py`'s `_process_watcher` calls `proc.terminate()` unconditionally on Cancel) never leaves a partial file for the next run's reuse check to pick up. `build_dub_track` has no such step — every backend's synth call (`_synthesize_cloned`, `synthesize_line_offline`, GPT-SoVITS, Chatterbox, TADA, `_synthesize_edge_tts_with_piper_fallback`) writes straight to `clip_path`. The only guard is a bare `try: AudioSegment.from_file(clip_path) except: pass` — which only helps if loading a truncated file actually raises, and often it won't: `synthesize_line_offline`'s `wave.open(out_path, "wb")` (confirmed: Python's `wave` module writes a placeholder header up front and only patches the real frame count on `close()`) leaves a technically-valid, zero-frame WAV file if terminated mid-write — `AudioSegment.from_file()` loads it successfully as silent, zero-length audio, no exception at all. `soundfile.write()` (used by OmniVoice/Chatterbox/TADA) has the same close-time-header-patch behavior. Trigger: click Cancel on a running dub job (or Ctrl-C a `cli.py dub` run) while a clip is mid-synthesis. Failure: that line's cache file is left silently corrupted or truncated, reused as-is on every future run with no error recorded and no indication to the user — the only fix is manually finding and deleting that one clip file.

**Bug 2 — the clip-cache signature can't tell a real edge-tts render from the silent Piper fallback, so a line rendered by the "lower quality" offline fallback voice is cached and reused indistinguishably from a normal edge-tts line, with no way to detect it or force a re-render once Microsoft's periodic block lifts (`dub.py`'s `_voice_for_signature`, ~line 546, vs. `_synthesize_edge_tts_with_piper_fallback`, ~lines 148-161).** The signature is computed *before* synthesis, from the intended engine/voice only — `_voice_for_signature(None, "edge_tts", voice, ...)` always returns `{"engine": "edge_tts", "voice": voice}` regardless of which engine actually produced the audio. `_synthesize_edge_tts_with_piper_fallback` silently switches to `synthesize_line_offline` (a completely different engine, model, and voice) on `EdgeTTSBlockedError`, writing to the exact same `clip_path` the edge-tts-labeled signature produced. Trigger: any dub run during a period edge-tts is blocked (Piper installed as fallback — the module's own docstring names this as a real, periodic occurrence). Failure: no record anywhere that a given line was actually rendered by Piper, so voice quality can silently vary across a track with no way to identify affected lines; once the block lifts, re-running the dub does not retry those lines with edge-tts — the unchanged signature means the stale Piper clip is reused indefinitely, discoverable only by manually deleting the file.

1. **Fix Bug 1**: apply the same temp-file/`os.replace()` pattern `build_narration_track`'s `generate()` already uses to every backend's synth call inside `build_dub_track`, so a kill mid-write can never leave a corrupted file at the final cache path.
2. **Fix Bug 2**: make the signature (or a marker stored alongside the clip) reflect which engine actually produced the audio, not just which one was intended — so a Piper-fallback-rendered clip is distinguishable from a normal edge-tts one and gets correctly re-tried once edge-tts recovers, rather than being cached under an indistinguishable signature forever.
3. **Re-verify before fixing**: confirm the exact current shape of both functions, and of every backend's synth call signature, before changing them.

**Exit:**
- A test confirms a simulated kill mid-write (the synth call raises partway through, after some but not all bytes are written to `clip_path`, not before any file exists at all — the existing `test_a_cancelled_run_still_resumes_from_its_finished_clips` test only covers the latter) leaves no corrupted file at the final cache path for `build_dub_track` to reuse.
- A test confirms a line rendered via the Piper fallback is retried with edge-tts on a subsequent run once edge-tts is no longer blocked, rather than reusing the stale Piper clip.
- Manual check: start a real dub job, kill it mid-synthesis (e.g. `kill -TERM` the worker process), confirm the interrupted line's clip isn't silently reused as corrupted/silent audio on the next run.

**Merged as PR #120 (2026-09-27).** Independently reviewed and verified by the planning session before merge: base matched current `baihe-subtitler` tip exactly, trial-merge against tip clean, full diff read for both fixes (`build_dub_track` now writes to a `.partial.wav` temp path and `os.replace()`s it into place, cleaning up on failure; `_synthesize_edge_tts_with_piper_fallback` now returns whether Piper actually rendered the clip, and both `build_dub_track`/`build_narration_track` cache a Piper-fallback clip under a distinct `.piper_fallback.wav` path so a later run retries edge-tts instead of reusing it forever) — confirmed the `clip_path` reassignment happens before `os.replace()` in both call sites, and that the later track-assembly loop reads the same mutated dict field, so the distinct path threads through correctly. New regression tests read and run directly: 66 passed (`tests/test_dub.py`), including a real kill-after-partial-bytes repro and both engines' Piper-fallback-then-recovery scenarios. Full suite independently re-run on the branch: **2717 passed, 46 skipped, 0 failed.** CI green. Merged via squash, `merged: true` confirmed via `pull_request_read`.

### Step 31 — Detect a content-moderation refusal distinctly, and offer a real retry

Found by direct code read, at the user's request, after asking whether the app can translate gore/explicit content and whether a fallback exists if a request is blocked. **The answer confirmed by reading the actual code: there is no content-moderation handling anywhere in this app** — no Gemini `safety_settings` override, no per-engine refusal detection, nothing distinguishing "the model refused this on safety grounds" from any other failure. The real severity, confirmed by tracing the actual call path rather than assumed: **a single blocked line can currently fail an entire translation batch of up to 20 lines**, not just itself.

**Confirmed across all three cloud LLM engines (Claude, DeepSeek, Gemini) — each bundles up to `batch_size` (default 20) lines into one request/response, and none reads any moderation-specific signal:**

1. **Hard block, uncaught (`translate_engines.py`'s `GeminiEngine.translate_batch`, ~line 946)** — `data["candidates"][0]["content"]["parts"][0]["text"]` is raw dict/list indexing with no defensive check. A real Gemini safety block returns either an empty `candidates` list (with `promptFeedback.blockReason` instead) or a candidate whose `finishReason` is `"SAFETY"` with no `content` key at all — both shapes raise a bare `IndexError`/`KeyError` here. That exception propagates straight out of `_id_keyed_batch_request` (`translate_engines.py`, ~line 593 — the shared `text = call_model_fn(...)` call has no try/except around it) and out of `_request_translations_with_retry`, reaching `translate_lines_with_engine`'s outer "a failed batch is retried once, then left untranslated" handling with nothing but a cryptic Python exception message — **not just the offending line, the whole batch's up-to-20 lines**. `DeepSeekEngine.translate_batch` (~line 823, `resp.choices[0].message.content.strip()`) has the same shape of risk if a refusal ever comes back with `content: null` (a real, documented shape for some OpenAI-compatible refusal responses).
2. **Soft refusal, silently swallowed (`ClaudeEngine`/`DeepSeekEngine.translate_batch`)** — a model that declines in prose instead of returning the requested JSON just makes `_parse_id_keyed_json` (~line 560) return `{}` — indistinguishable from an ordinary format hiccup. `_id_keyed_batch_request`'s retry-missing-ids loop retries once, then whichever ids never got a JSON entry are simply absent from the result — `_request_translations_with_retry` returns `""` for each, and the caller records the whole batch as failed with no reason ever surfaced. Neither Claude's own `stop_reason` field (which can read `"refusal"`) nor an OpenAI-style `refusal` field is ever read.
3. **The one path already safe by construction: Ollama.** Local models have no cloud-side content filter, so it's already the one engine in this app guaranteed not to refuse on these grounds — the natural fallback destination, not something to build from scratch.

1. **Detect the hard-block case structurally, per engine, using each provider's own real signal — not a guess.** For Gemini: check `data.get("candidates")` is non-empty and the first candidate has a `finishReason` other than `"SAFETY"`/`"PROHIBITED_CONTENT"` before indexing into it; if blocked, raise a new `ContentModerationBlocked(engine, reason)` exception carrying the real `blockReason`/`finishReason` string, not a bare `KeyError`. For DeepSeek/OpenAI-compatible: check for a `None`/empty `message.content` alongside a `refusal` field before calling `.strip()`, raising the same exception type with whatever reason field is present. **Re-verify the exact current response shapes against each provider's real, current API docs before writing the check** — this project's own "never guess" rule, especially since a safety-response shape can change between API versions.
2. **Best-effort detection for the soft-refusal case** — when a batch attempt returns non-empty raw text but zero ids parse out of it (a real, distinguishable state from "malformed JSON with some ids recovered"), don't just silently mark it a parse failure: check the raw text for the response's own `stop_reason`/`refusal` field first (a real signal, not a guess) and only fall back to a text-pattern heuristic (a short list of clear refusal-shaped openers, e.g. "I can't" / "I won't" / "I'm not able to") as a lower-confidence secondary signal — label this path as best-effort in the code's own comments, since a heuristic can both false-positive and false-negative.
3. **Isolate the failure to the actual blocked line(s), not the whole batch, where practical.** On a caught `ContentModerationBlocked` (or a detected soft refusal) for a batch of more than one remaining id, retry once by bisecting the batch into two halves before giving up — this narrows down which specific line(s) triggered it in the common case without a combinatorial full binary search, and leaves the rest of the batch's genuinely fine lines translated instead of blank. Keep this a bounded, one-level split (not full per-line bisection) to avoid multiplying API calls unboundedly on a large batch.
4. **Add `"content_blocked"` to `translate_engines.SYSTEM_FLAG_REASONS`** (same dict `"timing_uncertain"`/`"reading_speed"`/etc. already live in, ~line 1292), with the flag_note carrying the real engine name and the provider's own stated reason — surfaced through the existing Review-queue flag/flag_note display (already real UI, no new surface needed), instead of the line being left blank with an opaque batch-error string.
5. **A real "retry with a different engine" action** on a `content_blocked`-flagged line in the Review queue, defaulting the suggested engine to Ollama (the one already-safe path) but letting the user pick any configured engine — reusing whatever single-line retranslate path Review already has, with the engine overridden just for that retry rather than switching the whole drama's default engine.

**Exit:**
- A test confirms a mocked Gemini response shaped like a real safety block (empty `candidates` + `promptFeedback.blockReason`, and separately a candidate with `finishReason: "SAFETY"` and no `content`) raises `ContentModerationBlocked` with the real reason, not a bare `KeyError`/`IndexError`.
- A test confirms a mocked DeepSeek/OpenAI-style `content: null` + `refusal` response is caught the same way.
- A test confirms a batch where one line's response is refused doesn't blank out every other line in that batch — the bisection retry actually narrows it down and translates the rest.
- A test confirms a `content_blocked`-flagged line shows the real engine + reason in the Review queue, and that "retry with a different engine" actually re-translates just that line through the newly-chosen engine.
- Manual check: with a real Gemini key, feed a line likely to trip its safety filter (a genuinely graphic passage, not a synthetic test string) and confirm it comes back as a clearly-labeled "blocked by Gemini's content filter" flag rather than a raw error or a silently-blank line, with a working "retry with Ollama" action.

**Built, reviewed, and merged (2026-09-27, PR #170).** Independently reviewed: real diff read in full across all three engines (Claude `stop_reason`, DeepSeek `refusal` field, Gemini `blockReason`/`finishReason`), the bisection retry (bounded to one level, confirmed via the `allow_bisect=False` recursion guard), the `bulk_translate.py` persistence gap fix, and the Review-queue retry UI (default Ollama, scoped to one line, handles a re-block and a missing API key gracefully). Trial-merged clean, full suite run on the merged tree — 3261 passed, 49 skipped, 0 failed. All four automated Exit-criteria tests present and match; the fifth (a real Gemini key against a genuinely graphic passage) correctly left as a pending manual check. Self-flagged scope exclusions (Reflect mode, ~11 other `call_llm_json` sites, one wasted retry in `call_with_backoff`) are real and correctly left out of scope. CI green before squash-merge.

### Step 32 — Expose look-ahead context and batch size as adjustable; a bigger-context default for novel-narration mode

Found by direct code read, at the user's request, after asking whether translation accuracy for novels/long-form content could be improved by increasing context. **Confirmed there are three separate "how much surrounding text the model sees" knobs, and only one of the three is actually user-adjustable today:**

1. **Look-back context (`context_window`) — already exposed.** `tabs/workspace_tab.py`'s translation section has a real slider (~line 3055, `st.slider("Context lines shown from before each batch", 0, 20, 6, ...)`), threaded through `run_translate_job`/`translate_lines_with_engine` correctly.
2. **Look-ahead context (`context_window_ahead`) — hardcoded, no UI control at all.** `translate_lines_with_engine`'s own signature defaults it to `3` (`translate_engines.py`, ~line 2077); `run_translate_job` (`tabs/workspace_tab.py`, ~line 269) never passes an override, so every translation run uses the hardcoded default with no way to change it short of editing code. This is the one most directly relevant to novels: knowing what's coming up matters for resolving a pronoun or reference in long-form prose, at least as much as knowing what came before.
3. **Batch size (lines translated per single LLM call, live-mode path) — hardcoded, no UI control.** `translate_lines_with_engine`'s `batch_size` parameter defaults to `20` and is never overridden by its one live-mode caller. (Bulk mode's several separate paths in `bulk_translate.py` have their own independent hardcoded batch sizes — 20/30/40/60 depending on the feature — genuinely a separate subsystem; out of scope for this step, noted for a possible follow-up rather than conflated with it.)
4. **Novel-narration's own chunk size, distinct from all three above.** `core.chunk_novel_text(raw_text, max_chars=200)` is what actually splits an imported novel's raw text into the "lines" every other knob then operates on — hardcoded, no UI control. A larger chunk size means each unit already carries more context on its own, before context_window/context_window_ahead/batch_size even apply.

**A real, asymmetric cost worth stating plainly, not glossed over:** for the cloud engines (Claude/Gemini/DeepSeek), their real context windows are far larger than anything this app currently sends, so raising these defaults is close to free — a cost/latency tradeoff only. For **Ollama**, `_estimate_ollama_num_ctx` already dynamically sizes `num_ctx` to fit whatever prompt these knobs produce (no separate wiring needed there) — but a much larger context_window/context_window_ahead/batch_size combination pushes a local model's real VRAM/token-processing cost up correspondingly, the same real hardware constraint Step 5/5c's GPU-sizing guidance already established elsewhere in this roadmap. Increasing these defaults for novel-narration mode should not silently also raise Ollama's effective cost with no way to opt out.

1. **Add a look-ahead slider** next to the existing look-back one, same UI section, same pattern (`st.slider`, a similarly clear help string) — wire `context_window_ahead` through the same `run_translate_job` → `translate_lines_with_engine` call chain the existing look-back value already uses (`tabs/workspace_tab.py` ~lines 269/301/347/355/386).
2. **Add a batch-size control** for the live-translate path specifically (not bulk mode's separate paths) — a slider or number input, reasonable bounds (e.g. 5–40), same wiring pattern.
3. **A bigger-context default specifically for `content_mode == "novel_narration"`** — when a drama is in novel-narration mode, pre-select higher starting values for context_window/context_window_ahead/batch_size (and consider raising `chunk_novel_text`'s default `max_chars` for novels specifically) rather than reusing the audio-drama-oriented defaults — the user can still move any slider afterward, this only changes the starting point. Keep this a default, not a forced value, so a user who wants a smaller/cheaper novel run isn't blocked from choosing that.
4. **Surface the Ollama VRAM/latency cost explicitly** somewhere the user actually sees it before it bites them — e.g. a caption near the sliders noting that larger values cost more time/VRAM specifically when the selected engine is Ollama, not a silent effect.
5. **Re-verify before building**: confirm the exact current line numbers and default values for all four knobs above against the real file before wiring anything, per this project's own standing rule — this write-up is accurate as of this review, but later steps may have touched these exact lines.

**Exit:**
- A test confirms the look-ahead slider's value actually reaches `translate_lines_with_engine`'s `context_window_ahead` parameter, the same way the existing look-back slider already does for `context_window`.
- A test confirms the batch-size control's value actually reaches `translate_lines_with_engine`'s `batch_size` parameter.
- A test confirms a novel-narration drama's translation section pre-selects the higher starting values, while an audio-drama's still starts at today's defaults.
- Manual check: translate a long novel-narration chapter with the look-ahead slider raised and confirm a pronoun/reference near the start of a batch that depends on something stated just after it resolves correctly, where it previously wouldn't have (or would have needed a lucky context_window value to catch it retroactively).

**Built, reviewed, and merged (2026-09-27, PR #164).** Independently reviewed: real diff read in full, the "left `chunk_novel_text` alone" judgment call independently verified by diff (no changes to `core.py` at all, confirmed), trial-merged clean, full suite run on the merged tree — **3177 passed, 49 skipped, 0 failed** (the 5 `test_sources_mangaz.py` failures the implementing session reported were confirmed environment-specific to its own sandbox, not reproducible here). All three exit-criteria tests present and match. CI green before squash-merge. Manual check (translate a novel-narration chapter with the look-ahead slider raised, confirm a forward-resolved pronoun) still pending — real-app check, not verifiable from this session.

### Step 33 — Fix: `requirements-install.bat` hardcodes a personal Windows path

Flagged by the Step 16 implementing session while reading nearby files, not part of that step's own scope — independently confirmed by reading the real file at the repo root. **Its entire content is:**

```
cd C:\Users\Airbear\Documents\baihe-subtitler
python -m venv venv
venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

streamlit run app.py
```

This is stale personal-machine clutter, not what a real user's install actually runs — `start.bat` (Step 10's own launcher, confirmed the real fresh-install entry point already covered by Step 10b's CI bootstrap check) never calls this file, and nothing else in the repo references it either. Anyone who actually double-clicks `requirements-install.bat` on a machine that isn't `Airbear`'s gets a `cd` into a folder that doesn't exist, and the rest of the script silently runs from whatever the shell's own leftover working directory happens to be instead — not a clean failure, a wrong-directory install.

**Fix**: make the first line `cd /d %~dp0` — the standard Windows batch idiom that changes to the directory containing the running script itself (the `/d` also allows switching drive letters, which plain `cd` can't). This needs no prompt and no user-typed path: whatever folder the user cloned/extracted the repo into, the script finds itself and runs from there, matching what `start.bat` already does correctly. A prompt-for-location alternative was considered and rejected — it would add a step to every single install for something the shell can already determine for itself with zero ambiguity, and this app's own "fewer options over more" preference already argues against surfacing a choice nobody needs to make.

**Exit:**
- Manual check: from a folder other than `C:\Users\Airbear\Documents\baihe-subtitler`, run `requirements-install.bat` on a real Windows machine (or confirm via a Windows CI runner) and confirm it creates the venv and installs dependencies into the actual folder it was run from, not the old hardcoded path.
- Confirm no other file in the repo references the old hardcoded path (a plain repo-wide search for `Airbear` should return nothing after this fix).

### Step 35 — Fix: the ML bubble detector double-counts every balloon, and the free CV fallback is a silent near-no-op on color artwork

Reported directly by the user with a real measurement from running the ML detector against real artwork; independently traced through the actual code before writing this up (`scanlate.py`), not taken on the report alone.

**Bug 1 — double-counting, confirmed real.** `detect_bubbles_ml()` (`scanlate.py:149`) uses `ogkalu/comic-text-and-bubble-detector`, a 3-class model — its own docstring says "bubble / text-in-bubble / text-outside-bubble" — and returns every detected box from all three classes with a `"label"` field attached, but **nothing anywhere in the pipeline reads that field to filter or merge.** Confirmed by tracing the full call chain: `detect_and_ocr_page()` (`scanlate.py:1696`) calls `detect_bubbles()` and passes the raw `boxes` straight into `analyze_page_regions()` (`scanlate.py:1615`), which calls `classify_text_regions()` (`scanlate.py:1173`) — a *different*, independent bubble/narration/sign/sfx classifier that assigns its own `"kind"` field using local image geometry, entirely separate from the ML model's own 3-class `"label"`. At no point is IoU checked between boxes, and at no point is the ML model's own label used to drop the redundant class. Since a "bubble" box and a "text-in-bubble" box for the same physical balloon are near-identical in position and size by construction (one model, two classes describing the same object), both survive as independent `TextRegion`s, each gets its own `ocr_box_region()` call and its own translation slot. **Real measurement from the user's own run: 46 of 63 detected regions on one page overlapped another by more than 70%** — roughly double the OCR calls, roughly double the translation cost (translation is billed per line/region on every cloud engine this app supports), and two stacked, overlapping text-overlay boxes rendered on top of what should be a single balloon in the final output. This hits the Scanlate tab identically to any other caller, since `detect_and_ocr_page()` is the single shared entry point for both the per-page button and the whole-chapter batch path.

**Bug 2 — the free CV fallback is a silent, near-useless default on color artwork.** `detect_bubbles_cv()` (`scanlate.py:37`) is a pure OpenCV heuristic: Otsu-threshold for **light** pixels (floor of 180), close small gaps, take connected components, and keep only components that don't touch the page edge and are mostly-filled/convex. This is a real, working technique for the specific case of white/light speech bubbles on a typical black-and-white manga scan — but it has no mechanism at all for a colored bubble fill, a gradient, a textured/colored panel background, or webtoon-style full-color art, since its entire signal is "is this pixel above a light-value threshold." On real full-color artwork this isn't a "weaker" detector, it's close to a no-op — confirmed by reading the algorithm, not just the user's report, which matches: a colored bubble simply never clears the light-pixel threshold the same way a white one does. **This is also the silent default**, not just an available option: `detect_bubbles(backend="auto")` (`scanlate.py:266`) resolves to `"ml"` only if the model's weights are *already* cached locally, and to `"cv"` otherwise — meaning anyone who hasn't separately, manually triggered the ~multi-hundred-MB ML download in advance gets the weak heuristic on every page until they do, with the only in-app signal being a post-hoc "No bubbles detected on this page" error (`scanlate.py:1714`) that doesn't distinguish "this page has no bubbles" from "the free detector can't see color artwork at all."

1. **Dedupe overlapping detector boxes, keyed by geometry (IoU), not by the model's own class-label strings.** A label-string filter (e.g. "only keep boxes labeled `bubble`") is fragile if the checkpoint's label names ever change or a different checkpoint is swapped in later (this file's own `detect_bubbles_ml()` docstring already flags that possibility) — an IoU-based merge is robust to that and also naturally covers any future detector that has the same one-object/multiple-classes shape. Add this once, inside `detect_bubbles()` or immediately after `detect_bubbles_ml()` returns, so every caller (single-page Detect, whole-chapter batch) benefits without each needing its own fix. **Re-verify the real `id2label` class name strings from the actual checkpoint before deciding whether to also add a label-aware preference** (e.g., prefer the box literally labeled "bubble" over "text-in-bubble" when merging two overlapping boxes, for a cleaner crop boundary) — don't hardcode label strings from this write-up's paraphrase of the model card without checking the real `model.config.id2label` values first, per this project's own "re-verify before building" rule.
2. **Warn explicitly, in the UI, when `backend="auto"` is about to resolve to `cv`** — not just a post-hoc "no bubbles found" message once it's already failed. Something concrete: "Using the free detector (the trained ML model isn't downloaded yet) — this works well on black-and-white scans but often finds nothing on full-color art. [Download the ML backend]" surfaced before running detection, not just in the failure path. Reuse whatever "is this page mostly color vs. mostly grayscale" signal is cheapest to add (even a simple saturation-channel check) if it makes the warning specific rather than blanket — but a blanket warning whenever `auto` resolves to `cv` is an acceptable, simpler first cut if a real color-detection heuristic adds more complexity than it's worth.
3. **Re-verify the exact current line numbers and function boundaries above against the real file before building** — this write-up is accurate as of this review (2026-09-27), but later steps may have touched `scanlate.py` in the meantime.

**Exit:**
- A test using a synthetic/fixture pair of near-identical, high-IoU boxes (one per label, mimicking a real "bubble" + "text-in-bubble" pair for the same balloon) confirms `detect_bubbles()`/`detect_and_ocr_page()` returns exactly one region for the pair, not two.
- A test confirms two genuinely separate, non-overlapping bubbles on the same page are both kept — the dedupe must not merge real distinct bubbles that happen to be nearby.
- A test confirms the auto-resolves-to-cv warning actually appears when `backend="auto"` picks `cv` (ML weights not cached), and does not appear when it picks `ml`.
- Manual check: run the ML backend on a real chapter and confirm the returned bubble count roughly matches the actual balloon count on the page (not close to double), with exactly one overlay box per balloon in the review table.
- Manual check: with the ML weights not yet downloaded, open Scanlate on a real full-color manhua/webtoon page and confirm the UI states plainly that the free detector struggles on color art and offers the ML backend, rather than a bare "no bubbles detected."

## Steps 36–44: deliberately a later phase, not next-in-line

**These steps are gated on the rest of this roadmap's build-out substantially completing first — their sequential numbering is bookkeeping, not a build-order signal, and none of them should be sent to an implementing session while Steps 19–35 (and whatever's added after) are still the active work.** This distinction comes directly from how the source ChatGPT conversation itself framed this material, re-checked against the actual conversation text at the user's explicit request rather than assumed: it repeatedly separated "finish the heavy development" from "then make the application increasingly self-maintaining, reducing dependence on Claude/ChatGPT" — one exchange states plainly "you don't have to implement all of this before finishing your existing application... that lets your current app keep working while these capabilities are added around it," and another: "once the heavy development is finished, I'd design the app so subscriptions are optional rather than required." The whole point of this phase is to let the app maintain *itself* via API-only access (no ongoing Claude Code/ChatGPT Plus subscription) once it no longer needs heavy new-feature development — building them mid-development, while this project still actively depends on Claude Code sessions for its main build-out, would be solving a problem that hasn't arrived yet and would compete for review/implementation bandwidth against the actual current work.

**Internal ordering once this phase actually starts — taken directly from the source conversation's own explicit priority list, not this session's guess**: 1. provider abstraction (Step 36) → 2. local-model support (already substantially exists via Ollama; verify/extend, don't rebuild) → 3. caching/checkpointing (Step 41) → 4. automated tests (already this project's standing practice) → 5. golden translation datasets (Step 38's "application tier") → 6. benchmark/evaluation system (rest of Step 38) → 7. model registry + fallback system (Step 40) → 8. self-diagnostics (already substantially built — see the verified-gaps note below for what's actually still missing) → 9. AI maintenance chat (Step 42) → 10. automated dependency/model migration (also Step 40) → 11. packaging/updater (start.bat already does most of this — see Step 10/18c). Step 39 (Jellyfin) and Step 43 (soft-delete/rollback) and Step 44 (notifications) aren't in the source's own numbered list and can land independently at any point in this phase.

**Verified-gaps note (2026-09-27) — an independent code audit, not assumption, corrected several "already exists" claims from this session's own first review pass.** Cloned `baihe-subtitler` fresh and checked ten specific claims file-by-file rather than trusting memory, per the user's explicit "just because I have the feature doesn't mean the UI/function is all there" instruction:

### Step 36 — Capability-based AI task routing (provider abstraction refinement)

Prompted by an architecture proposal the user got from a separate ChatGPT conversation, independently reviewed against the real repo before writing this up. `translate_engines.py`'s `ENGINES`/`get_engine()` already gives every subsystem a real provider abstraction — that part isn't missing. What's missing is that every call site asks for a *specific engine name* (`"claude"`, `"gemini"`) rather than a *capability* — so swapping which real model backs a given job (e.g. when a provider deprecates a model, see Step 40) means touching every call site that hardcoded that engine name.

1. Add a thin capability registry — `resolve_capability("translation.high_quality")`, `resolve_capability("research.grounded_search")`, `resolve_capability("coding.strong")` — each mapping to a configured real engine, editable in Settings.
2. Additive layer over the existing engine registry, not a rewrite. Migrate call sites gradually; this step doesn't require converting everything at once.
3. Migrate at least one real call site (translation) to prove the pattern works end-to-end, rather than shipping an unused abstraction.
4. **Cost-tier capability variants, confirmed genuinely missing by direct code audit** (2026-09-27 — `translate_engines.py` has no economy/quality-mode toggle anywhere, checked across every tab). Add `translation.cheap`/`translation.high_quality` as distinct, independently-configured capabilities (not just one `translation` capability with a single backend) so a future economy-mode toggle in Settings is a real, wireable switch, not new infrastructure.
5. **Confidence-based escalation, confirmed genuinely missing by the same audit** (no code anywhere ties AI-response confidence to model choice — the app always calls whichever single engine is configured). Scope narrowly for v1: a capability can optionally declare a cheap-first/escalate-on-low-confidence chain (e.g. local model → cloud model), reusing whatever confidence/uncertainty signal the calling engine already returns rather than inventing a new scoring system. Don't build a general confidence-scoring framework speculatively — wire this for one real call site (Step 37's metadata research is the natural first candidate, since its own escalation ladder already needs this) and stop there for v1. **Explicit build-order dependency, made crisper on a redundancy/reordering review (2026-09-27)**: since this item's own real call site is Step 37's escalation ladder, build this item *after* Step 37 lands (or as part of the same work), not before — despite Step 36 being numbered first. Items 1–4 of this step have no such dependency and can build in numeric order as normal; only item 5 needs the reorder.
6. **Per-provider status/test-connection, confirmed genuinely missing by a direct read of `tabs/settings_tab.py` (2026-09-27), added after a user-raised question about whether existing AI mechanisms are actually user-configurable or only Python-editable.** The "API keys & endpoints" expander already lets the user enter every provider's key (real, existing UI) — that part isn't a gap. What's missing: no "Test Connection" action anywhere in the app (checked, zero hits), no per-provider enabled/disabled toggle, and no visible status (configured-and-working / configured-but-untested / not configured) next to each key field. Add a small, real UI addition to the same expander — a "Test" button per configured key that makes one cheap real call and shows pass/fail, plus a status indicator — not a new page, not a new backend system; this is a UI gap on an already-real backend capability, matching the same "backend exists, user-facing surface doesn't" pattern this step's own capability-registry work (items 1–5) is already fixing for capability→engine mapping.

**Exit:**
- A test confirms `resolve_capability()` returns the configured engine for a given capability name.
- A test confirms the migrated translation call site actually resolves through the capability registry, not a hardcoded engine name.
- A test confirms a capability configured with an escalation chain falls through to the second backend when the first reports low confidence (mocked).
- A test confirms the per-provider "Test" action (item 6) reports failure on a mocked bad key/endpoint and success on a mocked good one, without making a real network call in the test.
- Manual check (item 6): with a real, valid key entered for one provider and a deliberately wrong key for another, confirm "Test" correctly reports pass for the first and a clear failure (not a raw exception) for the second.
- Manual check: change a capability's configured backend in Settings and confirm the next translation actually uses the new engine with no code change.

### Step 37 — Gemini Search Grounding for metadata research

Prompted by the same architecture proposal, independently verified as a real, currently-missing gap: Discover tab / glossary building already do LLM-assisted metadata lookup (`title_library.py`, `metadata_lookup.py`) with plain, non-grounded calls — there's no grounded-search backend and no tracked daily free-search budget for it. Gemini 2.5 Flash/Flash-Lite's free-tier Search Grounding (500 requests/day free, shared across Flash variants) is a real, currently-unused fit for exactly what Discover already does manually (title/author/character verification, official-source lookup).

1. Add a grounded-search research backend using Gemini 2.5 Flash/Flash-Lite Search Grounding, behind a `research.grounded_search` capability (Step 36) so it's swappable later without touching call sites.
2. **Specific escalation ladder, from the source conversation's own more detailed design** (missed in this session's first extraction pass, added here on the full re-read): Flash-Lite → Flash → local/direct search fallback → an explicitly opt-in paid provider — never silently spend beyond the free tier. Don't attach billing to get this working initially; build around the free allowance and let the app ask before ever switching to anything that incurs real API cost.
3. Track a visible daily free-search budget in Settings/Diagnostics, reusing the existing `GEMINI_FREE_TIER_LIMITS` tracking pattern already built for translation calls (Step 1f) rather than inventing a new mechanism.
4. Cache every grounded research result (name/title/synopsis + sources) so a repeat lookup for the same entity never re-spends budget — same discipline as Discover's existing query-translation caching (Step 25w).
5. **Scope was backend-mechanics-only through item 4 — widen to the fuller "Metadata Research" design, flagged on a second re-check against the source material (2026-09-27, a separate re-paste of largely the same conversation).** This also directly answers a finding from the earlier "Independent repository review" (already in this roadmap's own history, §E "Important improvements"): "Source name and URL are stored for known titles, but provenance is not attached per field, and retrieval date, confidence, and verification status are absent." Store every researched field with its own provenance record — `value`, `source`, `source_url`, `retrieved_at`, `confidence`, `last_verified` — not just a single source/URL pair per title. Confirmed genuinely missing: `metadata_lookup.py`/`title_library.py` store a title-level source, not per-field evidence.
6. **Never silently overwrite existing metadata — always propose with a choice, per this app's own established soft-delete/confirm-and-review pattern (Step 43, Step 57's 🔴 tier).** A research result that conflicts with an existing value shows both side by side with sources and confidence, and offers Keep Existing / Replace / Save Both — never a silent overwrite, matching this app's own already-established rule that a researched fact is a proposal, not an automatic correction.
7. **Multi-source triangulation, not Gemini-search-only.** Query Wikidata and Wikipedia's own APIs directly (structured, often more reliable for basic facts than an LLM's synthesis of search results) alongside Gemini's grounded search, and let the researcher flag disagreement between sources explicitly rather than silently picking one.
8. **Three explicit modes**, reusing the same backend at different depth/cost: **Quick Search** (fast, a few sources, basic identity confirmation), **Deep Research** (more sources, follows into found pages, builds a fuller structured record), **Verify** (checks an existing field specifically — "is this spelling still correct" — rather than researching from scratch).
9. **Relationship discovery, scoped modestly for v1**: when researching a work, surface directly-related entities the sources themselves mention (e.g. a novel's manga/anime adaptations) as suggested additional lookups, not an automatic graph-crawl — the user chooses whether to research each suggested link.

**Exit:**
- A test confirms a grounded search result is cached, and a second identical lookup doesn't re-call the API.
- A test confirms the daily budget counter increments correctly and the UI reflects remaining free searches.
- A test confirms a research result conflicting with an existing field never silently overwrites it — the Keep/Replace/Save Both choice is always presented.
- A test confirms each stored field carries its own source/URL/retrieved-at/confidence, not just one title-level source.
- Manual check: look up a real, obscure title/character name through Discover with grounding enabled and confirm the sourced answer is more accurate than the current non-grounded call, with per-field sources shown, not just a single title-level citation.

### Step 38 — Benchmark Lab: decide and build the real scope (supersedes/extends Step 24's "benchmark A/B" item)

Prompted by the same architecture proposal. Step 24 (already sent to the implementing session as "translation memory, benchmark A/B, library status") is meaningfully smaller than a real evaluation system — no public-benchmark import, no persistent per-run database, no full-pipeline benchmarking. **Real risk flagged explicitly**: Step 24 is in flight right now without knowing this bigger scope exists — see this file's own NEXT pointer for the decision needed before either step goes further.

1. Import public CJK MT benchmark subsets as a "public" tier — WMT test sets, FLORES-200's jpn/kor/zho→eng slices, optionally JTransBench.
2. Keep the user's own corrected translations as an "application" tier, separate from the public tier.
3. Every manually-fixed translation mistake becomes a "regression" tier entry — offered, never automatic (matches this project's own confirm-before-consequential-action pattern, and the user's own explicit statement in the source conversation that they don't want everything auto-submitted to benchmark/memory).
4. **Scoped saves, not one flat "add to memory" toggle — from the source conversation's own more detailed design, missed in this session's first extraction pass.** Every correction offers an explicit scope choice: this segment only / this project / this series or channel / global — never assumed. Default is "do nothing" (the translation is simply part of the finished project); saving anywhere is always an opt-in action, matching item 3 above.
5. **A personal "Translation Profile," auto-derived from accumulated corrections over time** (also from the fuller source design) — patterns like consistently preferring certain honorifics kept, or a particular register/formality choice, surfaced as an editable style summary rather than buried implicitly across hundreds of individual corrections. Presented for the user to review, not silently applied.
6. Persistent `benchmarks/` database recording per-run results: model, prompt version, context settings, per-language score, latency, VRAM, cost — so a model/prompt change is provably better or worse, not just assumed.
7. Use COMET (or a similar reference-based/reference-free neural metric) as the scoring backend where feasible; fall back to a simpler heuristic where COMET can't run.
8. **Explicitly reject** the proposal's full multi-dimension human-rubric scoring UI (separate sliders for meaning/naturalness/tone/hallucination/etc.) as overbuilt for a personal app — one aggregate quality score per run, plus the raw per-example pass/fail, is enough.
9. **~~A real "Model Arena" side-by-side comparison view~~ — resolved (2026-09-27): reuse Step 24's already-merged "Compare engines on this case" panel (PR #136) as the real Model Arena, don't build a second one.** This item originally claimed the comparison UI was "confirmed genuinely missing," but that was checked before Step 24 shipped — Step 24's Diagnostics panel already runs one registered benchmark case through 2 selected engines and shows both outputs/scores side by side, exactly the core of what this item describes. **Don't rebuild it.** Extend that existing panel instead: widen it to read/write this step's persistent `benchmarks/` database (item 6) rather than only the older single-case run-history storage it currently uses, and widen it to the multi-content-type cases item 11 adds (ASR/OCR/diarization, not just translation) — this is real, additive work (a different data source, more case types to select from), but it's an extension of an existing screen, not a new UI gap to close from scratch.
10. **Overlap with Step 24 — resolved, not just flagged.** Confirmed directly: Step 24 built the engine-comparison panel (item 9 above) and the Favorite/On-Hold/Plan-to-Translate library tags — neither is a benchmark-*database*/public-import/regression-tier system, so items 1-8 and 11 of this step remain fully in scope, un-duplicated. Only item 9 needed reconciling, done above.
11. **Scope was translation-only through item 10 — widen to ASR/OCR/diarization test tiers, flagged on a re-check against the source material (2026-09-27).** The source architecture proposal's own "Benchmark Lab" design explicitly spans more than translation (its own tree: CJK Translation / ASR / OCR / Diarization / Subtitle QC / Metadata extraction / Full Pipeline), and this step's items 1-9 only ever built the translation branch. Reuse the same `benchmarks/` database and Model Arena UI (items 6, 9) rather than a second parallel system — an ASR benchmark case scores WER/CER against a known-good transcript the same way a translation case scores against a reference; an OCR case scores character accuracy; a diarization case scores speaker-assignment accuracy. `asr_benchmark.py` (a standalone CLI script, never wired into any tab, per item 9's own finding) is the natural starting point for the ASR branch specifically.

**Exit:**
- A test confirms a benchmark run persists a real row with model/prompt/scores in the benchmark database.
- A test confirms adding a correction to Translation Memory offers the scope choice (segment/project/series/global) and defaults to "do nothing" if the user doesn't pick one.
- A test confirms "Add as regression test," if accepted, includes that example in the next benchmark run.
- Manual check: run the benchmark against two different configured translation engines and confirm a real side-by-side Model Arena view shows a believable quality delta matching what manual reading of the outputs suggests.
- Manual check (item 11): run at least one non-translation benchmark case (ASR or OCR) through the same benchmark database/Arena view and confirm it scores against its own appropriate metric (WER/CER, not a translation-quality score reused incorrectly).

Prompted by the same architecture proposal. Step 27 already checks *package* freshness against PyPI — a different, already-solved problem. Real gap: when a configured cloud model (a specific Claude/Gemini model string) is deprecated or retired by its provider, the app has no way to notice before a real call starts failing partway through a job.

This step's own "flag a configured model no longer listed as current" surfacing likely belongs in that same panel, next to Step 47's existing rows, not a second, separate deprecation-status display.
