- **Full section-by-section re-analysis of both ChatGPT vision docs, at the user's direct request** ("did you fully analyze... and see if they're able to be implemented and would improve"). Honest answer to that question: the first pass was a triage (covered/deferred/new), not a full per-section feasibility+value check — this pass did that properly, reading real code for every claim rather than restating the first pass's categorization. Found real things the first pass missed, both directions: **Baihe already has more than credited** — `benchmark_cases`/`benchmark_runs` plus Diagnostics' "🎯 Accuracy benchmark" section is a real, working benchmark/regression system (automatic regression/improvement detection between runs already implemented), substantially covering the vision doc's benchmark-corpus and regression-testing sections, which the first pass wrongly implied were entirely unbuilt. `glossary_terms` already has `category`/`policy`/`enforce_exact` — richer structured control than a flat term list. `translation_versions` and the existing "Translation versions" comparison expander already cover most of the versioning section. **And real, confirmed-missing pieces the first pass didn't check for specifically:** `translate_engines.py` (grepped directly) and `adaptive_style.py` (read in full) confirm there is **no real translation memory** — `adaptive_style.py` learns aggregate style preferences, not phrase-level reuse of a specific previously-approved translation; these are genuinely different mechanisms. The benchmark system compares run-over-run, not side-by-side (Engine A vs. B on one case, one view) — a real, small, missing mode on an otherwise-solid system. `dramas.status` tracks processing pipeline, not personal organization (Favorites/On Hold/Plan to Translate) — a real, separate, smaller gap. All three became Step 24. Also corrected an unverified assumption from the first pass: the browser extension was bundled into the M8+ (FastAPI/React) dismissal without actually checking whether it needs that whole migration — it may only need a small local endpoint; flagged as unresolved rather than left as a confident but unchecked claim.

- **Keiyoushi extension citations checked for language mismatch, at the user's explicit request ("make sure its not an English source, or non support source (jp/kr/cn)") (2026-09-27).** Every `src/<lang>/<extension>` path cited anywhere in this document as technique-reference material was pulled (`grep -oE "src/[a-z]+/[a-zA-Z0-9_]+"`, 13 distinct paths) and its `<lang>` prefix checked against the real site it names, since Keiyoushi's own convention (`ja`/`zh`/`ko`/`en`/`all`) directly answers this question. **Two real, confirmed flags, both already disqualified for independent ToS reasons, so no roadmap outcome changes — but each is now also confirmed wrong-language, a second and independent reason neither was ever a usable source:** `src/en/kmanga` (K MANGA, `kmanga.kodansha.com`) — the `en` prefix confirms this is Kodansha's English-language international app, not the Japanese-original source this project needs to translate *from*; `src/all/mangaup` (Manga UP!, `global.manga-up.com`) — the `all`/multi-region path plus the `global.` domain prefix indicate the international/English version, not the original Japanese マンガUP！ app. **All 11 other cited paths checked out correctly** — `src/ja/piccoma`, `src/ja/sundaywebevery`, `src/ko/manatoki`, `src/ko/toonkor`, `src/zh/baozimanhua`, `src/zh/baozimhorg`, `src/zh/dongmanmanhua`, `src/zh/guazimanhua`, `src/zh/manhuagui`, `src/zh/miaoqu`, `src/zh/tencentcomics` — every prefix matches the real content language of the site it's cited for.

- **Real extraction-technique research for Diritto, Munpia, Bomtoon, and Manta (2026-09-27) — all four confirmed to need a headless-browser build, none has a working reference scraper.** Real, direct fetches this pass, not guessed. **Diritto (diritto.co.kr)**: no scraper tool exists anywhere (`diritto-corp`'s only GitHub repo is an archived ESLint config, unrelated). Confirmed live episode URLs (`/contents/{novelId}/episodes/{n}`) are a Next.js **App Router** page using React Server Components streaming — a full regex scan of the raw HTML, including inside the RSC flight-payload script tags, found **zero Korean text**; chapter content isn't in the server response at all, almost certainly gated behind auth. **Munpia (munpia.com)**: the previously-found `software-engineer-mj/novel-crawler` is genuinely Munpia-specific (targets `novel.munpia.com/page/hd.novel/group/nv.regular`) but that URL is now dead (302s to the plain homepage) — its Selenium-based selectors are stale. Current chapter pages (`m.munpia.com/novel/viewer/{novelId}/{episodeId}`) are a near-empty Vite-bundled React SPA shell over a Spring Boot/Thymeleaf backend — zero server-rendered body text. **Bomtoon (bomtoon.com)**: confirmed via direct fetch — Next.js Pages Router with `__NEXT_DATA__` present but `pageProps` empty even on `getServerSideProps` pages; a full scan of the free-chapter listing found **zero `<a href>` links** anywhere in the raw markup. 100% client-JS-generated navigation, no server-side content at all. **Manta (manta.net)** (already dropped from the batch for a separate content-fit reason): homepage confirmed Next.js Pages Router with `pageProps` containing only SEO/JSON-LD metadata, no comic/chapter data — no working content URL could be located this pass to test further. **Bottom line, applies to all three still-candidate sites**: any real adapter for Diritto, Munpia, or Bomtoon needs a genuine headless-browser build (Playwright, intercepting the client-side content-fetch call), not a plain-HTTP adapter like Mag-Comi/raw1001.net/Kakuyomu — recorded here so the eventual Step 23x entries for these three don't understate the build effort.

- **Fanqie, baozimh.com, and Bilibili Manga pushed again with genuinely new angles, at the user's request — all three stay unresolved, but with materially stronger evidence this pass (2026-09-27).** **Fanqie (fanqienovel.com)**: `/statement` returns a real `404` (confirmed the path itself doesn't exist, not just an SPA-empty response); `notice.fanqienovel.com/docs` is an empty SPA shell. A real secondary source (36kr, covering the 2024–2025 AI-supplement-agreement controversy) confirms the reader ToS document exists and is named, but that controversy is about the separate *author* agreement (AI-training/data-labeling consent), not the *reader* access terms this roadmap tracks — conflating the two would be exactly the overreach this project's discipline exists to catch. No app-store listing surfaced a direct ToS URL. **Still unresolved** — the document's existence is now corroborated, its content remains unread. **baozimh.com**: now the **third independent confirmation** of an environment-specific block — `www.baozimh.com` 403's with both a standard UA and `Accept-Encoding: identity` (ruling out that specific evasion); `cn.baozimhcn.com` (the real current domain behind the `cn.baozimh.com` redirect) resolves and redirects into the same 403; `m.baozimh.com` doesn't resolve at all (not a separate host). Combined with the earlier GreatFire "mixed" status and the working Keiyoushi extension confirmed by its own maintainers, the evidence now more strongly supports an **IP-reputation block specific to this research environment**, not a universal restriction. **Still unresolved from here**, but provisionally lower-risk if re-checked from a different vantage point. **Bilibili Manga**: directly fetched and inspected the real agreement page (`manga.bilibili.com/eden/app-agreement.html`) — confirmed via raw source read to be a genuine Vue SPA shell (`<div id="app-vm"></div>`); pulled the actual JS bundle behind it (5.9KB) and confirmed it's pure webpack chunk-loader boilerplate with no embedded clause text and no discoverable API endpoint string — the content is fetched dynamically at runtime, not recoverable by static inspection. The umbrella `bilibili.com/protocal/licence.html` agreement is separately confirmed to be the same kind of SPA shell. Targeted searches for quoted Chinese clause text surfaced only general Bilibili copyright-litigation commentary, not the manga ToS itself. **Still unresolved**, now confirmed via direct source/bundle inspection rather than repeated URL guessing — the document names and URLs are real and stable, just their content isn't recoverable this way.

- **copymanga, Comico, and yomonga.com re-checked with genuinely new angles, at the user's request — one resolves to candidate, two stay unresolved with stronger evidence (2026-09-27).** **copymanga (mangacopy.com) — resolved to candidate.** A real chapter URL with a proper UUID-style chapter id (found via search, since guessed slugs 404 on the app's own real 404 page) returned a clean HTTP `200` — no CAPTCHA, no auth wall, no 403/429, served over Cloudflare with a standard CSP. This confirms the earlier-found `robots.txt` `Disallow: /chapter/` is **not backed by any actual technical enforcement** — a crawler-etiquette request only, the same distinction already drawn for Kakuyomu's own disallow. No ToS still exists anywhere to check, but with the technical wall now ruled out, this is an open unauthenticated API with no stated terms rather than a blocked site. **Net: candidate**, on the same "no ToS to violate, no technical block" basis as raw1001.net. **Comico (comico.jp) — stays unresolved, with one real new fact.** The real Google Play listing links a genuine, distinct Comico-specific URL (`comico.jp/legal/privacy_policy`) that loads as real, non-shell content (198 lines, its own `<title>`) — confirming `/legal/` is a real path space, not pure SPA junk. But comico.jp's Nuxt app returns `200` for *any* path including nonsense ones, so `/legal/terms`/`/legal/kiyaku`/etc. are false positives (the same generic shell every time), not real pages. The site's actual sitemap (found via `robots.txt`, 13 real sub-sitemaps) lists manga-content URLs only, no legal/terms URL among them. **Net: still unresolved** — the privacy policy is now confirmed real and reachable, but the actual Terms of Service URL remains genuinely unlocated. **yomonga.com — stays unresolved, now confirmed as a long-term outage, not a transient one.** The `503` carries a `last-modified` header from March 2024 on the CloudFront error object itself — a stale, long-cached error page served for well over a year, not a fresh blip. Wayback Machine confirms the site was genuinely still live as recently as 2026-03-01 (six months ago) before going down; the archived page's actual content couldn't be retrieved (Wayback fetches blocked in this environment). No mirror domain found. **Net: still unresolved**, but now with real confirmation this is a real, extended outage of a site that did work, not a dead/fake domain.

- **zgzl.net (m.zgzl.net, "文海小说"/Wenhai Xiaoshuo, zh novels) vetted, from a user-supplied example chapter URL — candidate, at the same accepted risk tier as manhuagui/ToonKor/raw1001.net, with one real fact worth recording plainly.** The site's own homepage discloses it directly: **"本站所有作品都是转载小说，如有侵权请告知"** ("all works on this site are reprinted/reposted; contact us if infringing") — a self-admitted reprint/unofficial-aggregator posture, not an originals platform, the same category this project already knowingly accepted for manhuagui/ToonKor/raw1001.net/several raw-manga aggregators, not a new consideration this site introduces. No `robots.txt` exists at all (real `404` at `m.zgzl.net/robots.txt`; the root `zgzl.net` apex itself didn't resolve from this environment, only the `m.` subdomain was reachable) — no named-AI-bot block, but also no crawl guidance of any kind, because there's no file. No Terms of Service/user-agreement page exists anywhere in the footer navigation (only 首页/我的书架/阅读历史) — the reprint disclaimer above is the only policy-adjacent text found, and it addresses copyright notice-and-takedown, not automated access. Chapter pages (`/read_x9v/{id}.html`) are plain server-rendered HTML with `_2`/`_3`-suffixed pagination within a chapter and a `/info_x9v/` table-of-contents link — technically trivial, no JS rendering needed. No existing scraper/tool found for this specific site. **Net: candidate**, no ToS to violate and no technical block found, consistent with this project's own already-established acceptance of this exact risk tier for other raw/reprint aggregators — not a new or different bar being applied here.

  **Totals (re-tallied 2026-09-27, after zgzl.net added as a candidate):** 10 allowed/built, 26 further candidates (no blocking clause found, not yet built), 43 disqualified (an independently-confirmed policy finding), 5 blocked-in-current-environment (a purely technical wall, no separate policy finding — Qidian, 69shuba, Rawkuma, hachiraw.net, 17K小说网), 1 rejected for no payoff, 9 declined (named-AI-block principle, content-safety, deception, or instability findings), 16 unresolved/ambiguous/wrong-domain, 4 dropped (unconfirmable, out of scope, or a real content-fit mismatch — Manta). **Haitang (myhtebook.com) is now the single most-cleared standout candidate** — real, technically open, and its full ToS read directly with no blocking clause found, the only real candidate this session confirmed to explicitly host 百合/Yuri content. Mag-Comi (magcomi.com) is a real, confirmed second candidate, with the same Shonen Jump+-shaped personal-use carve-out and existing tooling.

- **`github.com/topics/*` discovery pass, round two (2026-09-26), at the user's request for new features/security/tabs to consider.** Checked video-dubbing, manga-translator, and audiobook topic pages, cross-referenced against the real current codebase rather than assumed still-missing. **Nothing genuinely new found — every standout feature turned out to already be built or already explicitly decided against**: Wav2Lip lip-sync (`youtube-auto-dub`, `PersoDub`) was already checked and rejected as out of scope in the round-one pass above, still holds. Synchronized read-along captions (`abogen`'s headline feature) — already built: `reader.py`'s own JS already highlights the line matching current playback position. Direct EPUB ingestion (`ebook2audiobook`'s headline feature) — already built: `epub_io.py`. Fully-local/offline operation, per-character voice assignment, LLM-driven script preprocessing — all already Baihe's existing design (Ollama/local TTS engines, Step 11b's per-character voice map, emotion detection driving delivery). **One small, genuinely new, not-yet-present idea, not added as a step**: RVC-style voice post-processing/enhancement (seen in `Pandrator`) as a quality pass after cloning — none of Baihe's TTS engines currently apply one. Minor, optional, not written up as its own step given "fewer options over more" and the already-large TTS-engine surface; worth remembering if a real quality gap shows up in practice. **Security check (same request)**: read `db.py` directly for SQL-injection risk — every f-string-interpolated part is either a hardcoded column/table name from Python literals or immediately followed by parameterized `?` placeholders for actual values; the one function taking a column name as a parameter (`distinct_values`) is only ever called with fixed literals (`"studio"`, `"author"`), never user input. Secret redaction (`translate_engines.redact_secrets`) is real and shared between stored-error display and the Diagnostics support-copy feature. File uploads use extension-only extraction plus a fixed filename prefix, not raw uploaded filenames — no path-traversal opening found. No new security gap found; the app's LAN-only/no-auth design (Step 10e) is a deliberate, already-documented tradeoff, not re-litigated here.

- **Full real hardware profile (2026-09-25), recorded here since this session has no separate memory store — the persistent record is this file.** User supplied real `nvidia-smi` and `systeminfo` output directly (not summarized secondhand). **GPU**: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080 Ti, 12,288MiB VRAM, driver reports CUDA 13.3 (the driver's max-supported CUDA version, not necessarily what any installed `torch` build targets — see below), WDDM driver model. **CPU**: 1 socket, AMD64 Family 26 Model 68 (AMD Zen 5-generation), ~4.7GHz. **RAM**: 65,141MB (~64GB) total, 47,672MB available at capture time. **OS**: Windows 10 Pro, build 19045 (22H2-class), installed 2020-07-17. **Python**: confirmed elsewhere this session as 3.14 (`pythoncore-3.14-64`), already flagged in Step 18c as ahead of the project's CI-pinned 3.11 and the README's unbounded "3.9+" claim. **Real, confirmed finding from cross-referencing this against a separately pasted error trace**: despite this real GPU, the user's actual installed `torch` build is `2.13.0+cpu` — the CPU-only wheel, not a CUDA build — meaning every GPU-touching stage (diarization, vocal separation, transcription, TTS) is currently running on CPU on a machine with a capable, idle 3080 Ti. Root-caused and added as Step 18 item 7 (an install-time gap: nothing in `requirements-install.bat`/`start.bat` ever selects PyTorch's CUDA-specific index) and cross-referenced from the new Step 4g (vocal-separation progress gap) as the reason that stage reads as unusually slow on this machine specifically. 12GB VRAM still comfortably confirms Step 5/5c's existing 8–12GB consumer-GPU design assumptions once a CUDA `torch` build is actually installed.

### 7.1 Translation engines: which language each is actually good for

From the real AQI benchmark checked in §6's "is ChatGPT good for translation" pass (Alconost, 2026) plus what's already documented about each engine elsewhere in this roadmap — not re-deriving anything, just laid out as the table the user asked for. Scores are Alconost's AQI (Accuracy Quality Index); "—" means not in that benchmark, described qualitatively instead.

| Engine | Japanese | Korean | Chinese (Simplified) | Chinese (Traditional) | Other languages |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Gemini** | 72.5 AQI — **#1** | 78.2 AQI — **#1** | 71.9 AQI — #2 | 74.4 AQI — **#1** | Broadest top-2 CJK coverage of any engine checked; general strength across most high-resource languages |
| **Claude** | 71.2 AQI — #2 (near-tie) | not top-2 in this benchmark | not top-2 in this benchmark | 74.2 AQI — #2 (near-tie) | Strongest for high-nuance/brand-sensitive prose per Lokalise's task-based framing; this project's own Step 5/11b research already treats it as the default-quality bar |
| **DeepSeek** | not top-2 in this benchmark | 70.7 AQI — #2 (small sample, n=7) | 72.2 AQI — **#1** | not top-2 in this benchmark | Chinese-trained, so its zh-CN edge is real and explainable, not noise; weaker evidenced elsewhere |
| **Ollama (`qwen3:8b`, local default)** | qualitative only | qualitative only | qualitative only | qualitative only | Qwen family is broadly CJK-capable by training design, but **not independently benchmarked against the three above at this size** — treat as "good enough local/free," not confirmed best-in-class for any one pair |
| **NLLB** | qualitative only | qualitative only | qualitative only | qualitative only | Breadth over depth — 200+ languages by design, non-commercial license; not a quality leader for any single pair, a coverage option |
| **LibreTranslate** | qualitative only | qualitative only | qualitative only | qualitative only | Already labelled "Basic quality" in Baihe's own free-tier engine picker (Step 1c) — the floor of the lineup, not a contender for CJK quality |
| **DeepL** | not evidenced for CJK | not evidenced for CJK | not evidenced for CJK | not evidenced for CJK | Reputation is strongest for European languages; no CJK-specialized claim found in this pass — not Baihe's use case anyway |
| **Google Translate** | qualitative only | qualitative only | qualitative only | qualitative only | Broadest raw language coverage (100+) of anything in the lineup, general-purpose baseline quality, not a CJK specialist |

**Free-tier accuracy specifically, at the user's follow-up request.** Tried directly to find hard CJK-specific numbers for the free-tier engines beyond what's in the table above (NLLB's own paper, Qwen's technical report, LibreTranslate's own community forum) — mostly couldn't, and saying so honestly rather than inventing precision:
- **Gemini (free-tier key) — the free option with real evidence, because it's literally the same model.** The free tier is a rate limit, not a lesser model — its accuracy is the same Gemini row above (#1 in JA/KO/ZH-TW, #2 in ZH-CN in the real AQI benchmark). The catch is entirely usage-shaped (~10 req/min on Flash), not quality-shaped.
- **Ollama (`qwen3:8b`) — a real, but not CJK-specific, improvement claim.** Step 5's own adoption cited real FLORES+ COMET/CEA100 numbers showing Qwen3-8B beats Qwen2.5-7B (e.g. en→ar COMET 19.74 vs. 17.39) — genuine evidence the swap was worth it, but that comparison isn't a CJK pair. Searched specifically for a Qwen3-8B zh/ja/ko FLORES number this pass and didn't find one in the accessible portions of Qwen's own technical report or the broader open-LLM-MT literature — the Alibaba Qwen-MT product page claims CJK strength, but that's their separate, API-only translation-tuned model (§6), not the chat model Baihe actually runs locally. Treat local accuracy as "confirmed better than the previous default, not confirmed how it stacks up against Gemini/Claude/DeepSeek for CJK specifically."
- **NLLB — a real aggregate claim, not a CJK-specific one.** Meta's own paper states NLLB-200 improved BLEU by an average of 44% over the prior state of the art across all 200+ languages on FLORES-200 — a genuine, large, real improvement, but averaged across mostly low-resource languages (the paper's own emphasis is African/Indian languages seeing the biggest gains); no Chinese/Japanese/Korean-specific number was found in the portions of the paper this pass could read. High-resource languages like CJK were already reasonably well-served before NLLB, so the aggregate number likely overstates NLLB's edge for CJK specifically.
- **LibreTranslate — the one where "no benchmark exists" is itself the honest finding.** Checked directly: its own underlying Argos Translate maintainer states on their community forum "I haven't done very much with BLEU scores... instead I've tried to use as much high quality data as possible and then manually tested" — there is no published accuracy number to cite, for any language pair. Independent reviews checked (`machinetranslation.com`, `langbly.com`) describe it as "usable" for major pairs including Chinese/Japanese but consistently rank it below Google Translate, and explicitly not recommended for fiction — directly relevant to Baihe's actual content (novels/manga), where LibreTranslate is the weakest option in the free lineup, already reflected by Baihe's own "Basic quality" label on it.

**Ranked by confidence of evidence, not just claimed quality**: Gemini free-tier (real, same-as-paid numbers) → Ollama `qwen3:8b` (real but non-CJK-specific improvement evidence) → NLLB (real but non-CJK-specific aggregate claim) → LibreTranslate (no published benchmark found anywhere, weakest by every qualitative review checked, already labelled "Basic" in-app).

**What this means for Baihe's actual defaults:** the three cloud engines already offered (Claude/Gemini/DeepSeek) are exactly the three that place top-2 somewhere in this benchmark — nothing to add. No source found makes a verified case to change the local default away from `qwen3:8b`.

### 7.2 Translation engines: price, cheapest to most expensive (checked September 2026, not re-derived from memory)

Token-based (LLM) and character-based (dedicated MT API) pricing aren't perfectly comparable — a translation prompt's tokens include more than just the source text, and a token isn't a fixed number of characters across languages — so treat the ordering as directional, not exact. Per 1M tokens (input/output) unless noted; DeepSeek's off-peak/peak split is real (its own pricing page, not a promotion) and can roughly halve or double the numbers shown depending on time of day (UTC).

| Rank | Engine (tier) | Price | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Ollama (local) | **$0** | Own hardware/electricity only — already Baihe's local default |
| 1 | NLLB (self-hosted) | **$0** | Non-commercial license |
| 1 | LibreTranslate (self-hosted) | **$0** | Hosted `libretranslate.com` API has a separate paid tier; self-hosting stays free |
| 1 | Test mode | **$0** | Fake output, not real translation |
| 1 | Gemini (free-tier key) | **$0** | Rate-limited (~10 req/min on Flash); Google may use the text to improve its products |

| 7 | DeepSeek V4.1 Flash | $0.15 / $0.60 (off-peak) → $0.30 / $1.20 (peak) | Previously the cheapest paid option; still the cheapest **verified-for-CJK** one (§7.1) |
| 8 | Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite Preview | $0.25 / $1.50 | Real, released March 2026 — a smaller/cheaper preview tier, not the flagship Flash line; no CJK-specific quality evidence found. **Added as a selectable, non-default model (Step 9 item 4), at the user's request — a cheaper option, not a quality claim.** |

Not currently a false claim anywhere in this roadmap (DeepL was never labelled "🧪 Free" in Step 1c's own engine-picker table — only Test mode/Ollama/Gemini-free/NLLB/LibreTranslate are), but worth knowing DeepL got meaningfully pricier to reach at all. |

Batch processing (Claude, Gemini) and prompt caching (both, plus DeepSeek's own cache-hit rate) cut these further — not reflected in the ranking above since Baihe's actual usage pattern (batched line translation, Step 9's caching work) would benefit from both, making real costs lower than this sticker-price ordering implies.

**GPT-6 Luna and Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite, checked at the user's request ("Torii reports these are good and cheap") — both confirmed real and cheap, neither with confirmed translation-quality evidence for Baihe's actual content.**
- **GPT-6 Luna** — OpenAI's own product page (`developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-6-luna`, read directly) describes it as "our most efficient model for focused, high-volume tasks," explicitly positioned alongside classification/lightweight-agentic/summarization use, not nuanced or creative text — and its dedicated translation endpoints (`v1/audio/translations`, realtime translation) are marked **"Not supported"** on that same page (this doesn't block using it for text translation the way Baihe calls every engine — via ordinary chat completion, not a dedicated translate endpoint — but it's a signal OpenAI itself didn't scope Luna around translation specifically). No CJK or general translation benchmark found for it in this pass. **Also not currently buildable as a drop-in**: `translate_engines.py` has no OpenAI-model engine at all today — the `openai` package is already a dependency, but only used to talk to DeepSeek's OpenAI-*compatible* endpoint, not OpenAI's own. Adding Luna would mean a new, real engine class (pointed at OpenAI's actual endpoint, with its own API key setting), not a config change.
- **Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite Preview** — real, released March 3, 2026, genuinely cheap, but it's a "Lite"/"Preview"-tagged smaller tier sitting below the flagship Flash line already checked in §7.1's AQI benchmark (that benchmark's "Gemini" rows are the flagship models, not this lighter preview variant) — no evidence found that this specific smaller model matches the flagship's CJK results.
- **What Torii's own claim is actually worth here**: Torii's marketing material recommends "Gemini 3 Flash" generally as "the best model for the job, and cheap" — a real quote, but it's Torii's own product recommendation for *image/manga OCR+translate* specifically, not an independent benchmark, and doesn't name Luna or the 3.1 Flash-Lite variant by name as translation-quality winners the way the user's message implied. Treating it as a lead worth checking (which this pass did), not as verified fact on its own — same discipline applied to every other secondary-source claim in this doc.

**Decision, given at the user's follow-up:** don't default to Flash-Lite, but do add it as a selectable, clearly-labelled-as-cheaper (not clearly-labelled-as-better) option — done, see Step 9 item 4. **GPT-6 Luna stays not-added** — the user didn't ask for it to be added the way they did for Flash-Lite, and it would need a real new engine class (no OpenAI-model support exists in `translate_engines.py` today) rather than a model-string change, so the bar for adding it without quality evidence is higher. Recommendation if Luna is wanted later: run one real head-to-head — translate the same CJK sample through Luna and through the existing defaults — same manual-check pattern already used for the PaddleOCR-VL-For-Manga vs. `manga-ocr` decision in Step 11.
